Often you need to convert strings (from JSON, user input, or config files) into your enum type. A common pattern is to create a map for lookup and a parse function that returns an error for invalid values.
Multiple Iota Expressions
You can use iota multiple times in the same line for complex patterns. Each occurrence of iota in a line has the same value, but you can use different expressions with it.

content.title: Keep Related Constants Together
content.message: Iota resets to 0 in each new const block. Always define all related enum values in the same const block to ensure they form a proper sequence.

content.text: Compile-Time Expressions
Constants must be computable at compile time. This means you can use arithmetic, bitwise operations, and some built-in functions, but not runtime values or most function calls.

Constants and iota provide Go's answer to enums. Use iota for sequential values, bit shifting for flags, and custom types with String() methods for type safety and readability. Remember that iota resets in each const block, and consider skipping zero to avoid the uninitialized variable gotcha.

sections.title: Concurrency Patterns: Worker Pools, Pipelines, and More

content.text: Go's goroutines and channels are powerful primitives, but complex problems require patterns. How do you limit concurrent operations? How do you chain processing stages? How do you handle errors from multiple goroutines? These patterns are battle-tested solutions.

This section covers six essential patterns: Worker Pool (bounded parallelism), Fan-Out/Fan-In (parallel processing with merged results), Pipeline (multi-stage transformations), Rate Limiting (controlling throughput), Semaphore (dynamic concurrency limits), and errgroup (error handling with cancellation).
Worker Pool: Bounded Parallelism

A worker pool maintains a fixed number of goroutines that pull jobs from a shared channel. This bounds resource usage: instead of spawning thousands of goroutines (one per task), you run a controlled number of workers.
The pattern: create a jobs channel and results channel, start N workers that range over jobs and send to results, send all jobs then close the jobs channel, close results after all workers finish.
Fan-Out / Fan-In: Parallel Processing

Fan-out means multiple goroutines read from the same channel, competing for work. Fan-in means multiple goroutines write to the same channel, merging their outputs. Together, they enable parallel processing of a stream.
This pattern is ideal when you have a stream of items to process independently and want to parallelize the work while merging results into a single output stream.

content.title: Order Not Preserved
content.message: Results arrive in completion order, not input order. If you need ordered results, include the original index with each item and sort at the end.

content.text: Pipeline: Chained Processing Stages

A pipeline connects stages where each stage's output channel is the next stage's input. Each stage runs concurrently: while stage 2 processes item A, stage 1 can be processing item B. This creates efficient streaming transformations.
Each stage is a function that takes an input channel, returns an output channel, and spawns a goroutine to do the transformation. The goroutine closes the output channel when done.
Rate Limiting: Controlling Throughput

Rate limiting prevents overwhelming external services or resources. The simplest approach uses time.Tick to create a channel that delivers values at a fixed rate. Each operation waits for a tick before proceeding.
For production code, use golang.org/x/time/rate which implements a token bucket algorithm with burst support. This allows occasional spikes while maintaining an average rate.

content.title: Production Rate Limiting
content.message: Use golang.org/x/time/rate for production. It provides rate.Limiter with Wait(), Allow(), and Reserve() methods, plus configurable burst size.

content.text: Semaphore: Dynamic Concurrency Limits

A semaphore limits concurrent operations without dedicated worker goroutines. Unlike a worker pool where you have N workers processing a queue, a semaphore allows up to N goroutines to run simultaneously while spawning goroutines dynamically.
The pattern uses a buffered channel as a counting semaphore: send to acquire (blocks when full), receive to release. This is simpler than a worker pool when each task is independent.
errgroup: Error Handling with Cancellation

The errgroup package (golang.org/x/sync/errgroup) solves a common problem: running multiple goroutines, waiting for all to complete, and handling the first error. It also provides automatic cancellation when any goroutine fails.
errgroup.WithContext returns a group and a context. When any goroutine returns an error, the context is cancelled, signaling other goroutines to stop. Wait() returns the first error encountered.
Or-Done Channel: Early Exit

The or-done pattern lets you receive from a channel while also respecting a done signal. Without this, you'd need to wrap every channel read in a select statement. The helper function handles this cleanly.
Tee Channel: Duplicate a Stream
The tee pattern splits one channel into two, sending each value to both outputs. This is useful when multiple consumers need the same stream, like logging while processing.
Choosing the Right Pattern

items.label: Worker Pool
items.description: Fixed batch of work with bounded concurrency. Best when you know the workload upfront.

items.label: Fan-Out/Fan-In
items.description: Streaming data needing parallel processing with merged results. Order not preserved.

items.label: Pipeline
items.description: Multi-stage transformations where stages can run concurrently.

items.label: Rate Limiter
items.description: External API limits or resource protection. Use time.Tick or x/time/rate.

items.label: Semaphore
items.description: Dynamic goroutines with a cap. Simpler than worker pool for independent tasks.

items.label: errgroup
items.description: Multiple goroutines with error handling and automatic cancellation on failure.

items.label: Or-Done
items.description: Reading from channels while respecting cancellation.

items.label: Tee
items.description: Duplicating a stream for multiple consumers.

content.text: These patterns compose beautifully. A real system might use errgroup to manage a worker pool with rate limiting, feeding a pipeline. Start simple, add patterns when you hit specific problems. Understanding these patterns is essential for writing production-grade concurrent Go code.

sections.title: File I/O: Reading, Writing, and Managing Files

content.text: File I/O is fundamental to almost every Go application. You'll read configuration files, write logs, process data files, and manage user uploads. Go's standard library provides simple functions for common tasks and powerful primitives for complex scenarios.

This section covers the os package for file operations, bufio for efficient reading/writing, the io interfaces that make Go's I/O so flexible, and the filepath package for cross-platform path handling.
Quick Read and Write with os.ReadFile and os.WriteFile

For simple tasks, os.ReadFile reads an entire file into memory and os.WriteFile writes data to a file. These functions handle opening, reading/writing, and closing automatically. They're perfect for small files like configuration or templates.
The permission argument (like 0644) uses Unix octal notation: owner read+write (6), group read (4), others read (4). We'll cover permissions in detail later.

content.title: When to Use Quick I/O
content.message: Use os.ReadFile/WriteFile for small files (configs, templates, JSON). For large files, streaming with os.Open avoids loading everything into memory.

content.text: File Handles with os.Open and os.Create

When you need more control, open files with os.Open (read-only) or os.Create (write, truncates existing). These return a *os.File handle that you must close when done. Always use defer file.Close() immediately after opening.
The Read method reads into a byte slice and returns the number of bytes read. When the file ends, it returns io.EOF. The Write and WriteString methods write data to the file.

content.title: Always Close Files
content.message: Use 'defer file.Close()' immediately after opening. Forgetting to close causes resource leaks and can lose data (unflushed writes). For writers, check the error from Close().

content.text: Flexible Opening with os.OpenFile
os.OpenFile gives you full control with flags: O_RDONLY (read), O_WRONLY (write), O_RDWR (both), O_CREATE (create if missing), O_APPEND (add to end), O_TRUNC (clear existing). Combine flags with |.
This is essential for appending to log files: you want to create the file if it doesn't exist, open for writing, and append rather than overwrite.
Understanding File Permissions
File permissions use Unix octal notation. Each digit (0-7) represents permissions for owner, group, and others. Each digit is a sum: 4 (read) + 2 (write) + 1 (execute). The leading 0 indicates octal.

items.description: Owner read+write only. Use for private files like SSH keys, secrets.
Owner read+write, others read. Standard for data files, configs.
Owner all, others read+execute. Use for directories and scripts.
Owner all, others nothing. Private directories.

content.text: Line-by-Line Reading with bufio.Scanner

bufio.Scanner is the easiest way to read a file line by line. It handles buffering automatically and provides a clean iteration pattern. The Scan() method advances to the next line and returns false at EOF or on error.
By default, Scanner splits on newlines. You can customize this with scanner.Split() for word-by-word or custom delimiters.
Buffered Writing with bufio.Writer

Writing many small pieces is inefficient because each Write() is a system call. bufio.Writer buffers writes in memory and flushes to the file in larger chunks. This can dramatically improve performance.
Critical: always call Flush() before closing to ensure buffered data is written. Data in the buffer is lost if you close without flushing.

content.title: Always Flush Buffered Writers
content.message: Call writer.Flush() before closing the file. Buffered data is lost if you don't flush. Consider using defer with a wrapper that flushes then closes.

content.text: The io.Reader and io.Writer Interfaces

Go's io package defines minimal interfaces that many types implement. io.Reader has one method: Read(p []byte) (n int, err error). io.Writer has Write(p []byte) (n int, err error). This simple design enables powerful composition.
Files, network connections, HTTP bodies, buffers, compressors, and encryptors all implement these interfaces. Code written against io.Reader/Writer works with all of them.
Useful io Functions

The io package provides utility functions that work with any Reader/Writer. io.Copy copies all data, io.CopyN copies exactly N bytes, io.ReadAll reads everything into memory, and io.LimitReader limits how much can be read.
Directory Operations

The os package provides functions for creating, listing, and removing directories. os.Mkdir creates one directory, os.MkdirAll creates nested directories (like mkdir -p), and os.ReadDir lists directory contents.
Cross-Platform Paths with filepath

Never concatenate paths with + and /. Use filepath.Join which handles OS-specific separators (/ on Unix, \ on Windows). The filepath package also provides functions to extract directory, filename, extension, and convert to absolute paths.
Checking Files and Getting Info
os.Stat returns file information: size, permissions, modification time, and whether it's a directory. Use errors.Is(err, os.ErrNotExist) to check if a file doesn't exist.
Temporary Files and Directories
os.CreateTemp creates a temporary file with a unique name. os.MkdirTemp creates a temporary directory. Both use the system's temp directory by default. Always clean up temp files when done.
Common File Operations

Go's file I/O is built on simple, composable primitives. Use os.ReadFile/WriteFile for simple cases, os.Open/Create for control, bufio for efficiency, and the io interfaces for flexibility. Always close files with defer, always flush buffered writers, and use filepath for cross-platform paths.

sections.title: JSON: Encoding, Decoding, and Struct Tags

content.text: JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) is the universal data format for web APIs, configuration files, and data exchange. Go's encoding/json package makes it easy to convert between Go values and JSON, with struct tags giving you precise control over the output.
This section covers marshaling (Go to JSON), unmarshaling (JSON to Go), struct tags for customization, handling dynamic JSON, custom encoding, and streaming for large data.
Basic Encoding with json.Marshal

json.Marshal converts any Go value to JSON bytes. It uses reflection to examine struct fields, converting field names to JSON keys. Only exported fields (starting with uppercase) are included in the output.
json.MarshalIndent produces formatted output with indentation, useful for debugging. In production, use json.Marshal for compact output that saves bandwidth.
Struct Tags: Controlling JSON Output

Struct tags customize how fields are encoded. The json tag specifies the JSON key name. Add omitempty to skip zero values, or use - to exclude a field entirely. Tags are the key to creating clean, idiomatic JSON APIs.

items.label: `json:"name"`
items.description: Use 'name' as the JSON key instead of the Go field name.

items.label: `json:"name,omitempty"`
items.description: Omit field entirely if it has a zero value (empty string, 0, false, nil).

items.label: `json:"-"`
items.description: Never include this field in JSON output. Use for internal/sensitive data.

items.label: `json:",string"`
items.description: Encode number as JSON string. Useful for large integers (JavaScript safety).

content.text: Decoding JSON with json.Unmarshal

json.Unmarshal parses JSON bytes into a Go value. You must pass a pointer so Unmarshal can modify the target. Unknown JSON fields are silently ignored, making your code forward-compatible with API changes.
Always check the error from Unmarshal. Common errors include malformed JSON, type mismatches (e.g., string where number expected), and invalid UTF-8.
Nested Structures and Arrays
Real-world JSON contains nested objects and arrays. Go handles this naturally: nested objects become nested structs, arrays become slices. The mapping is intuitive and works bidirectionally.
Dynamic JSON with map[string]any

When you don't know the JSON structure in advance, use map[string]any (or map[string]interface{} in older Go). This captures any JSON object. Numbers become float64, arrays become []any, and nested objects become nested maps.
Use type assertions to extract values. This approach is flexible but loses type safety, so use it only when the structure is truly unknown.
json.RawMessage for Deferred Parsing
json.RawMessage stores raw JSON without parsing it. This is useful when you need to delay parsing until you know the type, or when you want to pass through JSON unchanged.
Custom Marshaling and Unmarshaling
Implement json.Marshaler and json.Unmarshaler interfaces to control exactly how your types are encoded/decoded. This is essential for custom date formats, enums, or special representations.
Streaming with Encoder and Decoder
For large files or HTTP streams, use json.Encoder and json.Decoder instead of Marshal/Unmarshal. They work with io.Reader/Writer and process JSON incrementally without loading everything into memory.
This is especially useful for newline-delimited JSON (NDJSON), where each line is a separate JSON object. The decoder's More() method tells you if more objects are available.
Handling null Values
JSON null maps to Go's nil. For nullable fields, use pointers. A nil pointer encodes as null, and null decodes to nil. This distinguishes between "field not present" and "field explicitly null."

items.label: json.Marshal/Unmarshal
items.description: Works with []byte. Simple for small payloads. Loads entire JSON into memory.

items.label: json.Encoder/Decoder
items.description: Works with streams. Memory-efficient for large data. Supports NDJSON.

items.label: json.RawMessage
items.description: Defers parsing. Useful for type-switching or pass-through scenarios.

items.label: map[string]any
items.description: Dynamic parsing. Flexible but loses type safety. Use for truly unknown structures.

content.text: Go's JSON package is simple yet powerful. Use struct tags for clean API contracts, pointers for nullable fields, custom Marshaler/Unmarshaler for special types, and streaming for large data. Master these tools and you'll handle any JSON scenario confidently.

sections.title: HTTP Client: Making Requests and Handling Responses

content.text: Every modern application needs to communicate with web services: REST APIs, microservices, third-party integrations. Go's net/http package provides a powerful, production-ready HTTP client. Unlike many languages, Go's standard library is all you need for most HTTP tasks.
This section covers making requests, handling responses, setting headers, using timeouts and context for cancellation, configuring connection pooling, and building a reusable API client.
Simple GET Request

http.Get is the simplest way to fetch a URL. It returns a response and an error. Critical: always close the response body with defer resp.Body.Close() after checking the error. Failing to close causes connection leaks.
Warning: http.Get uses the default client which has no timeout. Requests can hang forever. We'll fix this shortly, but let's start simple.

content.title: Always Close Response Body
content.message: Close the body even if you don't read it. Unclosed bodies leak connections. Pattern: check error first, then defer close. Never defer close before checking error (resp might be nil).

content.text: POST Requests with JSON
For POST requests, use http.Post with a content type and body. For JSON APIs, marshal your data, wrap it in bytes.NewBuffer, and set content type to application/json.
Custom Client with Timeout

The default http.Client has no timeout, meaning requests can hang forever. For production, always create a custom client with an explicit timeout. The Timeout field covers the entire request: connection, TLS handshake, sending request, and reading response.
Create one client and reuse it. Each client maintains a connection pool, so reusing avoids the overhead of establishing new connections.

content.title: Reuse Your Client
content.message: Create one http.Client at startup and reuse it for all requests. Creating a new client per request wastes resources and defeats connection pooling.

content.text: Custom Headers with http.NewRequest

http.Get and http.Post are convenient but limited. For custom headers, different HTTP methods, or request bodies, use http.NewRequest (or better, http.NewRequestWithContext) to build a request, then execute it with client.Do().
Context for Cancellation and Deadlines

Context gives you fine-grained control over request lifecycle. WithTimeout sets a deadline, WithCancel lets you cancel manually. When context is cancelled, the request stops immediately, freeing resources.
This is essential for graceful shutdown: when your server is stopping, you can cancel all in-flight requests by cancelling their context.
Handling Different HTTP Methods
http.NewRequestWithContext works for any HTTP method: GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE, etc. Use the http.Method constants for clarity.
Configuring Transport for Connection Pooling

http.Transport controls low-level connection behavior: pooling, timeouts for connection phases, TLS settings, and proxy configuration. For high-throughput applications, tuning these settings is essential.

items.label: MaxIdleConnsPerHost
items.description: Default is 2, too low for high concurrency. Increase for APIs you call frequently.

items.label: IdleConnTimeout
items.description: How long to keep unused connections. 90s is reasonable for most cases.

items.label: TLSHandshakeTimeout
items.description: Max time for TLS handshake. 10s prevents hanging on slow/broken TLS.

items.label: ResponseHeaderTimeout
items.description: Max time waiting for response headers after sending request.

content.text: Building a Reusable API Client
For production code, wrap http.Client in a domain-specific API client. This encapsulates base URL, authentication, headers, and provides typed methods for each endpoint.
Error Handling and Retries
Network requests fail. Implement retries with exponential backoff for transient errors. Check for specific error types to decide whether to retry.

Go's HTTP client is powerful yet simple. Key practices: always set timeouts, always close response bodies, use context for cancellation, reuse clients for connection pooling, and implement retries for resilience. With these patterns, you can build reliable clients for any API.

sections.title: database/sql: Connecting to Databases and Running Queries

content.text: Go's database/sql package provides a unified interface for working with SQL databases. Whether you use PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite, or another database, the API is the same. You only need to import a driver for your specific database.

This section covers connecting, querying, executing statements, transactions, handling NULL values, using context for cancellation, and the repository pattern. Since we can't connect to a real database in these examples, we'll use SQLite with an in-memory database for demonstrations.
Opening a Database Connection

sql.Open creates a database handle but doesn't actually connect. It validates the driver name and connection string format. Connections are established lazily when needed. Always call db.Ping() to verify the database is reachable.
The *sql.DB type is safe for concurrent use. Create one at application startup and reuse it. Don't open a new connection for each query.

content.title: Always Ping After Open
content.message: sql.Open only validates arguments, it doesn't connect. Call db.Ping() immediately to verify the database is reachable and credentials are correct.

content.text: Connection Pool Configuration

*sql.DB manages a pool of connections automatically. Configure limits based on your database server capacity and application needs. Too few connections causes contention; too many overwhelms the database.

items.label: MaxOpenConns
items.description: Total connections (active + idle). Set based on database server limits divided by app instances.

items.label: MaxIdleConns
items.description: Connections kept ready for reuse. Higher = faster queries, more memory.

items.label: ConnMaxLifetime
items.description: Recycle connections periodically. Helps with load balancers and database failover.

content.text: Creating Tables and Basic Operations
Use db.Exec for statements that don't return rows: CREATE, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE. It returns a sql.Result with RowsAffected() and LastInsertId() methods.
Querying Multiple Rows

db.Query returns *sql.Rows for iterating over results. Critical: always close rows with defer rows.Close(). Failing to close leaks connections. Use rows.Next() to iterate and rows.Scan() to read values into variables.

content.title: Always Close Rows
content.message: Use 'defer rows.Close()' immediately after db.Query(). Unclosed rows leak connections back to the pool, eventually exhausting all connections and hanging your application.

content.text: Querying a Single Row
db.QueryRow is for queries that return exactly one row. It returns *sql.Row which has only a Scan method. If no rows match, Scan returns sql.ErrNoRows.
Preventing SQL Injection
Never concatenate user input into SQL strings. Always use parameterized queries with placeholders. The database driver escapes values properly, preventing SQL injection attacks.

items.label: SQLite: ?
items.description: Use ? for placeholders: SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ?

items.label: PostgreSQL: $1, $2
items.description: Use numbered placeholders: SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = $1

items.label: MySQL: ?
items.description: Use ? for placeholders: SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ?

content.text: Transactions

Transactions group multiple operations atomically: either all succeed (commit) or all fail (rollback). Use db.Begin() to start, tx.Commit() to save, and tx.Rollback() to abort. Always defer tx.Rollback() - it's safe to call after Commit().
Handling NULL Values
Database NULL requires special handling. Go provides sql.NullString, sql.NullInt64, etc. - structs with a Valid boolean. Alternatively, use pointers: nil represents NULL.
Using Context for Timeouts

Production code should use context-aware methods: QueryContext, ExecContext, QueryRowContext. This allows timeouts and cancellation, especially important for long-running queries or when handling HTTP requests.
Prepared Statements
Prepared statements parse SQL once and execute many times with different parameters. This improves performance for repeated queries and provides additional SQL injection protection.
Repository Pattern

The repository pattern encapsulates database access behind a clean interface. Each repository handles one entity type with methods like FindByID, Create, Update, Delete. Context is always the first parameter.

Go's database/sql provides everything for reliable database access. Key practices: always Ping() after Open(), always close Rows, use parameterized queries to prevent SQL injection, use transactions for atomic operations, handle NULL with sql.Null* types or pointers, and pass context for timeouts and cancellation.

Go has testing built into the language. The testing package provides everything you need without external dependencies. Tests live alongside code in files ending with _test.go and run with the go test command.
This section covers writing test functions, table-driven tests, subtests, test helpers, setup/teardown, and running tests with various flags. We'll write actual runnable test examples.
Your First Test
Test functions must start with Test followed by a capitalized name, and accept *testing.T. Use t.Error or t.Errorf to report failures without stopping, or t.Fatal/t.Fatalf to stop immediately.
The testing.T provides logging, failure reporting, and test control. When a test fails, Go shows the file, line number, and your error message.
t.Error vs t.Fatal

t.Error reports a failure but continues running the test. t.Fatal reports a failure and stops immediately. Use Fatal when continuing would cause panics or meaningless results (like a nil pointer after a failed setup).

items.label: t.Error / t.Errorf
items.description: Reports failure, continues test. Use when more checks provide useful info.

items.label: t.Fatal / t.Fatalf
items.description: Reports failure, stops test. Use when continuing would panic or be meaningless.

items.label: t.Skip / t.Skipf
items.description: Skips test with message. Use for conditional tests (e.g., needs network).

items.label: t.Log / t.Logf
items.description: Logs message, only shown with -v flag. Use for debugging info.

content.text: Table-Driven Tests

Table-driven tests define test cases in a slice of structs. This Go idiom reduces duplication, makes it easy to add cases, and clearly shows what's being tested. Each struct has inputs and expected outputs.
Subtests with t.Run
t.Run creates named subtests that appear individually in output and can be run separately with -run flag. Combined with table-driven tests, subtests make failures crystal clear.

content.title: Run Specific Subtests
content.message: Run a specific subtest with: go test -run TestDivide/positive_numbers (spaces become underscores)

content.text: Test Helpers
Test helpers are functions that perform common setup or assertions. Always call t.Helper() first - this makes failure messages point to the test that called the helper, not the helper itself.

content.title: Always Call t.Helper()
content.message: Without t.Helper(), failures show the line inside the helper, not where the test called it. This makes debugging much harder.

content.text: Setup and Teardown
Go 1.14+ provides t.Cleanup() for registering teardown functions that run after the test completes. For shared setup across tests in a file, use TestMain.
Parallel Tests
Call t.Parallel() to run tests concurrently. This can significantly speed up test suites. Be careful: parallel tests must not share mutable state.

content.title: Capture Loop Variables
content.message: In parallel tests, always capture the loop variable: tt := tt. Without this, all goroutines share the same variable and tests fail randomly.

content.text: Testing Error Conditions
Testing error cases is just as important as testing success. Check that functions return errors when they should, and optionally verify the error message or type.
Running Tests
The go test command compiles and runs tests. It supports many flags for filtering, verbosity, coverage, and more.

content.code:
# Run all tests in current package
go test

# Verbose output (shows all test names)
go test -v

# Run tests matching pattern
go test -run TestDivide

# Run specific subtest
go test -run TestDivide/positive_numbers

# Run all tests in all packages
go test ./...

# With race detector (catches data races)
go test -race ./...

# With coverage percentage
go test -cover

# Generate coverage report
go test -coverprofile=coverage.out
go tool cover -html=coverage.out

# Skip long tests (use testing.Short())
go test -short

# Set timeout (default 10m)
go test -timeout 30s

# Run N times (catch flaky tests)
go test -count=10

# Disable test caching
go test -count=1

content.text: Skipping Tests Conditionally
Use t.Skip to conditionally skip tests based on environment, flags, or other conditions. The -short flag sets testing.Short() to true.

items.label: go test
items.description: Run tests in current package

items.label: go test -v
items.description: Verbose: show all test names and t.Log output

items.label: go test -run Pattern
items.description: Run only tests matching regex pattern

items.label: go test -race
items.description: Enable race detector (use in CI!)

items.label: go test -cover
items.description: Show coverage percentage

items.label: go test -short
items.description: Set testing.Short() to true

items.label: go test ./...
items.description: Run tests in all packages

content.text: Go's testing package is simple yet powerful. Use table-driven tests for clarity, t.Run for subtests, t.Helper for cleaner helpers, t.Parallel for speed, and t.Cleanup for resource management. Run with -race in CI to catch data races early.

Go's testing package includes a powerful benchmarking framework. Unlike manual timing with time.Now(), Go benchmarks automatically run your code enough times to get statistically meaningful results. This eliminates guesswork and gives you reliable performance measurements.
This section covers writing benchmark functions, understanding b.N, measuring memory allocations, using sub-benchmarks, and avoiding common pitfalls that lead to misleading results.
Your First Benchmark

Benchmark functions start with Benchmark, take *testing.B, and live in _test.go files. The key is the b.N loop: Go's framework automatically adjusts N until it gets stable measurements (about 1 second of runtime).

content.title: Always Use b.N
content.message: Never hardcode the loop count. Always use 'for i := 0; i < b.N; i++'. Go automatically determines N for accurate measurements.

content.text: Running Benchmarks
Use go test -bench=. to run benchmarks. The output shows the function name, iterations (N), and time per operation. Add -benchmem for memory stats.

content.code:
# Run all benchmarks
go test -bench=.

# Run benchmarks matching pattern
go test -bench=Fibonacci

# Include memory allocation stats
go test -bench=. -benchmem

# Run for longer (more accurate)
go test -bench=. -benchtime=3s

# Run multiple times (check consistency)
go test -bench=. -count=5

# Skip regular tests, only benchmarks
go test -bench=. -run=^$

# Specify CPU count
go test -bench=. -cpu=1,2,4

content.text: Comparing String Concatenation Methods
A classic benchmark comparison: string concatenation with += vs strings.Builder. This demonstrates how benchmarks reveal performance differences that aren't obvious from code inspection.
Memory Allocation Tracking
Memory allocations often matter more than CPU time. Each allocation involves the allocator and creates garbage for the GC. Use -benchmem or b.ReportAllocs() to track allocations.
Setup Isolation with ResetTimer
When your benchmark needs expensive setup that shouldn't be timed, use b.ResetTimer() after setup. This zeroes out time and allocation counters.
Sub-Benchmarks for Different Sizes
Sub-benchmarks let you test how performance scales with input size. Use b.Run() to create named sub-benchmarks. This makes it easy to spot O(n) vs O(n²) behavior.
Avoiding Compiler Optimizations
If you don't use a function's result, the compiler might optimize away the entire call. Always store results in a package-level variable to prevent this.
Parallel Benchmarks
b.RunParallel tests how code performs under concurrent load. This is essential for code that will run in HTTP handlers or other concurrent contexts.
Comparing Results with benchstat
To compare before/after performance, save benchmark output and use benchstat. It calculates statistical significance and shows percentage changes.

content.code:
# Install benchstat
go install golang.org/x/perf/cmd/benchstat@latest

# Before changes: run 10 times for statistics
go test -bench=. -count=10 > old.txt

# Make your optimizations...

# After changes
go test -bench=. -count=10 > new.txt

# Compare with statistics
benchstat old.txt new.txt

# Output shows:
#   - Name
#   - Old time/op vs New time/op
#   - Delta (percentage change)
#   - P-value (statistical significance)

items.label: ns/op
items.description: Nanoseconds per operation. Lower is better.

items.label: B/op
items.description: Bytes allocated per operation. Lower means less GC pressure.

items.label: allocs/op
items.description: Number of allocations per operation. Fewer allocations = faster.

content.text: Common Benchmarking Mistakes

items.label: Discarding results
items.description: Compiler may optimize away unused results. Use a package-level sink variable.

items.label: Including setup in timing
items.description: Use b.ResetTimer() after setup, b.StopTimer()/StartTimer() for per-iteration setup.

items.label: Ignoring memory
items.description: Always use -benchmem. Allocations cause GC pressure that doesn't show in CPU time.

items.label: Running once
items.description: Use -count=5 or higher. Single runs can have noise from OS scheduling.

items.label: Noisy environment
items.description: Close other apps, disable turbo boost for consistent results.

content.text: Benchmarks are essential for optimization. Always measure before optimizing - intuition about performance is often wrong. Use -benchmem to track allocations, run multiple times with -count, and compare changes with benchstat.

sections.title: Logging: Structured Logs and Best Practices

content.text: Logging is essential for debugging, monitoring, and understanding application behavior. Go provides two approaches: the classic log package for simple use cases, and the modern log/slog package (Go 1.21+) for structured, production-ready logging.
This section covers basic logging with the log package, structured logging with slog, log levels, JSON output, adding context, and best practices for production systems.
The Standard log Package
Go's built-in log package provides basic logging. It writes timestamped messages to stderr by default. It's simple but lacks log levels and structured output.
Custom Loggers
Instead of using the global logger, create custom loggers for different parts of your application. Each logger can have its own prefix, flags, and output destination.

content.title: Fatal vs Panic
content.message: log.Fatal calls os.Exit(1) after logging - defers won't run. log.Panic calls panic() which can be recovered. In library code, return errors instead of using Fatal/Panic.

content.text: Structured Logging with slog (Go 1.21+)

The log/slog package brings structured logging to Go's standard library. Structured logs output key-value pairs that are easy to parse, search, and analyze with tools like Elasticsearch, Splunk, or CloudWatch.

items.label: log package
items.description: Unstructured text, no levels. Best for scripts, CLI tools, quick debugging.

items.label: log/slog
items.description: Structured key-value pairs with levels. Best for production services, APIs, microservices.

content.text: Configuring Log Levels
slog provides four levels: Debug, Info, Warn, Error. The default level is Info, so Debug messages are hidden. Create a custom handler to change the level.
JSON Output for Production
Production systems need JSON logs for log aggregation tools. Switch from TextHandler to JSONHandler for machine-readable output.
Adding Context with With()
Use Logger.With() to create child loggers with pre-set attributes. This is perfect for adding request IDs, user IDs, or other context that should appear in all related logs.
Redacting Sensitive Data
Never log passwords, API keys, or personal data. Use ReplaceAttr in HandlerOptions to automatically redact sensitive fields.
Adding Source Location
For debugging, you can include the source file and line number in log output using AddSource option.
High-Performance Logging
For hot paths, use LogAttrs with pre-built attributes to avoid allocations from variadic parameters. Also check Enabled() before expensive log construction.

items.label: TextHandler
items.description: Human-readable output for development. Easy to read in terminal.

items.label: JSONHandler
items.description: Machine-readable for production. Works with log aggregators.

content.title: Environment-Based Configuration
content.message: Use TextHandler for local development (human-readable) and JSONHandler for production (machine-parseable). Switch based on an environment variable.

content.text: The log/slog package brings production-ready structured logging to Go's standard library. Use the classic log package for simple scripts, but prefer slog for any service that needs proper observability.
Command-line tools are everywhere in Go: go build, docker run, kubectl apply. Go's standard library provides the flag package for parsing flags, while os.Args gives raw access to arguments.
This section covers raw argument access with os.Args, the flag package for typed parsing, custom flag types, subcommands, and combining flags with environment variables.
Raw Arguments with os.Args
os.Args is a string slice containing all command-line arguments. The first element (os.Args[0]) is always the program name. Use this for simple positional arguments.
Basic Flag Parsing
The flag package handles typed flags with default values and auto-generated help. Define flags with flag.String, flag.Int, flag.Bool, etc., then call flag.Parse().

content.title: Flag Syntax
content.message: Go accepts -flag, -flag=value, and -flag value. Boolean flags can use -verbose or -verbose=true. Use -- to stop flag parsing.

content.text: Binding to Existing Variables
Use StringVar, IntVar, BoolVar to bind flags to existing variables. This is cleaner when populating config structs.
Short and Long Flags
Go's flag package doesn't distinguish short (-v) and long (--verbose) flags. Both use single dash. To support both, define two flags pointing to the same variable.

content.code:
package main

import (
    "flag"
    "fmt"
)

func main() {
    var verbose bool
    var output string

    // Define both short and long versions
    flag.BoolVar(&verbose, "verbose", false, "verbose output")
    flag.BoolVar(&verbose, "v", false, "verbose output (shorthand)")

    flag.StringVar(&output, "output", "out.txt", "output file")
    flag.StringVar(&output, "o", "out.txt", "output file (shorthand)")

    flag.Parse()

    fmt.Printf("Verbose: %v\n", verbose)
    fmt.Printf("Output: %s\n", output)
}

content.text: Custom Flag Types
For complex types like slices or enums, implement the flag.Value interface: String() and Set(string) error. This lets you use -tag=a -tag=b to collect multiple values.
Subcommands Pattern
Tools like git and docker use subcommands (git commit, docker run). Create separate FlagSets for each subcommand, then parse based on os.Args[1].

content.code:
package main

import (
    "flag"
    "fmt"
    "os"
)

func main() {
    // Define subcommand flag sets
    serveCmd := flag.NewFlagSet("serve", flag.ExitOnError)
    servePort := serveCmd.Int("port", 8080, "port to listen on")
    serveHost := serveCmd.String("host", "localhost", "host to bind")

    buildCmd := flag.NewFlagSet("build", flag.ExitOnError)
    buildOutput := buildCmd.String("o", "./dist", "output directory")
    buildMinify := buildCmd.Bool("minify", false, "minify output")

    if len(os.Args) < 2 {
        fmt.Println("Usage: app <command> [options]")
        fmt.Println("Commands: serve, build")
        os.Exit(1)
    }

    switch os.Args[1] {
    case "serve":
        serveCmd.Parse(os.Args[2:])
        fmt.Printf("Server: %s:%d\n", *serveHost, *servePort)

    case "build":
        buildCmd.Parse(os.Args[2:])
        fmt.Printf("Output: %s, Minify: %v\n", *buildOutput, *buildMinify)

    default:
        fmt.Fprintf(os.Stderr, "Unknown command: %s\n", os.Args[1])
        os.Exit(1)
    }
}

content.text: Environment Variable Fallback
Production tools support both flags and environment variables. Use env vars as defaults, with flags taking precedence.
Custom Usage Message
Override flag.Usage to customize the help message shown with -h or -help.

items.label: os.Args
items.description: Raw string slice. Manual parsing. Best for simple positional arguments.

items.label: flag package
items.description: Typed parsing with defaults. Auto-generates -help. Best for most CLI tools.

items.label: Third-party (cobra, urfave/cli)
items.description: Nested subcommands, shell completion, advanced features. Best for complex CLIs.

content.title: Positional Arguments
content.message: Use flag.Args() to get non-flag arguments after parsing. Combine with flags for commands like: app -verbose file1.txt file2.txt

content.text: The flag package covers most CLI needs without external dependencies. For complex tools with nested subcommands, shell completion, or man page generation, consider cobra or urfave/cli.

Concurrency is the ability to handle multiple tasks at once. In Go, concurrency is not just a feature but a core design principle. Go makes concurrent programming accessible through goroutines and channels, abstractions that let you write concurrent code almost as easily as sequential code.
Think Like a Chef

Imagine a chef cooking dinner. They put pasta in boiling water (8 minutes), start the sauce simmering (5 minutes), and prep the salad (3 minutes). A sequential chef would wait for the pasta to finish, then start the sauce, then make the salad: 16 minutes total. A concurrent chef starts the pasta, then while it boils, starts the sauce, then preps the salad while both cook. Total time: about 8 minutes (the longest task).

content.code:
Sequential Chef (one thing at a time):
|-- Pasta [################] 8 min
|-- Sauce                    [##########] 5 min
|-- Salad                                [######] 3 min
+-- Total: 16 minutes

Concurrent Chef (multiple things in progress):
|-- Pasta [################]
|-- Sauce [##########]
|-- Salad [######]
+-- Total: 8 minutes (all finish together!)

content.text: The concurrent chef doesn't have more hands. They still do one action at a time: stir the sauce, check the pasta, chop vegetables. But by switching between tasks intelligently, all three dishes make progress together. This is concurrency: structuring work so multiple tasks can be in progress, even if you're only actively working on one at any moment.
Why Concurrency Matters

Modern programs rarely do just one thing. A web server handles thousands of requests simultaneously. A CLI tool might download files while showing a progress bar. A data pipeline processes records in parallel to finish faster. Without concurrency, these programs would be painfully slow, processing one thing at a time while the CPU sits idle waiting for network or disk.
Concurrency vs Parallelism

These terms are often confused. Concurrency is about structure: designing your program to handle multiple tasks. Parallelism is about execution: actually running multiple tasks at the same instant on different CPU cores. Back to our chef: one chef managing three dishes is concurrency. Three chefs each cooking one dish simultaneously is parallelism. A concurrent program can run on a single core (one chef), switching between tasks. A parallel program requires multiple cores (multiple chefs).

content.code:
Concurrency (structure)          Parallelism (execution)
    +---------------------+          +---------------------+
    |  Task A ....####..  |          |  Core 1: Task A ####|
    |  Task B ####....##  |          |  Core 2: Task B ####|
    |  Task C ..####....  |          |  Core 3: Task C ####|
    |     (one core)      |          |  (multiple cores)   |
    +---------------------+          +---------------------+
    Tasks interleaved over time     Tasks run simultaneously

content.title: Rob Pike's Definition
content.message: Concurrency is about dealing with lots of things at once. Parallelism is about doing lots of things at once. Go gives you concurrency; the runtime decides when to use parallelism based on available cores.

content.text: Go's Approach: Communicating Sequential Processes

Go's concurrency model is based on Communicating Sequential Processes (CSP), a theory from computer scientist Tony Hoare. The core idea is simple: instead of sharing memory and using locks to prevent conflicts, independent processes should communicate by passing messages. Think of it like a kitchen with multiple chefs: instead of everyone grabbing ingredients from the same counter (shared memory, might collide), each chef has their own prep station and they pass dishes to each other through a serving window (channels). In Go, goroutines are the chefs and channels are the serving windows.

items.label: Traditional Threading
items.description: Threads share memory and use locks (mutexes) to prevent conflicts. Requires careful coordination.

items.label: Go's Preferred Approach
items.description: Goroutines communicate by passing data through channels. Data has one owner at a time, reducing coordination complexity.

content.text: The Go proverb captures this: "Do not communicate by sharing memory; instead, share memory by communicating." Instead of two goroutines accessing the same variable with a lock, you have one goroutine own the data and others request it through channels. That said, Go also provides mutexes for cases where shared memory is simpler. You'll learn both approaches in this section.
When to Use Concurrency

rows: Each request runs in its own goroutine
Don't wait idle for slow operations
Fetch from 3 APIs concurrently, total time = slowest one
Process uploaded files while responding to user

content.text: Getting Started
Here's a function that simulates a network call. It takes 100ms to complete:

To run functions concurrently, use the `go` keyword. When you write `go fetchData(...)`, Go starts the function in the background and immediately moves to the next line without waiting. Let's run three fetches at once:

When you run this program, nothing happens. No output at all. Why? Main doesn't wait for goroutines. It launches them and immediately exits. When main exits, the program stops, killing any goroutines still running.
A simple fix: add `time.Sleep` to make main wait before exiting. This gives goroutines time to finish:

content.output:
$ go run with_sleep.go
Got data from api
Got data from database
Got data from cache
All done!

content.text: The output shows all three fetches completing almost simultaneously after about 100ms, followed by "All done!" The order of the fetch results varies between runs because goroutines run concurrently and their exact completion order depends on the scheduler.

Now it works! The three fetches run concurrently, completing in ~100ms instead of 300ms. But time.Sleep is unreliable. You're guessing how long to wait. Too short, and goroutines get killed. Too long, and you waste time. The upcoming sections teach proper ways to wait: WaitGroups and channels.
What You'll Learn

This Concurrency section covers Go's entire concurrency toolkit. You'll start with goroutines (lightweight threads) and channels (communication pipes), then learn synchronization primitives like WaitGroups and Mutexes. By the end, you'll understand production patterns like worker pools, pipelines, and graceful shutdown.

content.title: Concurrency Is Not Always the Answer
content.message: Adding concurrency to a program adds complexity. A simple sequential solution is often better than a complex concurrent one. Use concurrency when you have a clear performance need or when the problem is naturally concurrent (like handling multiple network connections). Don't use it just because Go makes it easy.

content.text: Ready to dive in? The next section introduces goroutines, Go's fundamental unit of concurrency.

A goroutine is Go's version of a lightweight thread. While a typical OS thread uses 1-2 MB of memory, a goroutine starts with just 2 KB. This means you can run thousands, even millions, of goroutines on a single machine. This isn't just a performance trick; it changes how you think about concurrency.
Creating a Goroutine
Starting a goroutine is remarkably simple: put the keyword 'go' before a function call. That's it. The function runs concurrently with the rest of your code.

content.output:
$ go run first_goroutine.go
Hello from main!
Hello from goroutine!

content.text: Run this multiple times. Sometimes you'll see the goroutine's message first, sometimes main's message first. This is concurrency in action: both functions are running, and the order depends on the scheduler.
How Goroutines Work

To understand goroutines, you need to know about threads. A thread is the basic unit that your operating system runs. Every program runs on at least one thread. Creating threads is expensive: each one uses 1-2 MB of memory, and your OS can only handle thousands of them.

Goroutines are different. When you call `go someFunction()`, Go doesn't ask the OS for a new thread. Instead, it creates a tiny data structure (just 2 KB) that tracks the function and where it left off. Go's runtime includes a scheduler that multiplexes goroutines onto threads. Multiplexing means running many goroutines on a few threads by switching between them. The scheduler decides which goroutine runs on which thread at any moment.

Think of it like a restaurant. Threads are waiters (expensive to hire, limited number). Goroutines are customer orders. You don't need one waiter per order. A few waiters can handle hundreds of orders by switching between tables. When one table is waiting for food, the waiter serves another. Go's scheduler does the same: when a goroutine waits (for network, file, or sleep), the scheduler runs a different goroutine on that thread.

items.label: OS Threads
items.description: 1-2 MB stack, expensive to create, OS schedules them, limited to thousands

items.label: Goroutines
items.description: 2 KB initial stack (grows as needed), cheap to create, Go schedules them, millions possible

content.text: Anonymous Goroutines
You don't need to define a separate function. Anonymous functions work perfectly with goroutines and are common for short concurrent tasks.

content.output:
$ go run anonymous_goroutines.go
Hello, Alice!
Running in goroutine

content.text: Both anonymous goroutines run concurrently. The order of output may vary because the scheduler decides which goroutine runs first. Notice how we pass `name` as an argument to the second goroutine, creating a copy that the closure can safely use.
When to Use Goroutines

rows: net/http starts a goroutine per request automatically
Send email after user signup without making them wait
Fetch from 5 APIs at once, total time = slowest one

content.title: Fire-and-Forget Has Risks
content.message: The background email example is simple but risky. If the server shuts down, the email is lost. If sending fails, no one knows. In production, use a WaitGroup to track goroutines, or better yet, use a job queue. We cover these patterns in later sections.

content.text: The Loop Variable Trap

This is one of the most common goroutine bugs in Go versions before 1.22. When you launch goroutines in a loop using the loop variable directly, all goroutines may see the same value. Go 1.22 fixed this, but understanding the bug helps when reading older code.

In Go versions before 1.22, the goroutine captures the variable i, not its value at that moment. By the time the goroutines run, the loop has finished and i equals 3. Go 1.22+ creates a new variable for each iteration, fixing this issue. The fixes below work in all Go versions:

content.title: Go 1.22 Loop Variable Fix
content.message: Starting in Go 1.22, each loop iteration creates a new variable by default, fixing this trap. If you're on Go 1.22+, the bug won't happen. But understanding it helps when reading older code or targeting earlier Go versions.

content.text: Main Goroutine Exits, Program Ends

When `main()` returns, the program stops immediately. Go doesn't wait for other goroutines to finish. They get killed without warning. Our examples use `time.Sleep()` as a temporary fix, but it's unreliable. The proper solutions are WaitGroups and channels, covered in upcoming sections.
Goroutines Don't Return Values

Unlike regular function calls, `go someFunction()` doesn't return a value. It tells Go to run the function in the background and immediately continues to the next line. Your code doesn't wait for the goroutine to start or finish. If you need results from a goroutine, use channels (covered next) or shared memory with synchronization.

content.code:
// This doesn't work - you cannot assign the result of 'go'
result := go computeSomething() // Compile error: syntax error

content.text: To get results from a goroutine, use a channel:

content.output:
$ go run return_via_channel.go
42

content.text: The main goroutine creates a channel, starts a goroutine that computes and sends the result, then blocks waiting to receive. When the goroutine sends 42 on the channel, main receives it and prints. This pattern, sending results through channels, is how goroutines communicate safely.
Runtime Functions
Go's `runtime` package provides functions to inspect and control goroutines:

content.output:
$ go run num_goroutine.go
Goroutines: 1
Goroutines: 3

content.text: Initially only main is running (1 goroutine). After starting two goroutines and waiting briefly for them to begin, the count increases to 3. This function is useful for debugging goroutine leaks, where the count grows unexpectedly over time.

`runtime.GOMAXPROCS(n)` sets how many OS threads can run Go code in parallel. This controls true parallelism: how many goroutines can execute at the exact same instant. By default, Go uses all CPU cores. You rarely need to change this, but it's useful to understand:

content.output:
$ go run gomaxprocs.go
GOMAXPROCS: 8

content.text: The output shows the default GOMAXPROCS equals the number of CPU cores (8 in this case). After setting it to 2, only two goroutines can execute simultaneously. The rest wait their turn on those two threads.

`runtime.Gosched()` tells the scheduler to pause the current goroutine and let others run. You rarely need this because Go's scheduler switches automatically. But it can help in tight loops that don't have natural pause points:
Quick Reference

content.title: Mental Model
content.message: Think of goroutines as tasks on a to-do list, and the Go runtime as a smart assistant with a few workers (OS threads). The assistant assigns tasks efficiently, switching when one is waiting. You describe what needs doing; Go figures out how to do it efficiently.

content.text: Goroutines are powerful, but how do you wait for them to finish? The next section introduces sync.WaitGroup, a simple counter that lets you wait for multiple goroutines to complete.

In the previous section, we used time.Sleep to wait for goroutines. That's unreliable: you're guessing how long to wait. Too short, and goroutines get killed. Too long, and you waste time. WaitGroup solves this. It waits until all goroutines actually finish, no guessing needed. Use WaitGroup when you just need to know when goroutines are done. If goroutines need to send data back, use channels instead (covered in the next section).
How It Works

A WaitGroup is a counter that tracks running goroutines. Think of it like a checklist: you add items before starting work, check them off when done, and wait until everything is checked off. Add(n) adds n items to the list. Done() checks off one item. Wait() blocks until the list is empty.

content.code:
+-----------------------------------------------+
|                                               |
|  wg.Add(3)                 counter: 3         |
|                                               |
|  goroutine 1: wg.Done()    counter: 2         |
|  goroutine 2: wg.Done()    counter: 1         |
|  goroutine 3: wg.Done()    counter: 0         |
|                                               |
|  wg.Wait()    blocks until counter == 0       |
|               unblocks, main continues        |
|                                               |
+-----------------------------------------------+

content.text: Declaring a WaitGroup
You declare a WaitGroup using var. The zero value is ready to use, no initialization needed.

content.code: var wg sync.WaitGroup    // Ready to use, counter starts at 0

content.text: Basic Usage

Here's the fundamental pattern. Notice that Add() is called before starting the goroutine, and Done() is deferred inside the goroutine. The defer keyword schedules a function to run when the surrounding function returns. This ensures Done() is always called, even if the goroutine panics.

content.output:
$ go run basic_waitgroup.go
Goroutine 1 working...
Goroutine 2 working...
Goroutine 1 done
Goroutine 2 done
All goroutines finished!

content.text: Goroutine 2 finishes last because it sleeps longer (200ms vs 100ms). The order of 'working' messages may vary since goroutines start concurrently, but 'All goroutines finished!' always prints last because wg.Wait() blocks until both call Done().
The Three Methods
Batch Add Pattern
When starting multiple similar goroutines, you can add the total count at once. This is cleaner and slightly more efficient than adding one at a time.

content.output:
$ go run batch_add.go
Processing: fetch products
Processing: fetch users
Processing: fetch orders
All tasks complete

content.text: The output order varies because goroutines run concurrently. The key pattern here is calling wg.Add(len(tasks)) once before the loop rather than wg.Add(1) inside each iteration. Both work, but batch adding is cleaner when you know the count upfront.

content.title: Critical: Add() Must Happen Before go
content.message: Always call Add() before starting the goroutine. If you call Add() inside the goroutine, there's a race: Wait() might see zero before the goroutine has a chance to increment the counter, and your program continues prematurely.

content.text: Parallel File Processing

Processing 4 files one by one takes 400ms (100ms each). Processing them in parallel takes only 100ms because all 4 run at the same time. WaitGroup lets you start all goroutines and wait for all of them to finish.

content.output:
$ go run parallel_files.go
Processed: config.yaml
Processed: users.json
Processed: report.csv
Processed: data.xml
Total time: 101.5ms

content.text: Notice the output order is different from the code order. That's because goroutines run concurrently and finish in unpredictable order. The Go scheduler decides which goroutine runs when. But WaitGroup doesn't care about order. It just waits until all goroutines call Done(), regardless of which finishes first. All 4 files finish in about 100ms, not 400ms. That's the power of parallel processing with WaitGroup.
Passing WaitGroup to Functions
When you pass a WaitGroup to a function, you must pass a pointer. WaitGroup contains internal state that must not be copied.

content.title: Negative Counter Causes Panic
content.message: If you call Done() more times than Add(), the counter goes negative and the program panics. This usually means you have a logic error: either calling Done() twice or not calling Add() enough times. Use defer wg.Done() to ensure exactly one Done() per goroutine.

content.text: When to Use WaitGroup

Use WaitGroup when you need to wait for goroutines to finish but don't need to collect results from them. If goroutines need to send data back, use channels instead (covered in the next section). Here are common scenarios:
Scenario 1: Download Files (Don't Need Content)
You want to download multiple files to disk. You don't need the content in your program, just need to know when all downloads finish.

content.output:
$ go run download_files.go
Downloading image2.png...
Downloading image1.png...
Downloading image3.png...
Saved image2.png to disk
Saved image1.png to disk
Saved image3.png to disk
All downloads complete!

content.text: All three downloads start almost simultaneously and each takes 100ms. Because they run in parallel, total time is about 100ms, not 300ms. WaitGroup ensures we don't print 'All downloads complete!' until every file is saved.
Scenario 2: Fire-and-Forget Tasks
You want to send emails or log events in the background. You don't care about the result, just need to make sure they complete before the program exits.

content.output:
$ go run fire_and_forget.go
Emails queued, waiting...
Sending email to carol@example.com...
Sending email to alice@example.com...
Sending email to bob@example.com...
Email sent to carol@example.com
Email sent to alice@example.com
Email sent to bob@example.com
All emails sent!

content.text: Notice 'Emails queued, waiting...' prints before any 'Sending' messages. That's because main prints it immediately after starting the goroutines, before they have a chance to run. The wg.Wait() then blocks until all emails finish sending.
Scenario 3: When NOT to Use WaitGroup
If you need to collect results from goroutines, WaitGroup alone is not enough. You need channels. This example shows the problem:

This code has a race condition. Here's what goes wrong: the line 'total += price' is not atomic. It actually does three steps: (1) read current value of total, (2) add price to it, (3) write the result back. When two goroutines do this at the same time, they might both read total as 0, both add their price, and both write back. One update gets lost. Expected total: 225 (100+50+75). Actual result: could be 100, 125, 150, or 225 depending on timing. WaitGroup only waits for goroutines to finish. It doesn't protect shared data. To collect results safely, use channels (covered in the next section).
