A method looks like a regular function, but with an extra parameter before the function name called the receiver. The receiver specifies which type the method belongs to. When you call user.Greet(), Go passes user as the receiver to the Greet method.

By convention, receiver names are short, often just the first letter of the type name. We use 'u' for User, 'c' for Counter, 's' for Server. Avoid using 'this' or 'self' like other languages. Go prefers short, consistent names.

content.output:
$ go run basic_method.go
Hello, Alice
Alice <alice@example.com>

content.text: Both methods work on the User struct. Greet() returns a greeting using the Name field, while DisplayEmail() formats both fields together. The key insight is that methods have direct access to all fields of their receiver.

content.title: Receiver Naming Convention
content.message: Use a short, consistent name for receivers. If you use 'u' for User in one method, use 'u' in all User methods. Consistency makes code easier to read.

content.text: Value vs Pointer Receivers
Here's where things get interesting. The receiver can be either a value (u User) or a pointer (u *User). This choice has a major impact on how your method behaves.

With a value receiver, the method gets a copy of the struct. Any changes it makes happen to the copy, and the original remains unchanged. With a pointer receiver, the method gets the memory address of the original struct, so changes affect the original.

Think of it like passing a document to someone. A value receiver is like giving them a photocopy. They can scribble all over it, but your original is safe. A pointer receiver is like giving them the original document with a pen.

items.label: Value Receiver (u User)
items.description: Works on a COPY of the struct. Changes don't affect the original. Use for read-only methods or small immutable types.

items.label: Pointer Receiver (u *User)
items.description: Works on the ORIGINAL via its memory address. Changes persist after the method returns. Use when modifying state or for large structs.

content.text: The Copy Problem

This is one of the most common mistakes for Go beginners. You write a method that should change something, but the change disappears when the method returns. Let's see this in action with a Counter that should track a number.

The IncrementWrong method uses a value receiver, so it gets a copy of the counter. It increments the copy, but the original counter stays at zero. The Increment method uses a pointer receiver, so it modifies the actual counter.

content.output:
$ go run receiver_demo.go
After IncrementWrong: 0
After Increment: 1
Is zero? false

content.text: This output demonstrates the critical difference. After IncrementWrong, the counter is still 0 because the method modified a copy. After Increment (pointer receiver), the counter becomes 1 because it modified the original. The IsZero method reads the current value correctly.

content.title: Value Receivers Create Copies
content.message: If your method needs to modify the struct, you MUST use a pointer receiver. This is the single most common mistake Go beginners make.

content.text: Automatic Pointer Conversion

You might wonder: if Deposit needs a pointer receiver, do I always need to write (&acc).Deposit()? No. Go handles this for you. When you call a method, Go looks at what the method needs and what you have, then converts automatically.

If you have a value and call a pointer method, Go takes the address for you. If you have a pointer and call a value method, Go dereferences it. Just write acc.Deposit() and Go figures out the rest. This convenience only applies to method calls though.

content.output:
$ go run auto_convert.go
Balance: 150
Balance: 225

content.text: Notice that we call Deposit() on both a value (acc) and a pointer (accPtr), and both work correctly. Go automatically takes the address of acc when calling the pointer method, and automatically dereferences accPtr when calling the value method.

content.title: Convenience, Not Magic
content.message: Auto-conversion only works for addressable values. You can't call Account{Balance: 100}.Deposit(50) directly because the temporary struct has no address to take.

content.text: When to Use Pointer Receivers
Choosing between value and pointer receivers is one of the most common decisions you'll make. Here are the guidelines that cover most cases:

items.label: Use Pointer Receiver (*T)
items.description: The method modifies the receiver. The struct is large and copying would be expensive. You want consistency with other methods on the same type.

items.label: Use Value Receiver (T)
items.description: The method only reads data. The struct is small (like Point{X, Y}). The type should be immutable (like time.Time).

content.text: If any method on a type needs a pointer receiver, it's often best to use pointer receivers for all methods on that type for consistency.

content.output:
$ go run when_pointer.go
Processed dataset
First record: 42
Distance squared: 25

content.text: The LargeData struct uses a pointer receiver to avoid copying 80KB+ of data on every method call. The Point struct uses a value receiver because it's only 16 bytes, cheaper to copy than to indirect through a pointer.
Nil Receivers: Handle with Care

Unlike many languages, Go allows you to call methods on nil pointers. The method receives nil as its receiver. This can be useful for recursive data structures like linked lists or trees, where nil represents an empty structure.
However, if you don't check for nil and try to access a field, your program will panic. Always check for nil at the start of methods that use pointer receivers if nil is a valid input.

content.output:
$ go run nil_receiver.go
Empty sum: 0
Empty length: 0
List sum: 6
List length: 3

content.text: The nil pointer doesn't cause a panic because both methods check for nil at the start. This is a common pattern for recursive data structures. The empty list returns 0 for both sum and length, while the list 1->2->3 correctly sums to 6 with length 3.
Method Chaining: The Builder Pattern

A powerful technique is to have methods return the receiver pointer, enabling fluent chaining. Each method call returns the same object, so you can immediately call another method on it. Instead of writing three separate statements, you write one continuous chain that reads naturally from left to right.

This is the foundation of the builder pattern. It's especially popular for constructing complex objects step by step, like building SQL queries, HTTP requests, or configuration objects. The pattern keeps related operations together and makes the code self-documenting.

content.output:
$ go run chaining.go
SELECT name, email FROM users WHERE active = true

content.text: Each method returns the QueryBuilder pointer, allowing the next method to be called immediately. The chain reads naturally from left to right, building up the query step by step. Notice how Build() at the end returns a string instead of the builder, signaling the end of the chain.
Methods on Non-Struct Types
Methods aren't just for structs. You can define methods on any type you create, including types based on strings, integers, or slices. This lets you add meaningful behavior to simple types.
For example, instead of passing a raw string for a username and validating it everywhere, you can create a Username type with validation built in. The type itself ensures correctness.

content.output:
$ go run methods_custom_types.go
Valid: true
Normalized: alice
Average: 87.6
Max: 95

content.text: The Username type adds validation and normalization behavior to a simple string. The Scores type adds statistical methods to a slice of integers. This pattern creates domain-specific types that carry their behavior with them, making code more expressive and self-documenting.
Quick Reference: Choosing a Receiver Type
Here's a quick summary to help you decide. When in doubt, use a pointer receiver. It's safer for modification and avoids unexpected copying for large structs.

items.label: Use Pointer Receiver (*T)
items.description: Method modifies the receiver. Struct is large (avoid copying). Consistency with other methods. Struct contains sync.Mutex or similar.

items.label: Use Value Receiver (T)
items.description: Method only reads data. Type is small (like Point{X, Y}). Type should be immutable (like time.Time). Slice or map (already reference types).

content.text: Methods are how Go attaches behavior to data. Use value receivers for read-only operations on small types, pointer receivers when you need to modify data or avoid copying. Keep receiver names short and consistent, and consider the builder pattern for fluent APIs.

In the previous sections, we learned that structs group data and methods attach behavior to types. But what if you want to write a function that works with multiple types? For example, a function that can print any object that has a String() method, regardless of whether it's a User, a Product, or a Robot.

This is where interfaces come in. An interface defines a contract: a set of methods that a type must have. Any type that has those methods automatically satisfies the interface. There's no 'implements' keyword. If it walks like a duck and quacks like a duck, Go treats it as a duck.

This approach, called structural typing or duck typing, makes Go incredibly flexible. You can write generic code that works with any type that has the behavior you need, and you can swap implementations without changing a single line of calling code.
Defining and Implementing an Interface

An interface is defined with the type keyword, followed by the interface name and the keyword interface. Inside the braces, you list the method signatures that types must have to satisfy this interface. No method bodies, just names, parameters, and return types.

To implement an interface, a type simply needs to have all the required methods with matching signatures. No explicit declaration is needed. In this example, both Person and Robot implement Greeter because they both have a Greet() method that returns a string.

content.output:
$ go run interface_basic.go
Hello, I'm Alice
Beep boop. I am R2-D2

content.text: Both Person and Robot work with the introduce function because they both implement Greeter. Go doesn't care about the types themselves, only that they have the required Greet() method. This is polymorphism: the same function call (g.Greet()) produces different behavior depending on the actual type. The word comes from Greek meaning 'many forms.' One interface, many implementations.

content.title: Implicit Implementation
content.message: Notice there's no 'implements Greeter' anywhere. If a type has all the methods an interface requires with matching signatures, it automatically implements that interface. This is called structural typing.

content.text: Example: Payment Processing

Let's see why interfaces are so powerful in practice. Imagine you're building an e-commerce system that needs to support multiple payment providers: Stripe, PayPal, maybe Apple Pay later. Without interfaces, you'd need separate checkout functions for each provider, or ugly switch statements everywhere.

With interfaces, you define what a payment processor must do (charge money, provide a name), then write your checkout logic once. Any payment provider that implements those methods works automatically. Adding a new provider means creating a new type, not changing existing code.

content.output:
$ go run payment_interface.go
Processing with Stripe...
Stripe: Charging $99.99
Processing with PayPal...
PayPal: Charging $49.99

content.text: The checkout function works identically with both Stripe and PayPal. To add a new payment provider like Apple Pay, you'd create a new struct with Charge() and Name() methods. The checkout function wouldn't change at all.
The Empty Interface: any

What if an interface has zero methods? Then every type in Go satisfies it, because every type has at least zero methods. This is called the empty interface, written as interface{} or, since Go 1.18, simply any.

The empty interface is Go's way of saying 'I'll accept anything.' Functions like fmt.Println use it to accept any type. However, once a value is stored in an empty interface, Go no longer knows its type at compile time. You lose type safety and need type assertions to do anything useful with the value.

content.output:
$ go run any_interface.go
Value: 42, Type: int
Value: hello, Type: string
Value: true, Type: bool
Value: [1 2], Type: []int
Value: <nil>, Type: <nil>

content.text: The function accepts any type, from integers to strings to slices. The %T format verb reveals the actual type stored in the interface. This flexibility comes at the cost of type safety, since the compiler can't verify operations on the value.

content.title: Use any Sparingly
content.message: Using any loses compile-time type safety. The compiler can't catch type errors, so bugs appear at runtime instead. Prefer specific interfaces that describe the behavior you actually need.

content.text: Type Assertions: Extracting the Concrete Type
When you have an interface value and need to access the underlying concrete type, you use a type assertion. The syntax is value.(Type), which extracts the concrete value if it matches the type.

There are two forms of type assertion. The single-value form v.(Type) panics if the type doesn't match. The two-value form v.(Type) returns a second boolean indicating success. Always use the two-value form unless you're absolutely certain of the type.

content.output:
$ go run type_assertion.go
It's a string: hello
Length: 5
Not an int

content.text: The two-value form lets us safely check whether the assertion succeeds. When it succeeds, str contains the actual string and we can call string methods like len(). When it fails, ok is false and num gets the zero value for int (0).

content.title: Avoid Single-Value Assertions
content.message: The expression v.(Type) without checking ok will panic if v doesn't hold that type. A panic crashes your program. Always use the two-value form: value, ok := v.(Type)

content.text: Type Switch: Handling Multiple Types

When you need to handle several possible types, chaining if statements with type assertions gets messy. Go provides a cleaner solution: the type switch. It looks like a regular switch, but the cases are types instead of values.

The special syntax switch x := v.(type) extracts the type of v and assigns the concrete value to x within each case. Inside the case int block, x is an int. Inside the case string block, x is a string. This gives you type-safe access to the value.

content.output:
$ go run type_switch.go
integer: 42 (doubled: 84)
string of length 5: "hello"
boolean: true
int slice, sum = 6
unknown type: float64

content.text: Each case handles a different type with type-safe operations. In the int case, we can double the value. In the string case, we can get its length. The default case catches types we didn't explicitly handle, like float64.
Interface Composition: Building from Small Pieces
Go encourages small, focused interfaces. The io.Reader interface has just one method: Read. The io.Writer interface has just one method: Write. But what if you need both reading and writing?

Interface composition lets you embed smaller interfaces into larger ones. The ReadWriter interface embeds both Reader and Writer, requiring types to implement all methods from both. This is how the standard library builds flexible abstractions without deep inheritance hierarchies.

content.output:
$ go run composition.go
Writing to test.txt
Closing test.txt

content.text: The File struct implements Read, Write, and Close, so it satisfies Reader, Writer, Closer, ReadWriter, and ReadWriteCloser. We can use it wherever any of these interfaces are expected. This is how io.Copy works with any Reader and Writer combination.
Common Standard Library Interfaces
The Go standard library defines several interfaces that you'll use frequently. Implementing these interfaces lets your types work seamlessly with the rest of the language.

The fmt.Stringer interface (String() string) controls how your type appears when printed with fmt.Println. The error interface (Error() string) is how Go handles errors. By implementing these interfaces, your types integrate naturally with Go's built-in functionality.

content.output:
$ go run common_interfaces.go
Alice <alice@example.com>
validation failed on age: cannot be negative

content.text: The User type implements fmt.Stringer, so fmt.Println automatically calls String() instead of printing the raw struct. ValidationError implements the error interface, so it can be returned from any function that returns error and handled with standard error-checking idioms.
Compile-Time Interface Check
Because interfaces are implemented implicitly, you might accidentally break one by renaming or removing a method. The compiler won't warn you until something tries to use that type as the interface.

To catch this early, you can add a compile-time assertion. This line does nothing at runtime, but it tells the compiler to verify that your type implements the interface. If it doesn't, compilation fails immediately with a clear error message.

content.output:
$ go run compile_check.go
(no output - this is a compile-time check)

content.text: The program produces no output because the var _ line is purely a compile-time assertion. If you comment out the Load method from FileStorage, the compiler will fail with a clear error explaining which method is missing. This catches interface drift early.

content.title: Interface Satisfaction Check
content.message: The pattern var _ Interface = (*Type)(nil) is commonly used in Go codebases. The underscore discards the value, so no memory is allocated. It's purely a compile-time check.

content.text: The Nil Interface Gotcha

This is one of Go's most confusing behaviors for newcomers. An interface value actually contains two things internally: a type descriptor and a pointer to the underlying value. An interface is only nil when BOTH components are nil.

If you store a nil pointer of a specific type into an interface, the interface is NOT nil. It has a type (the pointer type) even though the value is nil. This catches many developers off guard when returning errors.

content.output:
$ go run nil_interface.go
Broken: err is NOT nil!
  Type: *main.MyError, Value: no error
Fixed: err is nil as expected

content.text: The broken version returns (*MyError)(nil), which has a type but nil value. When compared with err != nil, Go sees that the interface has a type (so it's not truly nil). The fixed version returns a plain nil, which has neither type nor value, so it equals nil as expected.

content.title: The Nil Interface Gotcha
content.message: Never return a typed nil pointer as an interface. An interface holding (*MyError)(nil) is NOT equal to nil. Always return nil directly when there's no error.

content.text: Interface Best Practices
Go's interface philosophy differs from languages like Java or C#. In Go, smaller is better. Here are the guidelines that the Go community has developed over years of practice.

items.label: Keep interfaces small
items.description: The ideal interface has 1-2 methods. io.Reader has just Read(). Smaller interfaces are more reusable and easier to implement.

items.label: Define where used
items.description: Define interfaces in the package that uses them (the consumer), not the package that implements them. This keeps packages decoupled.

items.label: Accept interfaces, return structs
items.description: Function parameters should be interfaces for flexibility. Return concrete types so callers know exactly what they're getting.

items.label: Don't over-interface
items.description: Only create an interface when you have multiple implementations or need to mock for testing. YAGNI applies here.

content.text: Interfaces are Go's answer to polymorphism. They enable flexible, testable code without inheritance hierarchies. Remember: if a type has the methods, it implements the interface automatically. Keep interfaces small, compose them when needed, and watch out for the nil interface gotcha.

Imagine you're building an employee management system. Every employee is also a person with a name and age. You could copy all the person fields into the employee struct, but that creates duplication. What if you later add an address field to Person? You'd have to remember to update Employee too.

Go solves this with embedding. Instead of copying fields, you include one struct inside another. The inner struct's fields and methods automatically become available on the outer struct. It's like saying "an Employee has all the properties of a Person, plus some extra ones."

Now consider another problem: you write a function to find the maximum of two integers. Later, you need the same logic for floats. And then for strings. Do you write three nearly identical functions? That's where generics come in. With generics (added in Go 1.18), you write one function that works with any type that supports comparison.
This section covers both techniques: embedding for building types through composition, and generics for writing flexible, type-safe code that works across multiple types.
Struct Embedding

To embed a struct, you add the type name without a field name. Go automatically promotes the embedded struct's fields and methods to the outer type. This means you can access them directly, as if they were defined on the outer type itself. You can still access the embedded struct explicitly when needed.

content.code:
Struct Embedding: Composition, Not Inheritance

    +------------------+
    |     Employee     |
    +------------------+
    | Person           |  <-- Embedded (no field name)
    |   +------------+ |
    |   | Name string| |  <-- Promoted: emp.Name
    |   | Age  int   | |  <-- Promoted: emp.Age
    |   | Greet()    | |  <-- Promoted: emp.Greet()
    |   +------------+ |
    | EmployeeID string|  <-- Own field
    | Department string|  <-- Own field
    +------------------+

    emp.Name      -->  emp.Person.Name  (promoted)
    emp.Greet()   -->  emp.Person.Greet() (promoted)

    Note: Employee is NOT a Person. It HAS a Person.

content.output:
$ go run embedding.go
Name: Alice
Age: 30
Hi, I'm Alice
Via Person: Alice

content.text: Employee can access Name and Age directly even though they're defined in Person. The Greet() method is also promoted. This is composition that feels like inheritance, but Employee is not a Person; it has a Person.

content.title: Composition Not Inheritance
content.message: Embedding is composition, not inheritance. Employee is not a Person; it has a Person. But promoted methods make it feel like inheritance.

content.text: Method Shadowing

Sometimes you want to customize behavior from an embedded type. If the outer type defines a method with the same name as the embedded type, the outer method takes priority. This is called shadowing. The embedded method isn't gone though. You can still access it explicitly through the embedded field name when you need the original behavior.

content.output:
$ go run shadowing.go
[INFO] Basic message
[DEBUG] [TIME] Shadowed method
[DEBUG] Original method

content.text: TimestampLogger.Log shadows Logger.Log. When we call ts.Log(), it uses the outer type's method. We can still call the original via ts.Logger.Log(). This lets you override behavior while keeping access to the original.
Interface Embedding

Just like structs, interfaces can embed other interfaces. This lets you build larger interfaces from smaller ones. Instead of listing all methods in one big interface, you compose it from focused, single-purpose interfaces. Go's standard library uses this pattern extensively. For example, io.ReadWriter combines io.Reader and io.Writer, so any type that can both read and write automatically satisfies io.ReadWriter.

content.output:
$ go run interface_embedding.go
Read: hello

content.text: ReadWriteCloser combines three single-method interfaces. Buffer implements all three methods, so it satisfies ReadWriteCloser. This pattern from the standard library shows how to build flexible interfaces from small, focused pieces.
Generic Functions (Go 1.18+)

Before generics, if you wanted a function to work with multiple types, you had two choices: write separate functions for each type, or use interface{} and lose type safety. Generics give you the best of both worlds. You write the function once, and it works with any type you specify. The compiler still checks types at compile time, so you catch errors early. The syntax uses square brackets to declare type parameters before the regular parameters.

content.output:
$ go run generics_basic.go
Numbers:
  [0]: 10
  [1]: 20
  [2]: 30
Names:
  [0]: Alice
  [1]: Bob
First: 10
Last: Bob

content.text: The same PrintSlice function works for both []int and []string. Go infers the type parameter T from the argument. First and Last work on any slice type, returning the appropriate zero value when the slice is empty.
Type Constraints

When you use `any` as a constraint, your function accepts any type, but you can only do things that work on all types, like assign or print. If you want to add numbers or compare values, you need to tell Go which types support those operations. Constraints do exactly that. You define an interface listing the allowed types using the pipe symbol (|), and Go then permits operations those types support.

content.output:
$ go run constraints.go
Sum ints: 15
Sum floats: 7.5
Min(3, 7): 3
Max strings: banana

content.text: Constraints limit which types can be used. Number allows + operations, Ordered allows < comparisons. Sum works with both int and float64 because both are in the Number union. Max even works with strings because string is in Ordered.

content.title: Standard Library Constraints (Go 1.21+)
content.message: Go 1.21 added the `cmp` package with `cmp.Ordered` constraint and `cmp.Compare` function. Use these instead of defining your own. For slice operations, see the `slices` package: `slices.Contains`, `slices.Index`, `slices.Sort`, and more.

content.text: Generic Types

Generics aren't just for functions. You can also create generic structs. Think about a stack: the push and pop logic is identical whether you're storing integers, strings, or custom types. Without generics, you'd need separate IntStack, StringStack, and so on. With generic types, you write Stack[T] once and use it with any type. This is especially useful for data structures like stacks, queues, linked lists, and trees where the container logic doesn't depend on what's inside.

content.output:
$ go run generic_stack.go
Length: 3
Popped: 30
Top: second

content.text: Stack[T] is a type-safe container. Stack[int] holds only ints, Stack[string] holds only strings. No type assertions or empty interfaces needed. The compiler ensures type safety at compile time.
Multiple Type Parameters

Sometimes one type parameter isn't enough. Consider a Map function that transforms a slice of one type into a slice of another, like converting integers to strings. You need two type parameters: one for the input type, one for the output type. Similarly, a key-value pair needs separate types for the key and value. You can declare multiple type parameters by separating them with commas in the square brackets.

content.output:
$ go run multi_params.go
Mapped: [#1 #2 #3 #4 #5]
Evens: [2 4]
Pair: age = 30

content.text: Map uses two type parameters: T for input and R for output, allowing transformation between different types. Pair uses K and V for key-value pairs of any types. This enables type-safe functional programming patterns.
The comparable Constraint

Not all types can be compared with == and !=. Slices, maps, and functions can't be compared directly. If your generic function needs equality checks, like finding an item in a slice or removing duplicates, you need to tell Go that only comparable types are allowed. Go provides a built-in constraint called `comparable` for exactly this. It includes all types that support == and !=, which are also the types valid as map keys.

content.output:
$ go run comparable.go
Contains 3: true
Index of 2: 1
Unique: [1 2 3 4]
Unique names: [a b c]

content.text: The comparable constraint ensures types support == and can be used as map keys. Contains, IndexOf, and Unique work with any comparable type. Unique uses a map internally, which requires comparable keys.

items.label: Use Generics
items.description: Same algorithm, different types. Container types. Type-safe transformations. Compile-time checking.

items.label: Use Interfaces
items.description: Different behaviors, same signature. Dependency injection. Runtime polymorphism. Plugin systems.

items.label: Use Embedding
items.description: Reuse fields and methods. Compose behaviors. Implement interfaces automatically.

content.title: Don't Over-Generalize
content.message: Start with concrete types. Add generics only when you find yourself duplicating the same algorithm for different types. A little copying is better than wrong abstractions.

content.text: Quick Reference

Embedding and generics are powerful tools for building flexible, type-safe code. Use embedding for composition and method promotion. Use generics for algorithms that work across multiple types. Use interfaces for behavioral polymorphism. Start with concrete implementations, then generalize when you see repeated patterns. In the next section, we explore Go's broader approach to object-oriented design and how it differs from traditional OOP languages.

If you're coming from Java, Python, or C++, you might be looking for classes, inheritance hierarchies, and abstract base classes. Go doesn't have any of these. At first, this feels limiting. How do you build complex systems without inheritance? How do you share code between types?

Go takes a fundamentally different approach to object-oriented programming. Instead of building tall inheritance trees, you compose small pieces together. Instead of declaring which interfaces a class implements, types satisfy interfaces automatically by having the right methods. This leads to simpler, more flexible code.

This section explains Go's OOP philosophy and why it works. Understanding this mindset is essential before diving into design patterns and system design, because the patterns look different in Go than in traditional OOP languages.
Why Go Doesn't Have Classes

Classes bundle data and behavior together, which is good. But they also bring inheritance, which creates tight coupling between parent and child classes. Change the parent, and all children might break. The deeper the hierarchy, the harder it is to understand what any single class actually does.

Go's creators saw decades of inheritance-based code and decided there was a better way. Instead of classes, Go has structs (data) and methods (behavior attached to types). Instead of inheritance, Go has composition (embedding one type inside another). The result is flatter, more explicit code.
Composition Over Inheritance

The phrase 'composition over inheritance' is common advice even in traditional OOP. Go enforces it by not providing inheritance at all. When you need to reuse code, you embed one struct inside another. The embedded struct's methods are promoted to the outer struct.

This is not inheritance. The outer type doesn't become a subtype of the inner type. It just gains access to the inner type's methods. You can still access the inner type directly, and you can override any promoted method by defining your own.

content.output:
$ go run composition.go
[SERVER] Starting server on port 8080
[SERVER] Direct log call
[DB] Connecting to database

content.text: Both Server and Database gain logging capabilities by embedding Logger. There's no 'LoggableServer extends Loggable' hierarchy. Each struct is independent, and the relationship is explicit: Server has-a Logger, not Server is-a Logger.
Implicit Interface Satisfaction

In Java, a class must declare 'implements Runnable' to satisfy the Runnable interface. In Go, if a type has a Run() method, it satisfies any interface that requires Run(). No declaration needed. This is called structural typing or duck typing.

This has profound implications. You can define interfaces in your own package that types from other packages satisfy, even if those packages don't know about your interface. This enables loose coupling without sacrificing type safety.

content.output:
$ go run implicit_interface.go
=== Report ===
Q3 results...
[Image: chart.png (800x600)]

content.text: Document and Image never mention the Printer interface. They just have Print() methods. Go's compiler sees that they satisfy Printer and allows them to be used wherever Printer is expected. This is polymorphism without inheritance.
Accept Interfaces, Return Structs

This is one of Go's most important idioms. When writing functions, accept interfaces as parameters (for flexibility) but return concrete struct types (for clarity). This gives callers the freedom to pass any compatible type, while making it clear exactly what they'll receive.

content.output:
$ go run accept_return.go
Lines: 2, Words: 5, Chars: 22

content.text: Analyze accepts io.Reader, so it works with files, network connections, string readers, or any other reader. But it returns *Result, a concrete type, so callers know exactly what fields and methods are available.
Go vs Traditional OOP: Quick Comparison

items.label: Traditional OOP
items.description: Classes, inheritance hierarchies, abstract classes, explicit interface declarations. Deep trees, tight coupling between parent and child.

items.label: Go's Approach
items.description: Structs, composition via embedding, implicit interfaces, small focused interfaces. Flat structure, loose coupling, explicit relationships.

content.title: Think 'Has-A' Not 'Is-A'
content.message: When designing types in Go, ask 'what does this type have?' not 'what is this type?' A Server has logging capability. A User has an address. This mindset leads to better Go code.

content.text: When Traditional OOP Patterns Don't Fit
Some design patterns from traditional OOP translate directly to Go. Others need adaptation. And some aren't needed at all because Go's features solve the problem differently.

For example, the Template Method pattern (using abstract classes to define algorithm skeletons) doesn't work in Go because there are no abstract classes. But you can achieve the same goal with interfaces and composition. The Singleton pattern exists in Go but uses sync.Once instead of private constructors.

content.title: Don't Force Java Patterns into Go
content.message: If you find yourself creating deep struct embedding, writing lots of getter/setter methods, or defining interfaces with 10+ methods, you're probably thinking in Java, not Go. Step back and look for a simpler, more Go-idiomatic solution.

content.text: Go's OOP is different, not deficient. The language guides you toward simpler designs: small interfaces, flat composition, explicit dependencies. In the following sections, we'll see how to apply these principles to build well-designed systems using composition patterns, SOLID principles adapted for Go, and practical design patterns.

In the previous section, we saw that Go favors composition over inheritance. But how do you actually compose types effectively? When should you embed a struct versus hold a reference? How do you share behavior without creating tangled dependencies?

This section explores practical composition patterns in Go. You'll learn when embedding makes sense, how to combine interfaces for flexible APIs, and common mistakes to avoid. These patterns form the foundation for more advanced design patterns covered later.
Struct Embedding Deep Dive

When you embed a struct, its fields and methods become part of the outer struct's API. This is promotion. You can access embedded fields directly, and you can call embedded methods as if they were defined on the outer type.

Embedding is not inheritance. The outer type doesn't become a subtype of the embedded type. You can't pass an Employee where a Person is expected. But you can access emp.Person to get the embedded value if needed.

content.output:
$ go run embedding_deep.go
City: Boston
Address: 123 Main St, Boston 02101
ZIP via Address: 02101
Company: TechCorp - 456 Tech Blvd, SF 94102

content.text: Both Person and Company embed Address. Each gains the City, Street, ZIP fields and the FullAddress() method. But Person and Company are not related types. They just share common fields through composition.
Embedding Pointers vs Values

You can embed either a value or a pointer. Embedding a pointer lets multiple structs share the same embedded instance, and allows the embedded type to be nil. Embedding a value creates a copy, ensuring isolation.

content.output:
$ go run embed_pointer.go
Original: {Debug:true Level:5}
v1: Debug=false
After p1 change: cfg.Level=10
p2.Config is nil: true

content.text: Value embedding is safer because changes are isolated. Pointer embedding is useful when you want shared state or when the embedded type is large and copying would be expensive. Be careful with nil pointer embeddings.

content.title: Nil Pointer Embedding
content.message: If you embed a pointer and it's nil, accessing any promoted field or method will panic. Always initialize pointer embeddings or check for nil before use.

content.text: Method Shadowing

When the outer type defines a method with the same name as an embedded method, the outer method shadows the inner one. This lets you override behavior while still having access to the original through the embedded field name.

content.output:
$ go run shadowing_pattern.go
Extended: 42 (bonus)
Base: 42
value=42
---
Base: 42
Extended: 42 (bonus)

content.text: Extended.Display shadows Base.Display. When we call ext.Display(), we get the extended version. To access the original, we use ext.Base.Display() explicitly. Methods not shadowed, like Info(), are promoted normally.
Interface Embedding

Just as structs can embed structs, interfaces can embed interfaces. This combines method requirements. A type must implement all methods from all embedded interfaces to satisfy the composite interface.

content.output:
$ go run interface_compose.go
Copied: Hello, World!
Closed: true

content.text: File implements Read, Write, and Close, so it satisfies Reader, Writer, Closer, ReadWriter, and ReadWriteCloser. The CopyData function only requires what it needs: a Reader and a Writer. This is the power of small, composable interfaces.

content.title: Keep Interfaces Small
content.message: The Go standard library's io.Reader has just one method: Read. This makes it incredibly reusable. When designing interfaces, ask: what's the minimum behavior I need? Start small, compose when needed.

content.text: The Decorator Pattern via Embedding
Embedding enables the decorator pattern naturally. Embed an interface, override specific methods, and delegate the rest. This adds behavior to existing types without modifying them.

content.output:
$ go run decorator_embed.go
LOG: Fetching data...
LOG: Got 22 bytes
Result: [data from users.json]
---
First call:
Cache miss, fetching...
LOG: Fetching data...
LOG: Got 22 bytes
Second call:
Cache hit!

content.text: LoggingDecorator and CachingDecorator both embed DataSource. They override GetData() to add behavior, then delegate to the embedded source. You can stack decorators: cached wraps logged, which wraps file. Each adds a layer of functionality.
Common Composition Mistakes

content.title: Deep Embedding
content.message: Don't embed more than 1-2 levels deep. Deep embedding makes code hard to understand and can lead to surprising method resolution. If you need more levels, use regular fields instead.

items.label: Use Embedding When
items.description: You want to promote methods/fields. The relationship is 'has-a' and makes sense conceptually. You're decorating or extending behavior.

items.label: Use Regular Fields When
items.description: You don't want promotion. The relationship is just 'uses' not 'has-a'. You need multiple instances of the same type.

content.text: Composition patterns in Go are simple but powerful. Embed structs to share fields and methods. Embed interfaces to combine behaviors. Use shadowing to override while keeping access to originals. And remember: prefer regular fields when you don't need promotion.

Imagine you're building a server struct. It needs a host, port, timeout, TLS config, logger, and maybe more. You could make a constructor with 6 parameters, but that's ugly and error-prone. Which parameter is which? What if you only want to set the port and use defaults for everything else?

The functional options pattern solves this elegantly. Instead of passing values directly, you pass functions that modify the struct. Each option is self-documenting, optional, and can have sensible defaults. This pattern is used extensively in production Go code, including the standard library.
The Problem with Many Parameters

content.output:
$ go run many_params.go
&{Host:localhost Port:8080 Timeout:30 MaxConn:100}

content.text: A config struct is better than many parameters, but it still requires specifying all fields. What if you want defaults? You'd need to check for zero values everywhere. The functional options pattern provides a cleaner solution.
The Functional Options Solution

Define a function type that modifies your struct. Create functions that return this type. The constructor accepts variadic options and applies each one. This gives you named, optional parameters with defaults.

content.output:
$ go run functional_options.go
Default: localhost:8080 (timeout=30s, maxConn=100)
Custom port: localhost:9000 (timeout=30s, maxConn=100)
Production: 0.0.0.0:443 (timeout=60s, maxConn=100)

content.text: Each With* function is self-documenting: WithPort sets the port, WithTimeout sets the timeout. You only specify what you want to change. Defaults handle everything else. Options can be applied in any order.
Validation in Options
Options can validate their inputs. Return an error from the option, and let the constructor collect and return any errors. This keeps validation close to the option being validated.

content.output:
$ go run options_validation.go
Server: port=9000, timeout=30
Invalid port error: invalid port: 70000
Invalid timeout error: timeout must be positive

content.text: Now NewServer can fail if any option is invalid. The error message is specific to what went wrong. This pattern is used by database drivers, HTTP clients, and many other production Go packages.
Example: HTTP Server

content.output:
$ go run http_options.go
Development:
Starting server on :8080
  Read timeout: 5s
  Write timeout: 10s

Production:
Starting server on :443
  Read timeout: 30s
  Write timeout: 1m0s
  Logging: enabled

content.text: The development server uses all defaults. The production server overrides specific values. Each call is readable and self-documenting. This is how real Go applications configure servers, clients, and other complex objects.

content.title: When to Use Functional Options
content.message: Use functional options when: you have 3+ configuration parameters, most have sensible defaults, the configuration is optional, or you expect to add more options later. For simple cases with 1-2 parameters, regular function parameters are fine.

content.text: The functional options pattern is a cornerstone of Go API design. It provides clear, extensible, optional configuration without sacrificing type safety. You'll see it throughout the Go ecosystem, from database drivers to testing frameworks.

Go doesn't have constructors in the traditional sense. There's no special syntax that runs automatically when you create a struct. Instead, Go uses a convention: functions named NewTypeName that return initialized instances. This explicit approach is actually more flexible than magic constructors.

This section covers the common constructor patterns in Go: simple constructors, factory functions, builders for complex objects, and when to use each. These patterns ensure your types are always created in a valid state.
The NewXxx Convention

By convention, a constructor function is named New followed by the type name. NewServer creates a Server, NewClient creates a Client. If a package exports only one type, the constructor is often just called New.

content.output:
$ go run new_convention.go
ID: user_1234567890123456789
Name: Alice
Email: alice@example.com
Created: 06 Sep 26 10:30 IST

content.text: NewUser handles details the caller shouldn't worry about: generating the ID and setting the creation time. The caller just provides the business-relevant data. This ensures every User has a valid ID and timestamp.
Constructors with Validation
Constructors can validate inputs and return errors. This prevents invalid objects from ever being created. The pattern is: return (*Type, error) and check inputs before creating the struct.

content.output:
$ go run validated_constructor.go
Created: alice (alice@example.com) with balance 100
Bad email: invalid email format: not-an-email
Bad username: username must be at least 3 characters
Bad balance: initial balance cannot be negative

content.text: Every validation happens at construction time. If you have an Account, you know it has a valid username, a valid email, and a non-negative balance. Invalid states are impossible because the constructor rejects them.
Factory Functions

A factory function returns an interface instead of a concrete type. This is useful when you have multiple implementations and want to choose at runtime, or when you want to hide implementation details from callers.

content.output:
$ go run factory.go
Memory: hello
[FileStorage] Would save to /data/key2
[FileStorage] Would load from /data/key2
File: file data

content.text: NewStorage returns Storage, not *MemoryStorage or *FileStorage. Callers work with the interface and don't depend on implementation details. You can add new storage types without changing calling code.
The Builder Pattern

For complex objects with many optional fields, the builder pattern provides a fluent API. Each method sets one field and returns the builder, allowing method chaining. Call Build() at the end to get the final object.

content.output:
$ go run builder.go
SELECT name, email FROM users WHERE active = true ORDER BY name LIMIT 10
SELECT * FROM products WHERE price > 100

content.text: The builder pattern makes complex object construction readable. Each method does one thing and returns the builder for chaining. Build() creates the final object. This is ideal for DSLs, query builders, and configuration objects.
Choosing the Right Pattern

items.label: Simple Constructor (New*)
items.description: Use for most cases. Takes required parameters, returns pointer and optionally error. Best when there are few, clear parameters.

items.label: Functional Options
items.description: Use when you have many optional parameters with defaults. Self-documenting, extensible. Good for configuration-heavy types.

items.label: Factory Function
items.description: Use when returning an interface. Hides implementation, enables runtime selection between implementations.

items.label: Builder Pattern
items.description: Use for complex objects with many optional parts. Fluent API with method chaining. Good for DSLs and query builders.

content.title: Start Simple
content.message: Begin with a simple NewX constructor. Only move to functional options or builders when the simple approach becomes awkward. Premature abstraction adds complexity without benefit.

content.text: Go's constructor patterns are explicit and flexible. Use simple constructors for most cases, functional options for complex configuration, factories for interface-based design, and builders for fluent APIs. The right choice depends on your specific needs.

SOLID is a set of five design principles that help create maintainable, flexible software. Originally formulated for object-oriented programming, these principles apply to Go, though sometimes in different ways than in Java or C++.

Go's design naturally encourages some SOLID principles. Small interfaces support Interface Segregation. Implicit interface satisfaction enables Dependency Inversion. But understanding the principles explicitly helps you make better design decisions, especially when building larger systems.
The Five SOLID Principles

SOLID is an acronym for five principles: Single Responsibility, Open-Closed, Liskov Substitution, Interface Segregation, and Dependency Inversion. Each addresses a specific aspect of software design that, when violated, leads to code that's hard to change and test.

content.code:
S - Single Responsibility Principle (SRP)
    A type should have only one reason to change.
    In Go: One struct/package = one job.

O - Open-Closed Principle (OCP)
    Open for extension, closed for modification.
    In Go: Use interfaces to add behavior without changing existing code.

L - Liskov Substitution Principle (LSP)
    Subtypes must be substitutable for their base types.
    In Go: Any implementation of an interface must honor its contract.

I - Interface Segregation Principle (ISP)
    Clients shouldn't depend on methods they don't use.
    In Go: Keep interfaces small (1-3 methods).

D - Dependency Inversion Principle (DIP)
    Depend on abstractions, not concretions.
    In Go: Accept interfaces, return structs.

content.text: Go's Natural Alignment with SOLID

Go's design makes some SOLID principles easier to follow than in traditional OOP languages. There's no inheritance to create tight coupling. Interfaces are implicit, so you can define them where they're used. The standard library models small, focused interfaces.

items.label: Easier in Go
items.description: Interface Segregation (small interfaces are idiomatic), Dependency Inversion (implicit interfaces), Open-Closed (interfaces enable extension)

items.label: Requires Attention
items.description: Single Responsibility (still need discipline), Liskov Substitution (behavioral contracts must be honored)

content.text: When SOLID Helps

SOLID principles shine when building systems that need to evolve over time. They help when you have multiple implementations of behavior, when you need to test components in isolation, or when different teams work on different parts of the system.

For small scripts or simple CRUD applications, strict SOLID adherence can be overkill. The goal is maintainability, not principle purity. Apply SOLID where it reduces complexity, not where it adds it.

content.title: SOLID is Not Dogma
content.message: Don't create interfaces for every type or split every function for 'single responsibility.' These principles are guidelines for managing complexity, not rules to follow blindly. Simple code that works is better than complex code that's 'correct.'

content.text: Preview: SOLID in Go

In the following sections, we'll explore each principle with Go-specific examples. You'll see how SRP applies to packages, how OCP works with interfaces, why LSP matters for behavioral contracts, how Go's small interfaces embody ISP, and how DIP enables testable code.

content.title: The Go Philosophy
content.message: Go favors simplicity over cleverness. When applying SOLID, ask: does this make the code simpler to understand and change? If not, reconsider. The best Go code is obvious, not abstract.

content.text: The Single Responsibility Principle (SRP) says that a type should have only one reason to change. The Open-Closed Principle (OCP) says that software should be open for extension but closed for modification. Together, these principles create code that's focused and adaptable.
Single Responsibility Principle

Imagine a UserService that handles user registration, sends welcome emails, logs activity, and generates reports. When the email format changes, you modify UserService. When logging requirements change, you modify UserService. When report format changes, you modify it again. Every change risks breaking unrelated functionality.
SRP says each type should have one job. A UserRepository handles data access. An EmailSender handles emails. A Logger handles logging. Each can change independently without affecting the others.

content.output:
$ go run srp_violation.go
Sending welcome email to alice@example.com...
LOG: User Alice registered
REPORT: Total users: 1

content.text: This works, but it's fragile. Changing the email format requires modifying UserService. Testing user registration without sending real emails is difficult. Let's refactor to follow SRP.

content.output:
$ go run srp_correct.go
Sending welcome email to alice@example.com...
LOG: User Alice registered
Total users: 1

content.text: Now each type has one job. UserRepository manages data. EmailSender sends emails. Logger logs. UserService orchestrates but delegates. You can change email logic without touching data logic. You can test UserService with a mock EmailSender.
SRP at the Package Level

In Go, SRP applies to packages too. A package should have one clear purpose. The net/http package handles HTTP. The encoding/json package handles JSON. Mixing unrelated functionality in one package makes it hard to understand and maintain.

content.code:
Good package structure (SRP applied):

myapp/
├── user/           # User domain logic
│   ├── user.go     # User type and methods
│   ├── repository.go
│   └── service.go
├── email/          # Email sending
│   └── sender.go
├── auth/           # Authentication
│   ├── token.go
│   └── middleware.go
└── http/           # HTTP handlers
    └── handlers.go

Bad: One giant 'utils' package with everything.

content.text: Open-Closed Principle
OCP says software should be open for extension but closed for modification. You should be able to add new behavior without changing existing code. In Go, interfaces are the key to achieving this.

Imagine a payment system that supports credit cards. When you need to add PayPal, you shouldn't modify the existing credit card code. Instead, define an interface that both implement. New payment methods extend the system without modifying it.

content.output:
$ go run ocp_example.go
Processing with Credit Card...
Charging $99.99 to card ending in 1234
Payment successful!

Processing with PayPal...
Charging $99.99 to PayPal account user@example.com
Payment successful!

Processing with Crypto...
Sending $99.99 to wallet 0x123abc
Payment successful!

content.text: Adding Crypto didn't require changing CreditCard, PayPal, or Checkout. The system is closed for modification (existing code unchanged) but open for extension (new payment methods can be added). This is OCP in action.

content.title: Interfaces Enable OCP
content.message: When you find yourself adding if/else or switch cases for new types, that's a sign you're violating OCP. Extract an interface, and each type becomes its own implementation that can evolve independently.

content.text: Combining SRP and OCP

SRP and OCP work together. When types have single responsibilities, they're easier to extend without modification. When new behavior is added through new types rather than changes to existing types, single responsibility is preserved.

items.label: SRP Violation Signs
items.description: Large structs with many methods. Methods that don't use most fields. Frequent changes for unrelated reasons.

items.label: OCP Violation Signs
items.description: Switch statements that grow with new types. Functions with type assertions for behavior. Changes to existing code when adding features.

content.text: SRP keeps your code focused. OCP keeps it stable. Together, they create systems where new features are new code, not changes to working code. This reduces bugs and makes testing easier.

The Liskov Substitution Principle (LSP) says that if you have a function that works with a type T, it should also work correctly with any subtype of T. The Interface Segregation Principle (ISP) says that clients shouldn't be forced to depend on methods they don't use. In Go, these principles shape how we design and use interfaces.
Liskov Substitution Principle

LSP is about behavioral contracts. If your code expects an io.Reader, any type implementing io.Reader should work. But it's not just about having the right method signatures. The behavior must be compatible too.

The classic LSP violation is the Square-Rectangle problem. A Square could inherit from Rectangle since a square is a rectangle mathematically. But if SetWidth and SetHeight are separate methods, a Square can't implement them correctly because changing width must also change height.

content.output:
$ go run lsp_violation.go
Rectangle before: 5x10 = 50
Rectangle after: 5x10 = 50
Square before: side=5, area=25
Square after: side=10, area=100

content.text: The Square doesn't behave like a Rectangle. When DoubleWidth sets width and height independently, Rectangle works as expected but Square breaks the contract. This is why LSP matters: substituting Square for Rectangle produces wrong results.
LSP Compliant Design

The fix is to design interfaces around actual behavior, not inheritance hierarchies. Both rectangles and squares have areas, but they don't share the same setting behavior. Make the interface match what clients actually need.

content.output:
$ go run lsp_correct.go
main.Rectangle: area = 50
main.Square: area = 16
main.Circle: area = 27
Total area: 93

content.text: Now all shapes are truly substitutable. The interface only requires Area(), which all shapes implement correctly. No shape has to pretend to be something it's not. This is LSP-compliant design.
Interface Segregation Principle

ISP says don't force clients to depend on methods they don't use. A function that only reads shouldn't require a type that can also write. Go's standard library embodies this with io.Reader (just Read), io.Writer (just Write), and io.ReadWriter (both).

Fat interfaces are the opposite. If an interface has 10 methods but most callers only use 2, that's a violation. Every implementer must provide all 10 methods, even if some are meaningless for that type.

content.output:
$ go run isp_violation.go
cached: key1

content.text: ReadOnlyCache must implement 8 methods just to provide Read. Seven of them panic because they don't make sense. This is ISP violation: the interface is too fat.
ISP Compliant Design
Break fat interfaces into small, focused ones. Each client depends only on what it needs. Implementers only provide what makes sense for them.

content.output:
$ go run isp_correct.go
Data: cached value
Data: new record

content.text: Now ReadOnlyCache only implements Reader. Database implements Reader, Writer, and Deleter. FetchData accepts Reader, so both work. No panic methods, no wasted implementations.

content.title: Go's io Package is ISP
content.message: Study io.Reader, io.Writer, io.Closer, and their compositions like io.ReadCloser. This is ISP in practice: tiny interfaces combined as needed. Most functions accept the smallest interface that works.

items.label: LSP Violations
items.description: Substituting a type breaks behavior. Methods panic or return dummy values. Callers need type checks to handle special cases.

items.label: ISP Violations
items.description: Interfaces with 5+ methods. Implementers have panic/no-op methods. Functions depend on interfaces they barely use.

content.text: LSP ensures implementations honor contracts. ISP ensures interfaces stay small. Together, they create substitutable types that don't burden implementers. In Go, think: small interfaces that reflect actual behavior, not theoretical hierarchies.

The Dependency Inversion Principle (DIP) says high-level modules shouldn't depend on low-level modules; both should depend on abstractions. Dependency Injection (DI) is a technique to achieve this by passing dependencies in rather than creating them internally. Together, they create flexible, testable code.
The Problem: Tight Coupling

When a struct creates its own dependencies internally, it's tightly coupled to those specific implementations. You can't swap in a different database, use a mock for testing, or reuse the code in a different context.

content.output:
$ go run dip_violation.go
MySQL result for: SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = 123

content.text: UserService is welded to MySQLDatabase. Testing requires a real MySQL connection. Switching to PostgreSQL means changing UserService code. This violates DIP: high-level UserService depends directly on low-level MySQLDatabase.
The Solution: Depend on Abstractions

Define an interface for what you need. The high-level module depends on the interface. The low-level module implements the interface. Neither depends on the other directly; both depend on the abstraction.

content.output:
$ go run dip_correct.go
MySQL: SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = 123
PostgreSQL: SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = 456

content.text: Now UserService depends on Database (interface), not MySQLDatabase (concrete). We inject the dependency via the constructor. Switching databases is just passing a different implementation. UserService code never changes.
Dependency Injection for Testing
The biggest benefit of DI is testability. You can inject mock implementations that behave exactly as your test needs. No real databases, no network calls, no external services.

content.output:
$ go run di_testing.go
SMTP: Sending to user@example.com via smtp.example.com

Mock recorded:
 - test1@example.com: Notification
 - test2@example.com: Notification

content.text: MockSender records calls instead of sending emails. Tests can verify the right emails would be sent without actually sending them. This is why DI is essential for testing: you can inject behavior that suits each test case.
Constructor vs Method Injection

Constructor injection passes dependencies when creating the object. Method injection passes them to individual methods. Constructor injection is more common because the dependency is available for all methods.

content.output:
$ go run injection_types.go
LOG: ServiceA doing work
LOG: ServiceA doing more
LOG: ServiceB doing work

items.label: Constructor Injection
items.description: Pass in NewX(). Available to all methods. Use for dependencies needed throughout the object's lifetime.

items.label: Method Injection
items.description: Pass to each method call. Use when different calls need different implementations, or the dependency is optional.

content.text: Consumer-Defined Interfaces
In Go, the interface should be defined where it's used (by the consumer), not where it's implemented (by the provider). This is the opposite of Java-style interfaces and is key to Go's flexibility.

content.output:
$ go run consumer_interface.go
Processing: data for 123

content.text: We only need GetData, so we define an interface with just that method. ExternalService has many methods, but we don't depend on them. This is DIP + ISP combined: depend on a minimal abstraction that we define.

content.title: Accept Interfaces, Return Structs
content.message: Functions should accept interfaces (flexibility) and return concrete types (clarity). This lets callers pass any compatible implementation while knowing exactly what they receive.

content.title: Avoid Interface Pollution
content.message: Don't create interfaces for everything. An interface with only one implementation adds complexity without benefit. Create interfaces when you have multiple implementations or need to mock for testing.

content.text: Testing with Dependency Injection
DI's biggest benefit is testability. When dependencies are injected, tests can provide mock implementations that control behavior and verify interactions without external systems.

content.output:
$ go test -v di_test.go
=== RUN   TestUserService_UpdateEmail
=== RUN   TestUserService_UpdateEmail/successful_update
=== RUN   TestUserService_UpdateEmail/user_not_found
=== RUN   TestUserService_UpdateEmail/save_fails
--- PASS: TestUserService_UpdateEmail (0.00s)
    --- PASS: TestUserService_UpdateEmail/successful_update (0.00s)
    --- PASS: TestUserService_UpdateEmail/user_not_found (0.00s)
    --- PASS: TestUserService_UpdateEmail/save_fails (0.00s)
PASS
ok      command-line-arguments  0.002s

content.text: MockUserRepo implements UserRepository with configurable behavior. It records all calls for verification and can simulate errors. The tests cover success, not-found, and save-failure cases, all without touching a real database. This is the power of DI: your business logic is completely decoupled from infrastructure.

DIP and DI create loosely coupled, testable code. Depend on interfaces, inject implementations, define interfaces where used. This is how professional Go code achieves flexibility without sacrificing clarity.

Creational patterns control how objects are created. They hide the creation logic, making systems more flexible about what gets created, how, and when. Go's approach to these patterns differs from traditional OOP because there's no inheritance or constructors.
Factory Pattern

The Factory pattern creates objects without specifying the exact type. A factory function returns an interface, letting you swap implementations without changing client code. This is one of the most natural patterns in Go because interfaces are implicit.

Imagine you're building a notification system that sends alerts via email, SMS, or push notifications. Without a factory, every caller would need to know about all notification types. With a factory, callers just request a notifier by name.

content.output:
$ go run factory.go
Email to user@example.com: Server is down!
SMS to +1234567890: Server is down!
Push to device device-abc-123: Server is down!

content.text: The factory returns Notifier (interface), not the concrete types. Clients never import or mention EmailNotifier, SMSNotifier, or PushNotifier. Adding a new notification type means adding a case to the factory, not changing every caller.
Abstract Factory

An Abstract Factory creates families of related objects. Use it when you need to create multiple related types that must work together. In Go, this is typically an interface with multiple factory methods.

content.output:
$ go run abstract_factory.go
Light theme:
Button: [Light Button]
Checkbox: [ ] Light Checkbox

Dark theme:
Button: {{Dark Button}}
Checkbox: [X] Dark Checkbox

content.text: RenderUI works with any UIFactory. Light and dark components are guaranteed to be consistent within their family. Adding a new theme means creating a new factory, not changing RenderUI.
Builder Pattern

The Builder pattern constructs complex objects step by step. It's useful when an object has many optional fields or when the construction process has multiple steps. In Go, builders often use method chaining.

Consider building an HTTP request. You might need to set the method, URL, headers, body, timeout, and retry policy. A constructor with all these parameters would be unwieldy. A builder lets you set only what you need.

content.output:
$ go run builder.go
Simple request:
GET https://api.example.com/users
  Timeout: 30s, Retries: 3

Complex request:
POST https://api.example.com/orders
  Content-Type: application/json
  Authorization: Bearer token123
  Body: {"item": "widget", "qty": 5}
  Timeout: 10s, Retries: 5

content.text: Method chaining (each method returns *RequestBuilder) creates a fluent API. Callers set only what they need. Defaults handle common cases. Build() returns the final immutable object.

content.title: Builder vs Functional Options
content.message: Both patterns solve the many-parameters problem. Builders are better for complex construction with validation between steps. Functional options are better for simple configuration. Go libraries use both; choose what fits your use case.

content.text: Singleton Pattern

The Singleton pattern ensures a type has only one instance. In Go, this is typically done with package-level variables and sync.Once for thread-safe initialization. Use singletons sparingly; they can make testing harder.

content.output:
$ go run singleton.go
Initializing config (this happens only once)
Goroutine 4: MaxConns = 10
Goroutine 0: MaxConns = 10
Goroutine 1: MaxConns = 10
Goroutine 2: MaxConns = 10
Goroutine 3: MaxConns = 10
Same instance? true

content.text: sync.Once ensures the initialization function runs exactly once, even when called from multiple goroutines simultaneously. This is Go's idiomatic way to create singletons, avoiding the double-checked locking bugs common in other languages.

content.title: Singleton Drawbacks
content.message: Singletons make testing harder because you can't easily replace them with mocks. Consider passing dependencies explicitly (dependency injection) instead. Use singletons only for truly global state like configuration or logging.

items.label: Factory
items.description: Use when you need to create objects without exposing creation logic. Return interfaces. Best for: plugin systems, driver selection.

items.label: Builder
items.description: Use when objects have many optional fields or complex construction. Method chaining creates fluent APIs. Best for: requests, configs, queries.

items.label: Singleton
items.description: Use when exactly one instance should exist. Use sync.Once. Best for: configs, loggers, connection pools. Avoid for testability concerns.

content.text: Creational patterns in Go are simpler than in Java or C++. There's no inheritance, so factory hierarchies flatten. Constructors don't exist, so builders feel natural. Package-level variables with sync.Once replace complex singleton machinery.
Testing Creational Patterns
Factories that return interfaces are easy to test because you can verify the returned type and behavior. Builders can be tested by checking that the built object has the expected configuration.

content.output:
$ go test -v creational_test.go
=== RUN   TestFactory_ReturnsCorrectType
=== RUN   TestFactory_ReturnsCorrectType/email_notifier
=== RUN   TestFactory_ReturnsCorrectType/sms_notifier
--- PASS: TestFactory_ReturnsCorrectType (0.00s)
    --- PASS: TestFactory_ReturnsCorrectType/email_notifier (0.00s)
    --- PASS: TestFactory_ReturnsCorrectType/sms_notifier (0.00s)
=== RUN   TestFactory_UnknownType
--- PASS: TestFactory_UnknownType (0.00s)
=== RUN   TestBuilder_Defaults
--- PASS: TestBuilder_Defaults (0.00s)
=== RUN   TestBuilder_CustomConfig
--- PASS: TestBuilder_CustomConfig (0.00s)
PASS
ok      command-line-arguments  0.002s

content.text: Factory tests verify the correct type is returned and behaves as expected. Builder tests verify default values and that custom configuration is applied. The interface-based factory is particularly testable because we can verify behavior, not just type.

sections.title: Structural Patterns: Adapter, Decorator, Facade, Proxy

content.text: Structural patterns deal with how types are composed to form larger structures. They help you combine objects and classes into flexible, efficient structures. Go's embedding and interfaces make several structural patterns particularly elegant.
Adapter Pattern

The Adapter pattern makes incompatible interfaces work together. You have an existing type with one interface, but you need it to satisfy a different interface. An adapter wraps the existing type and translates calls.
Imagine you're using a third-party logging library that has its own interface, but your application expects the standard library's log interface. An adapter bridges the gap without modifying either.

content.output:
$ go run adapter.go
[MyApp] INFO: Starting work
[MyApp] INFO: Work completed

content.text: LoggerAdapter wraps ThirdPartyLogger and implements Logger. Your application code never knows it's using a third-party library. If you switch logging libraries, only the adapter changes.
Decorator Pattern

The Decorator pattern adds behavior to objects dynamically without changing their interface. Decorators wrap objects and add functionality before or after delegating to the wrapped object. In Go, embedding makes decorators clean.
Consider an HTTP handler that needs logging, authentication, and rate limiting. Instead of one giant handler, you can stack decorators that each add one concern.

content.output:
$ go run decorator.go
=== Request 1 ===
RATE: Request 1 of 2
AUTH: Checking credentials...
LOG: Incoming request: GET /users
LOG: Response: Processed: GET /users
Result: Processed: GET /users

=== Request 2 ===
RATE: Request 2 of 2
AUTH: Checking credentials...
LOG: Incoming request: GET /orders
LOG: Response: Processed: GET /orders
Result: Processed: GET /orders

=== Request 3 ===
Result: ERROR: Rate limit exceeded

content.text: Each decorator adds one concern. The order matters: rate limiting happens first, then auth, then logging. Request 3 is rejected by the rate limiter before reaching auth or logging. You can add, remove, or reorder decorators without changing any of them.

content.title: HTTP Middleware is Decoration
content.message: Go's http.Handler middleware pattern is the Decorator pattern. Middleware wraps handlers to add logging, auth, CORS, compression, etc. The func(http.Handler) http.Handler signature is the decorator factory.

content.text: Facade Pattern
The Facade pattern provides a simplified interface to a complex subsystem. Instead of exposing many classes with many methods, you expose one type with a few methods that orchestrate the subsystem.

Imagine a video conversion system with separate components for reading files, decoding video, encoding to new format, compressing, and writing output. A facade hides this complexity behind a simple Convert method.

content.output:
$ go run facade.go
Converting vacation.avi to vacation.mp4...
  Reading video file: vacation.avi
  Decoding video frames...
  Encoding to h264 format...
  Compressing at quality 80...
  Writing output: vacation.mp4
Conversion complete!

content.text: VideoConverter orchestrates five subsystem components. Clients call one method instead of coordinating five. The subsystem can change internally without affecting clients. Advanced users can still access individual components if needed.
Proxy Pattern

The Proxy pattern provides a surrogate for another object to control access to it. Proxies can add lazy initialization, access control, logging, or caching. The proxy implements the same interface as the real object.

content.output:
$ go run proxy.go
Created proxy for photo1.jpg (not loaded yet)
Created proxy for photo2.jpg (not loaded yet)
Created proxy for photo3.jpg (not loaded yet)

Displaying first image:
Loading photo1.jpg from disk...
[Image data for photo1.jpg]

Displaying first image again:
[Image data for photo1.jpg]

content.text: ImageProxy defers expensive loading until Display is called. Three proxies are created instantly. Only photo1.jpg is loaded (when displayed). The second Display call returns immediately since the image is already loaded. Images 2 and 3 are never loaded.

items.label: Adapter
items.description: Makes incompatible interfaces compatible. Wraps existing code to match expected interface. Use when integrating third-party libraries.

items.label: Decorator
items.description: Adds behavior without changing interface. Stackable. Use for cross-cutting concerns like logging, auth, metrics.

items.label: Facade
items.description: Simplifies complex subsystem. Provides high-level API. Use when hiding complexity from clients.

items.label: Proxy
items.description: Controls access to object. Same interface as real object. Use for lazy loading, caching, access control.

content.text: Structural patterns compose types into larger structures. Adapter translates interfaces. Decorator adds behavior. Facade simplifies. Proxy controls access. Go's implicit interfaces make all of these patterns straightforward to implement.
Testing Structural Patterns
Decorators and adapters are highly testable because they work through interfaces. You can test decorators by wrapping mock objects and verifying both delegation and added behavior.

content.output:
$ go test -v structural_test.go
=== RUN   TestLoggingDecorator
--- PASS: TestLoggingDecorator (0.00s)
=== RUN   TestValidatingDecorator
=== RUN   TestValidatingDecorator/valid_input
=== RUN   TestValidatingDecorator/input_too_short
=== RUN   TestValidatingDecorator/exact_length
--- PASS: TestValidatingDecorator (0.00s)
    --- PASS: TestValidatingDecorator/valid_input (0.00s)
    --- PASS: TestValidatingDecorator/input_too_short (0.00s)
    --- PASS: TestValidatingDecorator/exact_length (0.00s)
=== RUN   TestDecoratorChaining
--- PASS: TestDecoratorChaining (0.00s)
PASS
ok      command-line-arguments  0.002s

content.text: MockProcessor lets us test each decorator in isolation: verify it delegates correctly and adds its behavior. The chaining test shows how decorators compose. Testing validates both the added behavior and the delegation to the wrapped component.

sections.title: Behavioral Patterns: Strategy, Observer, Command, Template Method

content.text: Behavioral patterns focus on how objects communicate and share responsibilities. They define the patterns of communication between objects. Go's interfaces and first-class functions make behavioral patterns particularly expressive.
Strategy Pattern

The Strategy pattern defines a family of algorithms and makes them interchangeable. The algorithm varies independently from clients that use it. In Go, strategies are typically interfaces with one method, and you can use either struct implementations or function types.

Imagine a payment system that needs to support multiple payment methods. Each method has different processing logic. The Strategy pattern lets you swap payment methods without changing the checkout code.

content.output:
$ go run strategy.go
Cart total: $1029.98

Paid $1029.98 with credit card ending in 1234
Paid $1029.98 via PayPal (user@example.com)
Paid $1029.98 in crypto to 0x123456...

content.text: ShoppingCart doesn't know how payment works. It just calls Pay on whatever strategy is set. Adding a new payment method means creating a new strategy struct, not modifying ShoppingCart.
Strategy with Functions
For simple strategies with one method, Go's function types offer a lighter alternative. Instead of defining struct types, you can pass functions directly.

content.output:
$ go run strategy_func.go
Original: [-5 2 -8 1 9 -3]
Ascending: [-8 -5 -3 1 2 9]
Descending: [9 2 1 -3 -5 -8]
By absolute: [1 2 -3 -5 -8 9]
Odds first: [-5 -3 1 9 -8 2]

content.text: Function strategies are lighter when no state is needed. You can pass named functions or inline anonymous functions. This is idiomatic Go, taking advantage of first-class functions.
Observer Pattern

The Observer pattern defines a one-to-many dependency. When one object changes state, all its dependents are notified automatically. This is useful for event systems, UI updates, and publish-subscribe scenarios.

Imagine a stock price tracker. Multiple components (UI, alerts, logging) need to know when prices change. The Observer pattern lets the price tracker notify all interested parties without knowing who they are.

content.output:
$ go run observer.go
=== AAPL Update ===
[Main Screen] AAPL: $145.50
LOG: Price update - AAPL = 145.50

=== AAPL Update ===
[Main Screen] AAPL: $152.30
ALERT: AAPL exceeded $150.00 (now $152.30)
LOG: Price update - AAPL = 152.30

=== GOOG Update ===
[Main Screen] GOOG: $140.00
LOG: Price update - GOOG = 140.00
