content.text: StockTicker doesn't know about displays, alerts, or loggers. It just notifies all subscribers. Adding a new observer type doesn't require changing StockTicker. The second AAPL update triggers the alert because it exceeds the threshold.

content.title: Channels as Observers
content.message: In Go, you often use channels instead of the Observer pattern. Channels provide type-safe, concurrent communication. The Observer pattern is still useful when you need synchronous notification or when observers have different interfaces.

content.text: Command Pattern

The Command pattern encapsulates a request as an object. This lets you parameterize clients with different requests, queue requests, log them, or support undo operations. Commands decouple the invoker from the receiver.
Imagine a text editor with undo/redo. Each editing operation (insert, delete, replace) is a command object. The editor executes commands and can reverse them by calling Undo.

content.output:
$ go run command.go
Executed: Insert 'Hello'
Content: 'Hello'

Executed: Insert ' World'
Content: 'Hello World'

Executed: Delete 6 chars
Content: 'Hello'

--- Undo twice ---
Undone: Delete 6 chars
Content: 'Hello World'
Undone: Insert ' World'
Content: 'Hello'

--- Redo ---
Redone: Insert ' World'
Content: 'Hello World'

content.text: Each command stores what it needs for both Execute and Undo. DeleteCommand saves the deleted text so Undo can restore it. The Editor manages history without knowing command details. This pattern enables undo/redo, macros, and command logging.
Template Method Pattern
The Template Method pattern defines the skeleton of an algorithm in a base type, deferring some steps to subtypes. In Go without inheritance, we use composition and interfaces to achieve this.

content.output:
$ go run template.go
=== CSV Pipeline ===
Step 1: Extract
  Extracted 3 records
Step 2: Transform
  Transformed to 3 records
Step 3: Validate
  Validation passed
Step 4: Load
  Loaded 3 records to warehouse

=== API Pipeline ===
Step 1: Extract
  Extracted 2 records
Step 2: Transform
  Transformed to 2 records
Step 3: Validate
  Validation passed
Step 4: Load
  Loaded 2 records to warehouse

content.text: DataPipeline defines the algorithm structure (extract, transform, validate, load). DataMiner interface defines the variable parts. CSVMiner and APIMiner provide different implementations. The template (Run method) is fixed; the steps are pluggable.

items.label: Strategy
items.description: Interchangeable algorithms for one step. Client chooses algorithm. Use when you need multiple ways to do one thing.

items.label: Observer
items.description: One-to-many notification. Subject notifies observers on state change. Use for event systems, reactive updates.

items.label: Command
items.description: Encapsulates request as object. Enables undo, queuing, logging. Use when you need operation history or scheduling.

items.label: Template Method
items.description: Fixed algorithm skeleton with variable steps. Use when algorithm structure is fixed but steps vary.

content.text: Testing Behavioral Patterns

Behavioral patterns are highly testable because they depend on interfaces. You can inject mock strategies, fake observers, and stub commands. This demonstrates why good design and testability go hand in hand.

content.output:
$ go test -v strategy_test.go
=== RUN   TestCheckout_CalculatesTotal
=== RUN   TestCheckout_CalculatesTotal/single_item
=== RUN   TestCheckout_CalculatesTotal/multiple_items
=== RUN   TestCheckout_CalculatesTotal/empty_cart
--- PASS: TestCheckout_CalculatesTotal (0.00s)
    --- PASS: TestCheckout_CalculatesTotal/single_item (0.00s)
    --- PASS: TestCheckout_CalculatesTotal/multiple_items (0.00s)
    --- PASS: TestCheckout_CalculatesTotal/empty_cart (0.00s)
=== RUN   TestCheckout_PropagatesError
--- PASS: TestCheckout_PropagatesError (0.00s)
=== RUN   TestCheckout_ReturnsMessage
--- PASS: TestCheckout_ReturnsMessage (0.00s)
PASS
ok      command-line-arguments  0.002s

content.text: Notice we test the Checkout logic without any real payment processing. MockPayment records all calls and returns whatever we configure. This is Dependency Inversion in action: by depending on an interface, we can test business logic in complete isolation. No mocking framework needed, just a struct implementing the interface.

Behavioral patterns manage communication and responsibility. Strategy selects algorithms. Observer broadcasts events. Command captures operations. Template Method fixes structure. Go's interfaces and functions make these patterns natural to implement.

Low-Level Design (LLD) is the process of designing the internal structure of a system. While High-Level Design (HLD) defines components and their interactions, LLD specifies classes, interfaces, methods, and data structures. LLD questions are common in technical interviews and essential for writing maintainable code.
The LLD Process

A systematic approach to LLD helps you handle any design problem. Start by clarifying requirements, then identify entities, define relationships, design interfaces, and finally implement. Each step builds on the previous one.

content.code:
LLD Design Process

1. Clarify Requirements
   - What are the core features? (functional requirements)
   - What are the constraints? (non-functional requirements)
   - What's out of scope?

2. Identify Core Entities
   - What are the main objects/actors?
   - What data does each entity hold?
   - What operations does each entity perform?

3. Define Relationships
   - How do entities interact?
   - Is it one-to-one, one-to-many, many-to-many?
   - Who owns whom?

4. Design Interfaces
   - What behavior should be abstracted?
   - Where do we need flexibility for future changes?
   - What are the public APIs?

5. Apply Design Patterns
   - Which patterns solve the problems we've identified?
   - Don't force patterns; use them where they fit.

6. Consider Edge Cases
   - Concurrency? Thread safety?
   - Error handling?
   - Capacity limits?

7. Implement and Verify
   - Start simple, add complexity as needed.
   - Walk through a scenario to verify logic works.
   - Test early and often.

content.title: Interview Time Budget
content.message: LLD interviews typically run 45-60 minutes. For a 45-min round: Requirements (5 min), Entities (5 min), Class Design (15 min), Implementation (15 min), Extensions (5 min). For 60 min, expand Class Design and Implementation by 5-7 min each. Don't spend too long on setup or you'll run out of time for the interesting parts.

content.text: Requirements Gathering

Before writing any code, understand what you're building. In interviews, ask clarifying questions. In real projects, work with stakeholders. Split requirements into functional (what it does) and non-functional (how well it does it). Focus on four themes: primary capabilities (what operations must exist), rules and completion (success/failure conditions), error handling (invalid inputs), and scope boundaries (what's explicitly out).

content.code:
Example: Design an In-Memory Cache

Functional Requirements:
  1. Store key-value pairs
  2. Get value by key
  3. Delete key
  4. Support TTL (time-to-live) per entry
  5. Evict entries when capacity is reached (LRU)

Non-Functional Requirements:
  1. Thread-safe for concurrent access
  2. O(1) get/set operations
  3. Configurable maximum size
  4. Support for any value type (interface{})

Out of Scope:
  - Persistence to disk
  - Distributed caching
  - Cache invalidation callbacks

Key Questions to Ask:
  - What's the expected QPS (queries per second)?
  - What's the typical key/value size?
  - Should expired entries be cleaned proactively or lazily?
  - Is the cache shared across goroutines?

content.text: Entity Identification

Extract nouns from requirements. They often become structs. Look for actors (who uses the system), resources (what the system manages), and concepts (abstract ideas that need representation). Apply a simple filter: if something maintains changing state or enforces rules, it deserves to be its own struct. If it's just information attached to something else, it's probably a field on another struct.

content.output:
$ go run entities.go
Entry: user:123
Expired: false
Value: map[name:Alice]

content.text: Entry holds the cached data and metadata. Cache manages entries. EvictionPolicy is an interface because we might want different policies (LRU, LFU, FIFO). Starting with interfaces for variable behavior is key to flexible design.
Relationship Mapping

Draw relationships between entities. Use composition (has-a) rather than inheritance (is-a). In Go, this means embedding structs or holding references. Think about ownership: who creates, updates, and destroys each entity?

content.code:
Cache System Relationships

┌────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                     Cache                      │
│                                                │
│  ┌───────────┐      ┌───────────┐              │
│  │  entries  │─────▶│   Entry   │  (1:many)    │
│  │ map[k]*E  │      │ Key,Value │              │
│  └───────────┘      │ Timestamps│              │
│                     └───────────┘              │
│                                                │
│  ┌───────────┐                                 │
│  │  policy   │─────▶ EvictionPolicy (interface)│
│  └───────────┘             │                   │
│                      ┌─────┴─────┐             │
│                      │           │             │
│                     LRU         LFU            │
│                                                │
│  ┌───────────┐                                 │
│  │   mutex   │      (for thread safety)        │
│  └───────────┘                                 │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Ownership:
  - Cache OWNS entries (creates, updates, deletes them)
  - Cache USES policy (injected, doesn't create it)
  - Entry is self-contained (no external references)

content.text: Interface Design

Design interfaces based on how clients will use your system. Keep interfaces small and focused (Interface Segregation). Define them where they're used (consumer-defined interfaces). Think about what can change and abstract that.

content.output:
$ go run interfaces.go
Set name = Alice
Found: Alice
Not found
Cache size: 1

content.text: Small interfaces (Getter, Setter, Deleter) let functions accept only what they need. Composed interfaces (ReadWriter, Cache) combine them. Functions like readFromCache accept Getter because they don't need write access. This is Interface Segregation in practice.

content.title: Interview Strategy
content.message: In LLD interviews, verbalize your thought process. Start with requirements, sketch entities, discuss tradeoffs. A clear design process is as important as the final code. Ask clarifying questions to show you think about edge cases.

items.label: HLD (High-Level Design)
items.description: System architecture, component interactions, technology choices. Answers: what services exist and how they communicate.

items.label: LLD (Low-Level Design)
items.description: Class structure, interfaces, data structures, algorithms. Answers: how each component is implemented internally.

content.text: LLD bridges requirements and code. A good LLD makes implementation straightforward, testing easy, and future changes localized. The following sections apply this methodology to concrete problems.

Imagine you're building a social media feed. Every time a user opens the app, you fetch their profile, friend list, and recent posts from the database. The database query takes 50ms. With millions of users refreshing their feeds, your database is overwhelmed, response times spike to seconds, and users complain about a slow app.

Now imagine storing the most popular profiles in memory. Memory access takes microseconds, not milliseconds. When a celebrity's profile is requested 10,000 times per second, you hit the database once and serve the rest from memory. This is caching: trading memory for speed by keeping frequently accessed data close at hand.

But memory is finite. You can't store everything. When the cache fills up, which item do you remove to make room for new data? This decision is the eviction policy, and getting it right is the difference between a cache that helps and one that wastes memory on data nobody needs.
Why LRU?

LRU (Least Recently Used) eviction is based on a simple observation: if you haven't accessed something recently, you probably won't need it soon. Think of your browser tabs. The tab you used 5 minutes ago is more likely to be needed than the one you opened last week and forgot about. LRU captures this temporal locality pattern that appears everywhere in computing.

items.label: FIFO (First In First Out)
items.description: Remove oldest inserted item. Simple but ignores access patterns. A frequently used item inserted early gets evicted.

items.label: LRU (Least Recently Used)
items.description: Remove least recently accessed item. Captures temporal locality. Most common choice for general-purpose caches.

items.label: LFU (Least Frequently Used)
items.description: Remove item with lowest access count. Good for stable access patterns but slow to adapt to changes.

items.label: Random
items.description: Remove random item. Surprisingly effective and simple. No overhead tracking access patterns.

content.text: How LRU Works

Picture a stack of papers on your desk. Every time you use a document, you put it on top of the stack. When the stack gets too tall, you throw away papers from the bottom, the ones you haven't touched in ages. The paper on top is your most recently used (MRU), and the one at the bottom is your least recently used (LRU).

content.code:
LRU Cache Operations (capacity = 3)

Initial: empty cache

1. Set(A, 1)     [A] ← A is MRU and LRU

2. Set(B, 2)     [B, A] ← B is MRU, A is LRU

3. Set(C, 3)     [C, B, A] ← Full! C is MRU, A is LRU

4. Get(A)        [A, C, B] ← A accessed, moves to front
                             Now B is LRU

5. Set(D, 4)     [D, A, C] ← D added, B evicted (was LRU)
                  ↑
               B removed!

6. Get(C)        [C, D, A] ← C accessed, moves to front

Key insight: Get() updates recency, not just Set()

content.text: The challenge is making both operations fast. A simple list gives O(n) lookup. A hash map gives O(1) lookup but can't track order. The solution combines both: a hash map pointing to nodes in a doubly linked list. The hash map finds the node in O(1), and the linked list moves it to front in O(1).
Requirements

Before writing code, let's clarify what our cache needs to do. In an interview, this is where you ask questions: What operations are needed? How many concurrent users? What's the expected hit rate? For our cache, we'll support the standard operations plus two features that real systems need.

First, TTL (time-to-live) lets entries expire automatically. A user profile cached for 5 minutes stays fresh. Without TTL, you'd serve stale data indefinitely or need external invalidation logic. Second, thread safety is essential because web servers handle requests concurrently. Multiple goroutines will read and write the cache simultaneously.

content.code:
Functional Requirements:
  1. Get(key) - Retrieve value, return (value, found)
  2. Set(key, value) - Store key-value pair
  3. Delete(key) - Remove key
  4. TTL support - Entries expire after a duration
  5. LRU eviction when capacity reached

Non-Functional Requirements:
  1. O(1) Get and Set operations
  2. Thread-safe for concurrent access
  3. Configurable capacity

content.text: The O(1) requirement is critical. If Get takes O(n) time, the cache becomes a bottleneck instead of an optimization. This constraint drives our data structure choice: we need a hash map for O(1) key lookup, but a hash map alone can't track access order. We combine it with a doubly linked list.

content.code:
Data Structure: HashMap + Doubly Linked List

┌────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  Hash Map                 Doubly Linked List   │
│  ┌─────┐                                       │
│  │ k1  │───────────────────▶ [MRU]             │
│  ├─────┤                        ↕              │
│  │ k2  │───────────────────▶ [   ]             │
│  ├─────┤                        ↕              │
│  │ k3  │───────────────────▶ [LRU] ← evict     │
│  └─────┘                                       │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Why this combination?
  - HashMap: O(1) lookup by key
  - Doubly Linked List: O(1) move to front, O(1) remove from end
  - HashMap values point to list nodes, so we can:
    1. Find any node in O(1) via the map
    2. Move it to front in O(1) via list pointers
    3. Remove from back in O(1) for eviction

content.text: The hash map stores key-to-node pointers. When we access a key, we find its node in O(1), then move that node to the front of the list in O(1) using the doubly linked list's prev/next pointers. When we need to evict, we remove from the back in O(1). Go's container/list package provides a ready-made doubly linked list.
Implementation

Now let's translate our design into code. We'll build the cache in layers: first the entry struct that holds cached data, then the LRUCache struct that manages entries, and finally the public methods. The implementation uses Go's container/list package for the doubly linked list, so we don't need to implement list operations ourselves.

Pay attention to how each method maintains the LRU invariant: Get moves accessed items to front, Set adds new items at front and evicts from back, and both check TTL expiration. The mutex protects all shared state. We'll walk through the output to see the LRU behavior in action.

content.output:
$ go run lru_cache.go
After adding a, b, c: size=3
Got a=1
After adding d: size=3
  a: 1
  b: not found (evicted)
  c: 3
  d: 4

TTL demonstration:
Before expiry: temp=expires soon
After expiry: temp not found

content.text: The cache uses a hash map for O(1) key lookup and a doubly linked list for O(1) order operations. When 'd' is added, 'b' is evicted because it's the least recently used (a was accessed after b). The TTL demonstration shows entries expiring after their time limit.
Concurrency Testing

Thread safety claims are worthless without proof. Go's race detector finds data races by instrumenting memory access during execution. If two goroutines access the same memory without synchronization, and at least one is a write, the race detector reports it. Running go run -race is how you verify your mutex strategy actually works.

We'll stress test the cache with 10 writers and 5 readers running simultaneously, each making 100 operations. This creates thousands of concurrent accesses. If there's a race condition, the -race flag will catch it. If the cache corrupts under load, we'll see wrong sizes or panics.

content.output:
$ go run -race cache_concurrent.go
Concurrent test complete. Cache size: 100
No race conditions detected!

content.text: Running with -race flag verifies thread safety. 10 writers and 5 readers access the cache concurrently. The mutex ensures no data races. The final size is 100 (capacity limit) because eviction works correctly under concurrent load.

content.title: RWMutex Pitfall
content.message: We use a full Lock() even for Get because it modifies the list order. Using RLock() would cause races. Only truly read-only operations like Len() can use RLock(). Always verify with go run -race.

content.text: Testing the Cache

A well-designed cache is easy to test because its interface is simple: Get, Set, Delete. We test the core operations, eviction behavior, TTL expiry, and concurrent access. Table-driven tests make it easy to cover all scenarios.

content.output:
$ go test -v lru_cache_test.go
=== RUN   TestLRUCache_BasicOperations
=== RUN   TestLRUCache_BasicOperations/set_and_get
=== RUN   TestLRUCache_BasicOperations/get_non-existent_key
=== RUN   TestLRUCache_BasicOperations/overwrite_existing_key
--- PASS: TestLRUCache_BasicOperations (0.00s)
    --- PASS: TestLRUCache_BasicOperations/set_and_get (0.00s)
    --- PASS: TestLRUCache_BasicOperations/get_non-existent_key (0.00s)
    --- PASS: TestLRUCache_BasicOperations/overwrite_existing_key (0.00s)
=== RUN   TestLRUCache_Eviction
--- PASS: TestLRUCache_Eviction (0.00s)
=== RUN   TestLRUCache_TTLExpiry
--- PASS: TestLRUCache_TTLExpiry (0.06s)
PASS
ok      command-line-arguments  0.068s

content.text: The tests cover three critical scenarios: basic get/set operations with table-driven tests, LRU eviction order verification, and TTL expiry behavior. The table-driven approach in TestLRUCache_BasicOperations makes it trivial to add new test cases. Notice we test the eviction order specifically, confirming 'a' survives because we accessed it, while 'b' gets evicted.
Cache Metrics

A cache is only useful if it actually serves data from memory. The hit rate measures this: hits divided by total requests. A 90% hit rate means 9 out of 10 requests are served from cache, reducing database load by 90%. Monitor these metrics to know if your cache is working.

content.code:
Cache Performance Metrics

1. Hit Rate = Hits / (Hits + Misses)
   - 90%+ is good for most applications
   - Below 50% suggests wrong eviction policy or too small capacity

2. Miss Rate = 1 - Hit Rate
   - Each miss means a slow backend call

3. Eviction Rate = Evictions / Time
   - High rate suggests cache is too small
   - Increase capacity or reduce TTL

4. Memory Usage = Current Size / Capacity
   - Track to prevent OOM
   - Set alerts at 80%+ utilization

Example: API serving 10,000 req/sec
  - 95% hit rate = 9,500 cache hits, 500 DB queries
  - 50% hit rate = 5,000 cache hits, 5,000 DB queries
  - Difference: 10x more DB load with poor caching

content.text: The example shows why hit rate matters so much. At 95% hit rate, your database handles 500 queries per second. At 50%, it handles 5,000, a 10x increase. If your database can only handle 1,000 QPS, a drop from 95% to 50% hit rate takes your system from healthy to overloaded. Track these metrics and alert when they degrade.
Production Considerations

Production caches face challenges not seen in simple implementations. Cache stampede occurs when a popular key expires and hundreds of requests simultaneously hit the database. Stale data can cause bugs if TTL is too long. Memory pressure can crash your service if the cache grows unbounded.

content.title: Cache Stampede
content.message: When a popular key expires, many requests miss cache simultaneously and overwhelm the database. Solutions: probabilistic early expiration (refresh before TTL), single-flight pattern (one goroutine fetches, others wait), or background refresh (never let popular keys expire).

content.code:
Cache Write Strategies

1. Cache-Aside (Lazy Loading)
   Read: Check cache -> if miss, read DB, write to cache
   Write: Write to DB, invalidate cache
   Pro: Only caches what's needed
   Con: First request always slow (cold cache)

2. Write-Through
   Write: Write to cache AND DB simultaneously
   Read: Always from cache
   Pro: Cache always fresh
   Con: Write latency increased

3. Write-Behind (Write-Back)
   Write: Write to cache, async write to DB later
   Read: Always from cache
   Pro: Fast writes
   Con: Data loss risk if cache crashes

Most common: Cache-Aside for reads, invalidate on writes

content.text: Cache-Aside is the most common pattern because it's simple and safe. On read miss, fetch from database and populate cache. On write, update database and invalidate cache (don't update cache, which can cause race conditions). The cache implementation we built supports this pattern: the application controls when to call Get and Set.

content.title: Quick Reference
content.message: Data structures: HashMap + Doubly Linked List for O(1) operations. Thread safety: sync.Mutex (not RWMutex because Get modifies order). TTL: check on access (lazy) or background goroutine (eager). Capacity: set based on memory budget, monitor eviction rate.

content.title: Extension Ideas
content.message: Real caches add: background TTL cleanup, cache statistics (hits/misses), eviction callbacks, LFU as an alternative policy, sharding for reduced lock contention.

content.text: Imagine you're running a popular API that serves millions of requests daily. One morning, you notice your servers grinding to a halt. A single client, whether due to a bug, a misconfigured script, or malicious intent, is hammering your endpoints with 10,000 requests per second. Your database connections are exhausted, legitimate users can't access the service, and your infrastructure costs are skyrocketing.

Without rate limiting, your API is defenseless. A single misbehaving client can monopolize resources meant for thousands of users. Denial-of-service attacks become trivial. Costly operations like database queries or third-party API calls can run unbounded. You have no way to enforce fair usage across free and paid tiers.

In this section, we'll build a rate limiter from scratch. You'll learn two algorithms: Token Bucket (which allows controlled bursts) and Sliding Window Counter (which provides smoother limiting). Both are thread-safe and used in real systems like Stripe, GitHub, and AWS API Gateway.
Why Rate Limiting?

Rate limiting is about fairness and protection. Think of it like a bouncer at a club who controls how many people enter per hour. Without the bouncer, a mob could rush in and overwhelm the venue. With the bouncer, everyone gets a fair chance to enter, and the club stays at a manageable capacity.

The key insight is that rate limiting trades immediate availability for long-term stability. By rejecting some requests now, you ensure the system remains healthy for everyone. This is a fundamental tradeoff in distributed systems: you sacrifice perfect availability for graceful degradation under load.

items.label: Token Bucket
items.description: Allows bursts up to bucket capacity, then enforces steady rate. Best for APIs where occasional spikes are acceptable. Simple to implement. Used by AWS, Stripe.

items.label: Sliding Window Log
items.description: Stores exact timestamp of each request. Most accurate but memory grows with request rate. Good for low-volume, high-precision scenarios.

items.label: Sliding Window Counter
items.description: Combines fixed windows with weighted calculation. Memory-efficient approximation of sliding window. Used by Cloudflare, Redis.

items.label: Leaky Bucket
items.description: Processes requests at constant rate regardless of arrival pattern. Good for smoothing traffic to downstream services. Queues rather than rejects.

content.text: How Token Bucket Works

The Token Bucket algorithm is elegant in its simplicity. Picture a bucket that holds tokens. The bucket has a maximum capacity (say, 10 tokens). Tokens are added at a steady rate (say, 2 per second). Each request consumes one token. If the bucket is empty, the request is rejected.

content.code:
Token Bucket Algorithm

Initial State (bucket capacity=5, refill=2/sec):

    [*] [*] [*] [*] [*]     <- 5 tokens (full)
    ─────────────────────
           BUCKET

After 5 rapid requests:

    [ ] [ ] [ ] [ ] [ ]     <- 0 tokens (empty)
    ─────────────────────
           BUCKET
    
    Request 6: REJECTED (no tokens)

After waiting 1 second (refill 2 tokens):

    [*] [*] [ ] [ ] [ ]     <- 2 tokens
    ─────────────────────
           BUCKET
    
    Requests 6-7: ALLOWED
    Request 8: REJECTED

Key Properties:
  - Allows bursts up to bucket capacity
  - Sustained rate limited to refill rate
  - Simple state: just (tokens, lastRefillTime)

content.text: The visualization shows the core behavior: bursts are allowed up to the bucket capacity, but sustained traffic is limited to the refill rate. This makes Token Bucket ideal for APIs where you want to allow occasional spikes (like a user rapidly loading a page) while preventing sustained abuse.
Requirements

Before coding, let's clarify requirements. In an interview, you should ask these questions: Is this single-server or distributed? What's the expected request rate? Should limits be per-user, per-IP, or global? Do we need different limits for different endpoints? How should we communicate rate limit status to clients?

content.code:
Functional Requirements:
  1. Allow(key) - Returns true if request is allowed, false otherwise
  2. Configurable rate: requests per time window
  3. Per-key limiting: each user/IP has independent limits
  4. Multiple algorithms: Token Bucket and Sliding Window

Non-Functional Requirements:
  1. Thread-safe: concurrent requests must not corrupt state
  2. Low memory: O(1) per key, not O(requests)
  3. Accurate: no significant over/under counting
  4. Fast: O(1) per Allow() call

Why These Requirements Matter:
  - Thread-safe: API servers handle concurrent requests
  - Low memory: millions of keys (users) must fit in RAM
  - Accurate: billing/quota decisions depend on counts
  - Fast: rate limiting adds to every request's latency

content.text: Notice that we're building an in-memory, single-server rate limiter. This is the foundation. Real systems extend this with Redis for distributed rate limiting, but the algorithms are identical.
Data Structure Choice

The choice of data structure depends on the algorithm. For Token Bucket, we need to store the current token count and last refill time per key. A map from key to bucket gives us O(1) lookup. For Sliding Window Counter, we store the previous and current window counts plus the window start time.

content.code:
Token Bucket Data Structure:

    RateLimiter
        |
        +-- buckets: map[string]*TokenBucket
                         |
                         +-- "user1" --> TokenBucket{
                         |                  capacity: 10
                         |                  tokens: 7.5
                         |                  refillRate: 2.0
                         |                  lastRefill: time.Time
                         |               }
                         |
                         +-- "user2" --> TokenBucket{...}

    Time Complexity:
      - Allow(key): O(1) - map lookup + arithmetic
      - Space: O(K) where K = number of unique keys

    Why map[string]*TokenBucket?
      - O(1) lookup by key (user ID, IP address)
      - Each bucket is independent (no cross-key locking)
      - Pointer allows bucket-level mutex for fine-grained locking

content.text: Using a pointer to TokenBucket is important for performance. It allows us to lock individual buckets rather than the entire map, enabling concurrent requests for different users to proceed without blocking each other.
Token Bucket Implementation

Let's implement the Token Bucket algorithm. The key insight is lazy refill: instead of running a background goroutine to add tokens, we calculate how many tokens should have been added since the last request. This makes the implementation simpler and avoids goroutine management.

Watch for these details in the code: the mutex protects against concurrent access, tokens are stored as float64 to handle partial refills, and we cap tokens at capacity to prevent unbounded accumulation.

content.output:
$ go run token_bucket.go
Burst test (capacity=5):
  Request 1: true
  Request 2: true
  Request 3: true
  Request 4: true
  Request 5: true
  Request 6: false
  Request 7: false

Waiting 2 seconds for refill...
After refill:
  Request 1: true
  Request 2: true
  Request 3: true
  Request 4: true
  Request 5: false
  Request 6: false

Different user (user2):
  Request 1: true
  Request 2: true
  Request 3: true
  Request 4: true
  Request 5: true
  Request 6: false

content.text: The output demonstrates three key behaviors. First, the burst test shows that exactly 5 requests are allowed before the bucket empties. Second, after waiting 2 seconds at 2 tokens/second, 4 tokens accumulated (capped at capacity would be 5, but we consumed from empty so it's exactly elapsed * rate = 4). Third, user2 has an independent bucket that starts full, proving per-key isolation.
How Sliding Window Counter Works

The Sliding Window Counter is a memory-efficient approximation of the Sliding Window Log. Instead of storing every request timestamp, it keeps just two counters: the previous window's count and the current window's count. It then weights the previous window based on how far into the current window we are.

content.code:
Sliding Window Counter Algorithm

Time: 0.0s to 2.5s, Window size: 1 second, Limit: 10 req/sec

    Window 1 (0-1s)     Window 2 (1-2s)     Window 3 (2-3s)
    +-----------+       +-----------+       +-----------+
    | 10 reqs   |       | 8 reqs    |       |  ?        |
    +-----------+       +-----------+       +-----------+
                                       ^
                                  Current: 2.5s

At t=2.5s, we're 0.5s into Window 3:
  - Previous window (Window 2): 8 requests
  - Current window (Window 3): 0 requests so far
  - Weight of previous: 1.0 - 0.5 = 0.5 (50%)
  
Weighted count = (8 * 0.5) + 0 = 4
Limit = 10
Remaining = 10 - 4 = 6 requests allowed

Why This Works:
  - At window start (t=2.0s): 100% of prev counts
  - At window end (t=2.99s): ~0% of prev counts
  - Smooth transition, no fixed window boundary spikes

content.text: The key insight is the weighted calculation. At the start of a new window, requests from the previous window still count fully. As time progresses, their weight decreases linearly. This prevents the boundary spike problem of fixed windows, where users could make 10 requests at 0:59 and 10 more at 1:01.
Sliding Window Counter Implementation

The implementation tracks two counts per key: the previous window's requests and the current window's requests. When the window rolls over, the current count becomes the previous count, and a new current count starts at zero. The Allow() check calculates the weighted sum and compares against the limit.

content.output:
$ go run sliding_window.go
Sliding Window Rate Limiter (10 req/sec)

First burst:
  Request  1: true
  Request  2: true
  Request  3: true
  Request  4: true
  Request  5: true
  Request  6: true
  Request  7: true
  Request  8: true
  Request  9: true
  Request 10: true
  Request 11: false
  Request 12: false

Waiting 1.5s (full window + half)...
After 1.5s (previous window weighted ~50%):
  Request  1: true
  Request  2: true
  Request  3: true
  Request  4: true
  Request  5: true
  Request  6: true
  Request  7: false

content.text: The output shows the sliding window behavior. In the first burst, exactly 10 requests are allowed. After waiting 1.5 seconds, we're in a new window with the previous 10 requests weighted at roughly 50% (5 effective requests). This leaves room for about 5 more requests. Due to timing precision, you may see slight variations in the exact cutoff point.
Comparing the Algorithms

items.label: Token Bucket
items.description: Allows bursts up to bucket size. Good for APIs where occasional bursts are acceptable. Simple state: tokens + lastRefill. Used by: AWS API Gateway, Stripe.

items.label: Sliding Window Counter
items.description: Smoother limiting, no large bursts. Better for strict rate enforcement. Slightly more complex: prevCount + currCount + windowStart. Used by: Cloudflare, Redis.

content.text: Testing Rate Limiters

Rate limiters need tests for boundary conditions: exactly at the limit, one over, and after reset. Testing time-based behavior requires either short durations (as we use here) or mocking time. The concurrent test is critical since rate limiters are always accessed by multiple goroutines in real systems.

content.output:
$ go test -v -race rate_limiter_test.go
=== RUN   TestTokenBucket_BurstLimit
--- PASS: TestTokenBucket_BurstLimit (0.00s)
=== RUN   TestTokenBucket_Refill
--- PASS: TestTokenBucket_Refill (0.15s)
=== RUN   TestTokenBucket_Concurrent
--- PASS: TestTokenBucket_Concurrent (0.00s)
PASS
ok      command-line-arguments  2.129s

content.text: The tests verify three key behaviors. BurstLimit confirms exactly 5 requests are allowed. Refill confirms tokens accumulate over time. Concurrent runs 200 goroutines against 100 tokens and verifies exactly 100 succeed, proving thread safety. The -race flag confirms no data races in the implementation.
Production Considerations
The implementations above are correct but incomplete for real systems. Here are the gaps you'd need to address before deploying to production.

content.title: Memory Growth
content.message: The map of buckets grows unbounded as new keys arrive. In production, add a background goroutine that periodically removes buckets that haven't been accessed recently. Use a lastAccess timestamp and evict after a TTL (e.g., 10 minutes of inactivity).

content.title: Distributed Rate Limiting
content.message: Our implementation is single-server. If you have multiple API servers, each has its own bucket state. A user could get 5x the limit by hitting 5 servers. For distributed limiting, use Redis with INCR and EXPIRE, or a dedicated service like Envoy's rate limit service.

content.title: HTTP Response Headers
content.message: Good APIs tell clients their rate limit status via headers: X-RateLimit-Limit (max requests), X-RateLimit-Remaining (requests left), X-RateLimit-Reset (when limit resets, Unix timestamp), Retry-After (seconds to wait if limited). Return 429 Too Many Requests status when limited.

content.title: Tiered Limits
content.message: Real APIs have different limits per tier: free users get 100 req/min, paid users get 1000 req/min, enterprise gets unlimited. Store the limit configuration per user/API key and look it up when creating the bucket. Consider allowing burst multipliers for higher tiers.

content.code:
Production Rate Limiter Checklist:

[ ] Memory management
    - TTL-based eviction of inactive buckets
    - Maximum bucket count with LRU eviction

[ ] Distributed rate limiting
    - Redis backend for shared state
    - Consistent hashing for sharded limiters

[ ] Observability
    - Prometheus metrics: requests_total, requests_limited
    - Logging when limits are hit (with sampling)

[ ] Client communication
    - X-RateLimit-* headers on every response
    - 429 status code with Retry-After header
    - Clear error message in response body

[ ] Configuration
    - Per-tier limits (free, paid, enterprise)
    - Per-endpoint limits (auth stricter than read)
    - Dynamic config reload without restart

[ ] Graceful degradation
    - Fail open vs fail closed decision
    - Circuit breaker for Redis connection
    - Local fallback when distributed limiter unavailable

content.text: The checklist above represents what real rate limiters need. The core algorithms we implemented are production-worthy, but the surrounding infrastructure requires additional work. Start with the simple in-memory version, then add distributed support when you scale to multiple servers.
Key Takeaways

Rate limiting is a fundamental building block for API protection. Token Bucket is simple and allows controlled bursts, making it ideal for most APIs. Sliding Window Counter provides smoother limiting at the cost of slightly more complexity. Both algorithms are O(1) time and O(1) space per key, making them suitable for high-throughput systems. The core implementations are straightforward, but production deployment requires memory management, distributed coordination, and proper client communication.

Imagine you're building software for a multi-story parking garage in a busy downtown area. Vehicles arrive constantly: motorcycles, sedans, SUVs, and delivery trucks. Each vehicle needs to find an appropriate spot quickly. The garage has different spot sizes: compact spots for motorcycles, regular spots for cars, and oversized spots for trucks. Customers expect to drive in, get a ticket, park, and later pay based on how long they stayed.

Without a well-designed system, chaos ensues. Attendants manually track which spots are free by walking the floors. Cars circle looking for spots while empty ones sit unnoticed on another level. Trucks try to squeeze into regular spots, blocking traffic. The payment desk has no idea when a vehicle entered or where it parked. During peak hours, the system collapses under the load.

In this section, we'll design a parking lot management system from scratch. We'll model vehicles, spots, and floors as distinct entities, define clear rules for which vehicles can use which spots, track parked vehicles for instant lookup, and calculate fees on exit. The system will be thread-safe for concurrent operations and efficient enough for real-time use.
Why This Problem?

The parking lot is a classic LLD interview problem because it tests multiple skills simultaneously: object-oriented modeling (entities with behavior), enumeration design (vehicle types, spot sizes), polymorphism (different vehicles sharing common interfaces), composition (lots contain floors contain spots), and thread-safety (concurrent park/leave operations). It's complex enough to reveal design thinking but small enough to implement in an interview.

Think of it like a hotel reservation system, but for cars. The core insight is that the system must answer two questions instantly: "Where can this vehicle park?" and "Where is this vehicle parked?" The first requires tracking available spots by size. The second requires mapping license plates to spots. Designing data structures that answer both questions in O(1) time is the key challenge.
How Parking Lot Works

Let's walk through a typical parking session to understand the state changes involved. A car enters, the system finds an available medium spot, records the entry time, and returns the spot ID. When the car leaves, the system looks up the spot by license plate, calculates the duration, computes the fee, and returns the spot to the available pool.

content.code:
Parking Flow (Car "ABC-123" arrives):

1. ENTRY: Car arrives at gate
   +---------------------------+
   | availableSpots[Medium]: 6 |  vehicleToSpot: {}
   | availableSpots[Large]: 2  |
   +---------------------------+
                |
                v
2. FIND SPOT: Pop from availableSpots[Medium]
   Spot F1-S3 selected (Medium size)
                |
                v
3. RECORD: Create Vehicle, link to Spot
   +---------------------------+
   | availableSpots[Medium]: 5 |  vehicleToSpot: {"ABC-123": F1-S3}
   | availableSpots[Large]: 2  |
   +---------------------------+
   Spot F1-S3.Vehicle = {plate: "ABC-123", entry: 14:30}
                |
                v
4. TICKET: Return spot ID "F1-S3" to driver

---

Exit Flow (Car "ABC-123" leaves at 16:45):

1. LOOKUP: vehicleToSpot["ABC-123"] -> F1-S3
                |
                v
2. CALCULATE: 16:45 - 14:30 = 2.25 hours
   Fee = ceil(2.25) * $5/hour = $15
                |
                v
3. RELEASE: Return spot to pool
   +---------------------------+
   | availableSpots[Medium]: 6 |  vehicleToSpot: {}
   | availableSpots[Large]: 2  |
   +---------------------------+
   Spot F1-S3.Vehicle = nil

content.text: The ASCII diagram shows the two critical data structures: availableSpots (a map from spot size to list of free spots) and vehicleToSpot (a map from license plate to occupied spot). Together, these provide O(1) lookup for both finding a spot and finding a parked vehicle.
Requirements

In a real interview, you'd ask clarifying questions before coding. What types of vehicles? How many floors? Do we need reservations? Is the fee structure time-based or flat? Do we need to track which spots are occupied for a display board? For this design, we'll assume the following requirements gathered through such questions.

content.code:
Functional Requirements:

  1. Multiple floors, each with multiple spots
     WHY: Real garages have levels. Customers need to know which floor.

  2. Different spot sizes: Small, Medium, Large
     WHY: Optimize space. Small spots fit more motorcycles.

  3. Different vehicles: Motorcycle, Car, Truck
     WHY: Each has different size constraints.

  4. Park vehicle in smallest fitting spot
     WHY: Preserve large spots for trucks that need them.

  5. Remove vehicle and calculate time-based fee
     WHY: Core business model. Fee = hours * rate.

  6. Query available spots by size
     WHY: Display boards, attendant tools, capacity planning.

Spot-Vehicle Matching Rules:
  +------------+-----------------------------------+
  | Vehicle    | Can park in                       |
  +------------+-----------------------------------+
  | Motorcycle | Small, Medium, or Large           |
  | Car        | Medium or Large                   |
  | Truck      | Large only                        |
  +------------+-----------------------------------+

Non-Functional Requirements:

  1. Thread-safe operations
     WHY: Multiple gates, concurrent entry/exit.

  2. O(1) parking if spot available
     WHY: Gate throughput. Cars shouldn't wait.

  3. O(1) vehicle lookup by license plate
     WHY: Exit lane needs instant fee calculation.

content.text: Data Structure Choice

The key insight is using two maps to enable O(1) operations for both parking and leaving. The first map, vehicleToSpot, maps license plates to spots for instant lookup on exit. The second map, availableSpots, maps each spot size to a slice of free spots, enabling O(1) spot allocation by popping from the end of the slice.

content.code:
Data Structure Design:

  vehicleToSpot: map[string]*Spot
  +--------------------+     +----------------+
  | "ABC-123" -> *Spot | --> | ID: F1-S3      |
  | "XYZ-789" -> *Spot |     | Size: Medium   |
  +--------------------+     | Vehicle: {...} |
                             +----------------+
  WHY map: O(1) lookup by license plate on exit.

  availableSpots: map[SpotSize][]*Spot
  +-------------------+
  | Small  -> [S1,S2] |  Pop from end: O(1)
  | Medium -> [S3,S4] |  Append to end: O(1)
  | Large  -> [S5]    |
  +-------------------+
  WHY slice per size: O(1) allocation by popping last element.
  WHY grouped by size: Find smallest fitting spot in O(1).

Complexity Analysis:
  +------------+--------+--------+
  | Operation  | Time   | Space  |
  +------------+--------+--------+
  | Park       | O(1)   | O(1)   |
  | Leave      | O(1)   | O(1)   |
  | Available  | O(1)*  | O(1)   |
  +------------+--------+--------+
  * O(number of sizes), which is constant (3)

content.text: Implementation

Now we'll implement the parking lot system. The code defines SpotSize and VehicleType as enum-like constants with String methods for display. Vehicle and Spot are simple structs. ParkingLot contains the core logic with mutex protection for thread safety. Notice how Park() iterates through spot sizes starting from the minimum required, ensuring we use the smallest fitting spot.

content.output:
$ go run parking_lot.go
=== Parking Lot Simulation ===
Available: Small:4, Medium:6, Large:2

Parking vehicles:
  MOTO-1 (Motorcycle): parked in F2-S8 (Small)
  CAR-1 (Car): parked in F2-S11 (Medium)
  CAR-2 (Car): parked in F2-S10 (Medium)
  TRUCK-1 (Truck): parked in F2-S12 (Large)
  TRUCK-2 (Truck): parked in F1-S6 (Large)

Available after parking: Small:3, Medium:4, Large:0

Vehicle leaving:
  CAR-1 left, fee: $5.00

Available after CAR-1 leaves: Small:3, Medium:5, Large:0

Trying to park third truck:
  TRUCK-3: no available spot

content.text: The output shows the system working as designed. The motorcycle parks in a Small spot, preserving Medium and Large spots for bigger vehicles. Cars take Medium spots. Both trucks successfully park in Large spots, but the third truck fails because both Large spots are occupied. After CAR-1 leaves, one Medium spot returns to the available pool.

Notice how the design achieves O(1) complexity: Park() pops from the end of a slice (O(1)), and Leave() looks up by license plate in a map (O(1)). The vehicleToSpot map enables instant lookup, while availableSpots grouped by size enables efficient spot selection without scanning all spots.

Production Considerations

While this implementation covers the core logic, deploying a parking system requires addressing several real-world concerns. Understanding these helps you discuss trade-offs in an interview and shows you think beyond the happy path.

content.title: Edge Cases to Handle
content.message: Lost tickets (vehicle in lot but no record), power failures (persist state to disk), midnight fee rollover (day-based billing), overstay vehicles (abandoned cars), and invalid license plates (validation needed).

items.label: Persistence
items.description: In-memory data is lost on restart. Real systems persist to database and recover state on startup.

items.label: Distributed Locks
items.description: Multiple gate servers need distributed coordination. Use Redis locks or database transactions.

items.label: Spot Sensors
items.description: Physical sensors detect actual occupancy. System must reconcile sensor data with booking state.

items.label: Payment Integration
items.description: Credit card processing, receipts, refunds, and payment failures add significant complexity.

content.title: Design Extensions
content.message: Advanced features to discuss: reservation system (book spots in advance), dynamic pricing (surge during events), handicapped spot priority, electric vehicle charging spots with different rates, monthly passes, valet parking mode, and integration with navigation apps for real-time availability.

content.text: Imagine you're on-call at 3 AM when alerts start firing. Your payment service is failing, but the logs just say "error processing request." No request ID, no user context, no stack trace. You're flying blind, manually correlating timestamps across three different services while customers can't complete purchases. After an hour of grep gymnastics, you finally trace the issue to a malformed credit card token, but only because you happened to spot a pattern in the noise.

This nightmare happens when logging is an afterthought. Scattered fmt.Println calls, inconsistent formats, no log levels, no context propagation. In development, you can attach a debugger. In production, logs are your only window into what happened. Without structured, leveled, contextual logging, debugging becomes archaeology.

In this section, we'll design a logging framework that solves these problems. You'll learn how to use the Strategy pattern for pluggable outputs, how to propagate context through request lifecycles, and how to build a thread-safe, extensible system that makes debugging a breeze instead of a nightmare.
Why Build a Logging Framework?

Before jumping into code, let's understand what separates a toy logger from one you'd actually want in production. The core insight is that logging has two distinct concerns: what to log (levels, messages, context) and where to log it (console, file, network). Mixing these concerns creates inflexible code. Separating them via interfaces unlocks powerful composition.

items.label: fmt.Println
items.description: Zero infrastructure. No levels, no timestamps, no structure. Fine for CLI tools, useless for debugging distributed systems.

items.label: Basic Logger
items.description: Adds timestamps and levels. Better for debugging, but output format is hardcoded. Adding JSON output means rewriting.

items.label: Structured Logger
items.description: Key-value fields, pluggable handlers, context propagation. Query logs with tools like jq. What we're building.

content.text: Think of a logging framework like a mail sorting facility. Messages come in with metadata (priority, destination). The sorting system (our logger) routes each message based on its priority (log level) to the right output channels (handlers). Some mail goes to the recycling bin (filtered by level), some gets special handling (JSON format for log aggregators), and some triggers alerts (error-level with specific fields).
How It Works

When code calls logger.Info("user logged in"), several things happen in sequence. First, the logger checks if INFO meets the minimum level threshold. If not, the call returns immediately with zero allocation. If it passes, the logger constructs an Entry struct containing the level, message, timestamp, and any context fields. Finally, the entry is passed to each registered Handler, which formats and writes it according to its own rules.

content.code:
Log Flow:

  Code: log.With("user", "alice").Info("login")
           │
           ▼
    ┌──────────────────┐
    │  Level Check     │    minLevel=INFO
    │  INFO >= INFO?   │────▶ Yes, continue
    └──────────────────┘
           │
           ▼
    ┌──────────────────┐
    │  Build Entry     │    Entry{
    │  - level: INFO   │      Level: INFO,
    │  - msg: "login"  │      Message: "login",
    │  - fields: {...} │      Fields: {user: "alice"},
    │  - time: now()   │      Timestamp: 14:30:00
    └──────────────────┘    }
           │
           ▼
    ┌──────────────────┐
    │  Fan Out to      │
    │  Handlers        │
    └──────────────────┘
         │         │
         ▼         ▼
    ┌────────┐  ┌────────┐
    │Console │  │  JSON  │
    │Handler │  │Handler │
    └────────┘  └────────┘
         │         │
         ▼         ▼
    14:30:00       {"time":"...",
    [INFO]          "level":"INFO",
    login           "msg":"login",
    user=alice      "user":"alice"}

content.text: The flow diagram shows how a single log call fans out to multiple handlers. The Handler interface is the key abstraction: it decouples the logger from output concerns. ConsoleHandler formats for human readability. JSONHandler formats for machine parsing. You can add a SlackHandler for alerts or a DatadogHandler for metrics without touching the core logger.
Requirements

In an interview, before writing any code, clarify requirements. Ask: What log levels do you need? Where do logs go (stdout, files, remote)? Is the application concurrent? Do you need structured fields or just messages? How do you handle slow outputs? These questions reveal the scope and help you avoid over-engineering.

content.code:
Functional Requirements:

  1. Multiple log levels (Debug, Info, Warn, Error)
     WHY: Filter noise in production. Debug for development,
          Error for alerts. Reduces log volume and costs.

  2. Multiple outputs (Console, File, JSON, Remote)
     WHY: Console for development, JSON for log aggregators
          like Datadog or ELK. Different consumers need
          different formats.

  3. Configurable minimum level
     WHY: Debug in development, Info/Warn in production.
          Change at runtime without redeployment.

  4. Structured logging with key-value fields
     WHY: Enable queries like "show all logs where user_id=123"
          instead of regex parsing unstructured text.

  5. Timestamps on every entry
     WHY: Correlate events across services. Essential for
          distributed tracing and incident timelines.

Non-Functional Requirements:

  1. Thread-safe: Multiple goroutines log concurrently.
     Logging must not corrupt output or panic.

  2. Minimal allocation: Hot path should avoid heap
     allocations when level is filtered out.

  3. Extensible handlers: Adding new outputs should not
     require modifying core logger code (OCP).

content.text: The requirements split into two categories. Functional requirements describe what the system does: levels, outputs, fields. Non-functional requirements describe how well it does them: thread safety, performance, extensibility. In interviews, explicitly stating both shows systems thinking.
Data Structure Design

The core data structures are Entry (what we log) and Handler (where we log). Entry is a value type holding message, level, timestamp, and fields. Handler is an interface with a single method. This simple design enables powerful composition: multiple handlers, handler wrappers for buffering or filtering, context loggers with pre-filled fields.

content.code:
Core Types:

    ┌───────────────────────────────────────────┐
    │                  Logger                   │
    │  ┌─────────────────────────────────────┐  │
    │  │ handlers  []Handler                 │  │
    │  │ minLevel  Level                     │  │
    │  │ fields    map[string]any            │  │
    │  │ mu        sync.RWMutex              │  │
    │  └─────────────────────────────────────┘  │
    │                                           │
    │  Methods:                                 │
    │    AddHandler(h Handler) *Logger          │
    │    SetLevel(l Level) *Logger              │
    │    With(key, value) *Logger  (returns new)│
    │    Debug/Info/Warn/Error(msg, args...)    │
    └───────────────────────────────────────────┘
                        │
                        │ passes Entry to
                        ▼
    ┌───────────────────────────────────────────┐
    │              Handler (interface)          │
    │                                           │
    │   Handle(entry Entry) error               │
    │                                           │
    └───────────────────────────────────────────┘
            ▲               ▲              ▲
            │               │              │
    ┌───────────────┐ ┌───────────┐ ┌─────────────┐
    │ConsoleHandler │ │JSONHandler│ │ FileHandler │
    │               │ │           │ │             │
    │ Writer io.W   │ │ Writer    │ │ file *File  │
    │ mu sync.Mutex │ │ mu        │ │ mu          │
    └───────────────┘ └───────────┘ └─────────────┘

    Entry (value type):
    ┌─────────────────────────────────────────┐
    │  Level     Level          (int enum)    │
    │  Message   string                       │
    │  Fields    map[string]any               │
    │  Timestamp time.Time                    │
    └─────────────────────────────────────────┘

content.text: Handler is the Strategy pattern in action. The Logger doesn't know or care how handlers format output. It just calls Handle() on each one. This achieves O(n) complexity where n is the number of handlers, and O(1) for the level check. The With() method returns a new Logger to avoid mutating shared state, making it safe for concurrent use.
Implementation

Now let's implement the design. We'll build Level as an int enum with a String() method for readable output. Entry holds all log data as a simple value struct. The Handler interface has just one method, keeping it small per Go idiom. ConsoleHandler and JSONHandler demonstrate two different formatting strategies sharing the same interface.

Watch for these key patterns in the code: mutex protection in handlers (each handler locks independently), the With() method creating a new Logger instead of mutating (immutability for thread safety), and the early return when level is below threshold (the fast path that avoids allocation).

content.output:
$ go run logger.go
=== Basic Logging ===
14:30:00 [DEBUG] Starting application
14:30:00 [INFO] Server started on port 8080
14:30:00 [WARN] Memory usage high: 85%
14:30:00 [ERROR] Failed to connect: timeout

=== With Context Fields ===
14:30:00 [INFO] User logged in user_id=u123 request_id=req-456
14:30:00 [INFO] Processing order user_id=u123 request_id=req-456

=== JSON Format ===
{"level":"INFO","message":"Request received","service":"api","time":"2024-01-15T14:30:00Z"}
{"latency_ms":42,"level":"INFO","message":"Request completed","time":"2024-01-15T14:30:00Z"}

=== Level Filtering (min=Warn) ===
14:30:00 [WARN] This will appear
14:30:00 [ERROR] This will appear too

content.text: The output demonstrates all four key features working together. Basic logging shows each level with timestamp and severity tag. Context fields appear as key=value pairs, automatically included in every subsequent log call from that logger. JSON output shows the same data in machine-parseable format, ready for log aggregators like Elasticsearch or Datadog. Level filtering silently drops Debug and Info when minimum is set to Warn.

Notice how With() creates a child logger. The parent log variable still works without fields, while userLog carries user_id and request_id through its entire lifecycle. This pattern is perfect for request-scoped logging: create a child logger at the start of a request handler, add request ID and user ID, pass it through the call chain.
Testing the Logger

Good design enables good testing. Because Handler is an interface, we can inject a MockHandler that captures entries instead of writing to I/O. This lets us verify log levels, field propagation, and handler behavior in isolated unit tests. No file system, no stdout capture, just direct struct inspection.

The tests below demonstrate table-driven testing with test doubles. MockHandler records every entry it receives, letting us assert on level, message, and fields. Notice how we test both positive cases (logs appear when expected) and negative cases (logs filtered when below minimum level).
