TestLogger_With verifies immutability: the child logger has fields, the parent remains clean. TestConsoleHandler_Output verifies the formatting without involving the full logger.

This is the power of the Handler interface: we can swap implementations for testing. No mocking framework needed, no complex test setup. Just create a struct that implements Handle(), inject it, and inspect what it captured. This testability comes directly from following the Strategy pattern and Dependency Inversion.
Production Considerations
Our implementation covers the core design, but real systems need additional hardening. Here are the critical gaps and how production loggers address them.

content.title: Never Log Secrets
content.message: Passwords, API keys, credit card numbers, and PII must never appear in logs. Add a field sanitizer that redacts known sensitive keys (password, secret, token, ssn) before logging. Better yet, use typed wrappers that implement fmt.Stringer to return "[REDACTED]".

content.output:
$ go run redaction_example.go
API Key: [REDACTED]
Actual value: sk_live_abc123xyz

content.text: The Secret type automatically redacts itself when printed via fmt or log packages. This makes accidental secret logging impossible: you'd have to explicitly call Expose() to get the raw value.

items.label: Async Handlers
items.description: Buffer log entries in a channel and write in a background goroutine. Prevents slow I/O from blocking application code. Flush on shutdown.

items.label: Log Rotation
items.description: Rotate files by size or time. Keep last N files. Compress old logs. Libraries like lumberjack handle this for file handlers.

items.label: Sampling
items.description: At high volume, log 1-in-N entries for common events. Always log errors. Reduces cost while preserving signal.

items.label: Caller Info
items.description: Add file:line to entries using runtime.Caller(). Skip frames to get the actual call site, not the logger internals.

content.title: Go Standard Library
content.message: Go 1.21 introduced log/slog, a structured logger in the standard library. It uses the same Handler interface pattern we built here. Once you understand this design, you can use slog (or zerolog, zap, logrus) effectively because they all follow the same principles.

content.text: Imagine you're building an e-commerce platform. When a customer places an order, multiple systems need to react: the inventory service decrements stock, the shipping service schedules delivery, the notification service sends a confirmation email, and the analytics service logs the purchase. How do you wire all these systems together?

Without a messaging system, the order service would need to call each downstream service directly. This creates tight coupling: if the email service is slow, the entire checkout hangs. If you add a new service (say, fraud detection), you must modify the order service code. Worse, if one service fails, you might lose the event entirely. Each new integration makes the system more fragile and harder to change.

A Publish-Subscribe (Pub/Sub) system solves this by decoupling producers from consumers. The order service publishes a single "order.created" event to a topic, and every interested service receives a copy. Publishers don't know (or care) who's listening. Subscribers can be added, removed, or fail independently without affecting publishers. This is the foundation of event-driven architectures used by systems like Kafka, RabbitMQ, and Google Cloud Pub/Sub.
Why Pub/Sub?

The core insight behind Pub/Sub is that producers and consumers have different concerns that shouldn't be mixed. A producer knows what happened (an order was created), but it shouldn't need to know who cares. A consumer knows what to do with certain events, but it shouldn't need to coordinate with producers. Pub/Sub introduces a broker in the middle that handles routing, making each side simpler and more independent.

Think of it like a newspaper subscription. The newspaper (publisher) doesn't deliver to your door personally; it goes to a distribution center (broker). You (subscriber) don't visit the printing press; you sign up for topics you care about (Sports, Business) and papers arrive. If the newspaper adds a new section, they don't need your permission. If you move, you update your subscription without calling the editor.

items.label: Direct Calls
items.description: Producer calls each consumer. Tight coupling, slow if any consumer is slow, must modify producer to add consumers. Simple but doesn't scale.

items.label: Message Queue
items.description: One consumer per message (competing consumers). Good for work distribution, load balancing. Each message processed once.

items.label: Pub/Sub
items.description: All subscribers get every message. Loose coupling, parallel delivery, easy to add subscribers. Each message delivered to all interested parties.

content.text: How It Works

Let's walk through a concrete example. We have a broker managing topics, and services subscribing to topics they care about. When a message is published, the broker fans it out to all subscribers of that topic.

content.code:
Step 1: Services subscribe to topics

    OrderService         InventoryService      EmailService
         |                      |                    |
         |                      |                    |
         v                      v                    v
    +---------------------------------------------------------+
    |                         BROKER                          |
    |  +----------------+  +----------------+                 |
    |  | orders.created |  | orders.shipped |                 |
    |  |  Subscribers:  |  |  Subscribers:  |                 |
    |  |  - Inventory   |  |  - Email       |                 |
    |  |  - Email       |  |  - Analytics   |                 |
    |  |  - Analytics   |  +----------------+                 |
    |  +----------------+                                     |
    +---------------------------------------------------------+

Step 2: OrderService publishes "order.created"

    OrderService -----> Publish("orders.created", {id: 123})
                                    |
                                    v
                               BROKER looks up
                               "orders.created"
                                    |
                        +-----------+-----------+
                        |           |           |
                        v           v           v
                   Inventory    Email      Analytics
                   (decrement)  (send)     (log)

Step 3: Each subscriber processes independently

    Inventory: receives {id: 123} -> updates stock
    Email: receives {id: 123} -> sends confirmation
    Analytics: receives {id: 123} -> logs event

    (All happen in parallel, failures are isolated)

content.text: Notice that the OrderService sends one message, and the broker handles delivery to three different services. Each subscriber has its own channel, so a slow email service doesn't block inventory updates. If Analytics fails, Order and Inventory are unaffected. Adding a new subscriber (say, FraudDetection) requires zero changes to OrderService.
Requirements

Before coding, let's clarify requirements. In an interview, you'd ask: How many topics? How many subscribers per topic? What's the message rate? Do we need persistence? Acknowledgments? Let's design for an in-memory system first, then discuss production extensions.
Functional Requirements

content.code:
1. Create/delete topics
   Why: Organize messages by domain (orders, inventory, notifications)

2. Subscribe/unsubscribe to topics
   Why: Services can dynamically join/leave without redeployment

3. Publish messages to topics
   Why: The core operation - producers emit events

4. Multiple subscribers per topic
   Why: Fan-out pattern - one event triggers multiple actions

5. Message delivery to all subscribers
   Why: Each subscriber gets a copy (not competing consumers)

content.text: Non-Functional Requirements

content.code:
1. Thread-safe operations
   Why: Multiple goroutines publish/subscribe concurrently

2. Non-blocking publish
   Why: Publisher shouldn't wait for slow subscribers

3. Subscriber isolation
   Why: One slow/failing subscriber doesn't affect others

content.text: Data Structure Choice

content.code:
Broker
  +-- topics: map[string]*Topic     O(1) topic lookup by name
  +-- mu: sync.RWMutex               Protects topic creation/deletion

Topic
  +-- name: string
  +-- subscribers: map[string]*Subscriber   O(1) subscriber lookup
  +-- mu: sync.RWMutex                       Protects subscriber list

Subscriber
  +-- id: string
  +-- ch: chan Message (buffered)    Non-blocking delivery
  +-- topics: map[string]bool        Track subscriptions
  +-- mu: sync.RWMutex                Protects topic tracking

Why maps? O(1) lookup for topics and subscribers is critical for high
throughput. Why buffered channels? They decouple publish speed from
consume speed. If the buffer fills, we drop messages rather than block
the publisher (configurable behavior).

content.text: Implementation

Now let's implement the Pub/Sub system. We'll build three core types: Message (the data being sent), Subscriber (receives messages via a channel), and Broker (routes messages to subscribers). The key insight is using Go channels as the delivery mechanism: each subscriber has a buffered channel, and publishing is a non-blocking send.

Watch for these patterns in the code: (1) RWMutex for concurrent access, where reads are frequent but writes are rare; (2) copying the subscriber slice before sending to avoid holding locks during delivery; (3) select with default for non-blocking sends that drop messages when buffers are full.

content.output:
$ go run pubsub.go
=== Publishing Messages ===
[sub1] Received on orders: map[item:Widget order_id:1001]
[sub2] Received on orders: map[item:Widget order_id:1001]
[sub2] Received on orders: map[item:Gadget order_id:1002]
[sub1] Received on orders: map[item:Gadget order_id:1002]
[sub2] Received on inventory: map[item:Widget stock:50]
[sub3] Received on inventory: map[item:Widget stock:50]

=== Unsubscribe sub2 from orders ===
[sub1] Received on orders: map[item:Gizmo order_id:1003]

Done

content.text: The output demonstrates the core Pub/Sub behavior: sub1 and sub2 both receive orders (they're subscribed to the same topic), while sub2 and sub3 receive inventory updates. After sub2 unsubscribes from orders, only sub1 receives the third order. Notice that sub2 continues receiving inventory messages because unsubscription is per-topic, not global.

The key implementation details to understand: (1) The broker uses RWMutex, allowing multiple goroutines to read topics concurrently while serializing writes; (2) Before sending messages, we copy the subscriber slice under a read lock, then release the lock before delivering, so slow subscribers don't block topic modifications; (3) The select-with-default pattern tries to send but immediately falls back if the channel is full, preventing any subscriber from blocking the publisher.
Testing the Pub/Sub System

Testing concurrent systems is tricky because timing varies between runs. We use two strategies: (1) For delivery tests, use timeouts with select to wait for expected messages; (2) For the non-blocking test, verify synchronously that messages were dropped. The tests cover subscription tracking, correct message routing, unsubscribe behavior, and backpressure handling.

content.output:
$ go test -v pubsub_test.go pubsub.go
=== RUN   TestBroker_Subscribe
--- PASS: TestBroker_Subscribe (0.00s)
=== RUN   TestBroker_Publish
--- PASS: TestBroker_Publish (0.05s)
=== RUN   TestBroker_Unsubscribe
--- PASS: TestBroker_Unsubscribe (0.05s)
=== RUN   TestBroker_NonBlockingPublish
  [WARN] Dropped message for subscriber sub1
  [WARN] Dropped message for subscriber sub1
--- PASS: TestBroker_NonBlockingPublish (0.00s)
PASS
ok      command-line-arguments  0.102s

content.text: The test output shows four passing tests, each verifying a critical aspect of the system. TestBroker_Subscribe confirms that subscription state is tracked correctly in both the Topic and the Subscriber. TestBroker_Publish verifies fan-out delivery and topic isolation (sub1 doesn't receive inventory). TestBroker_Unsubscribe confirms that unsubscription stops delivery. TestBroker_NonBlockingPublish is the most important: notice the WARN logs showing messages were dropped when the buffer was full, proving the publisher didn't block.
Production Considerations
Our implementation demonstrates the core Pub/Sub pattern, but real systems need additional features. Let's examine what's missing and why it matters.

content.title: Message Loss
content.message: Our implementation drops messages when subscriber buffers are full. In systems where every message matters (financial transactions, audit logs), you need either larger buffers, backpressure (slow down publishers), or persistent queues that survive restarts.

content.title: No Acknowledgments
content.message: We deliver messages fire-and-forget. If a subscriber crashes while processing, the message is lost. Real systems use acknowledgments: the subscriber confirms processing, and unacknowledged messages are redelivered. This requires tracking message state per subscriber.

content.title: No Persistence
content.message: All state is in memory. If the broker crashes, topics, subscriptions, and in-flight messages are lost. Production systems persist to disk (like Kafka's log segments) or use distributed consensus (like NATS JetStream) for durability.

content.code:
Feature                   Our Implementation    Production System
----------------------------------------------------------------------
Message Persistence       Memory only           Disk + replication
Delivery Guarantee        At-most-once          At-least-once or exactly-once
Acknowledgments           None                  Per-message ACK/NACK
Dead Letter Queue         None                  Failed messages routed to DLQ
Message Ordering          Per-subscriber        Partition-based ordering
Subscriber Groups         All get all           Competing consumers option
Topic Wildcards           Exact match only      orders.* matches orders.created
Backpressure              Drop messages         Flow control / rate limiting
Distributed               Single node           Broker cluster with failover

content.text: Common Pitfalls

content.code:
1. Goroutine Leaks
   If subscribers never drain their channels and aren't cleaned up,
   goroutines waiting on full channels accumulate indefinitely.
   Solution: Use context cancellation and close channels on unsubscribe.

2. Holding Locks During I/O
   Never send to channels while holding mutex locks.
   Solution: Copy subscriber list, release lock, then send.

3. Map Iteration During Modification
   Go maps are not safe to modify while iterating.
   Solution: Copy keys/values to slice before iteration.

4. Blocking on Full Channels
   Blocking sends can deadlock if consumer is also blocked.
   Solution: Use select with default or timeout.

5. Forgetting to Handle Closed Channels
   Reading from a closed channel returns zero values.
   Solution: Use the two-value receive: msg, ok := <-ch

content.title: When to Use This Pattern
content.message: Use in-memory Pub/Sub for: event-driven communication within a single process, decoupling components in a monolith, local testing without infrastructure. Use a real message broker (Kafka, RabbitMQ, NATS) for: cross-service communication, durability requirements, high throughput, or when messages must survive restarts.

content.text: Quick Reference

content.code:
Pub/Sub Pattern Summary:

  Publisher -----> Broker -----> Subscribers
     |               |                |
  Sends events   Routes by       Receive copies
  to topics      topic name       independently

Key Operations:
  broker.Subscribe(topic, subscriber)   -> Add subscriber to topic
  broker.Unsubscribe(topic, subscriber) -> Remove subscriber
  broker.Publish(topic, payload)        -> Fan-out to all subscribers

Thread-Safety:
  - RWMutex on Broker.topics (protect topic map)
  - RWMutex on Topic.subscribers (protect subscriber map)
  - RWMutex on Subscriber.topics (track subscriptions)

Message Delivery:
  - Buffered channels for async delivery
  - Non-blocking send with select/default
  - Dropped messages when buffer full

Time Complexity:
  - Subscribe: O(1) map insertions
  - Unsubscribe: O(1) map deletions
  - Publish: O(n) where n = subscribers to topic

content.text: Imagine you're running an e-commerce platform during Black Friday. Your checkout service calls a payment gateway, an inventory service, and a shipping calculator. Suddenly, the payment gateway becomes slow, taking 30 seconds instead of 200ms. Your checkout service has 100 worker threads, and they're all waiting on payment responses. Within minutes, your entire checkout is frozen. Users can't buy anything.

Without protection, a single failing dependency cascades through your system. Each slow call ties up a goroutine. The backlog grows. Timeouts don't help because you're still sending requests to a struggling service, making its recovery harder. Your healthy services (inventory, shipping) become unreachable because checkout can't respond. One sick service infects everything.

What if your checkout could detect that payments are failing and stop calling them entirely? Instead of waiting 30 seconds per request, it could fail immediately with a clear message: "Payment temporarily unavailable." The payment service gets breathing room to recover. Your checkout stays responsive for other operations. This is exactly what a circuit breaker provides, and in this section we'll build one from scratch.
Why Circuit Breaker?

The circuit breaker pattern comes from electrical engineering. When current exceeds safe levels, a physical circuit breaker trips, cutting power to prevent fires. Software circuit breakers work the same way: when failures exceed a threshold, they trip, cutting calls to the failing service to prevent cascade failures. The key insight is that failing fast is better than failing slow.

Consider the alternatives. You could use timeouts alone, but timeouts still send requests to a sick service, consuming resources and slowing recovery. You could use retry logic, but retrying a failing service just multiplies load. You could use bulkheads to isolate resources, but bulkheads limit damage without stopping the problem. Circuit breakers complement all of these by detecting failure patterns and proactively stopping calls.

items.label: Timeout Only
items.description: Limits wait time but still sends every request. Failing service gets hammered. Resources tied up waiting.

items.label: Retry with Backoff
items.description: Helps with transient errors. Bad for sustained failures, multiplies load on struggling services.

items.label: Bulkhead
items.description: Isolates resources per dependency. Limits blast radius but doesn't stop calls to failing services.

items.label: Circuit Breaker
items.description: Detects failure patterns, stops calls proactively. Gives failing service time to recover. Fails fast.

content.text: Real systems use all of these together. A timeout ensures you don't wait forever. Retries handle transient blips. Bulkheads contain damage. And a circuit breaker detects when a service is truly sick and stops calling it until it recovers.
How It Works

A circuit breaker is a state machine with three states. In the CLOSED state, requests flow normally. The breaker counts failures. When failures exceed a threshold (say, 5 failures in 10 seconds), the breaker trips to OPEN. In OPEN state, all requests fail immediately without calling the dependency. After a timeout (say, 30 seconds), the breaker moves to HALF-OPEN. In HALF-OPEN, a limited number of test requests are allowed through. If they succeed, the breaker closes and normal traffic resumes. If they fail, the breaker opens again.

content.code:
Circuit Breaker State Machine:

  Request arrives
        |
        v
  +----------+
  | CLOSED   |  <-- Normal operation
  +----------+      - Requests pass through
        |           - Count consecutive failures
        | failure count >= threshold
        v
  +----------+
  |  OPEN    |  <-- Protection mode
  +----------+      - All requests rejected immediately
        |           - Timer starts
        | timeout expires
        v
  +----------+
  | HALF-OPEN|  <-- Testing recovery
  +----------+      - Allow limited test requests
        |           - Success -> CLOSED
        |           - Failure -> OPEN
        v
  Decision point:
    - Test succeeds -> back to CLOSED
    - Test fails    -> back to OPEN

content.text: The state diagram shows the lifecycle. CLOSED is the happy path where everything works. OPEN is the protection state where we fail fast. HALF-OPEN is the recovery probe where we carefully test if the service is healthy again. The transition from HALF-OPEN is critical: a single failure sends us back to OPEN, while enough successes restore normal operation.

Let's trace through a concrete example. Say our payment service starts failing. Request 1: fail (failures=1). Request 2: fail (failures=2). Request 3: fail (failures=3, threshold reached, OPEN). Request 4: instant reject. Request 5: instant reject. 30 seconds pass. Request 6: allowed through as test, succeeds (HALF-OPEN). Request 7: test, succeeds. Request 8: test, succeeds (3 successes, CLOSED). Now traffic flows normally again.
Requirements

Before coding, let's clarify requirements. In an interview, you'd ask: "What triggers a trip? Consecutive failures or failures within a time window?" "How do we count success in half-open, one success or multiple?" "Should different error types (timeout vs 500) be treated differently?" These questions show you understand the design space.

content.code:
FUNCTIONAL REQUIREMENTS

  FR1: Three States
       - Closed: normal operation, requests pass through
       - Open: failing fast, requests rejected immediately
       - Half-Open: testing, limited requests allowed

  FR2: Failure Tracking
       - Count consecutive failures in Closed state
       - Trip to Open when count exceeds threshold
       - Why: consecutive failures indicate sustained problems,
              not transient blips

  FR3: Timeout-Based Recovery
       - After timeout in Open state, transition to Half-Open
       - Why: gives failing service time to recover before we
              hammer it with test requests

  FR4: Half-Open Testing
       - Allow limited requests (e.g., 3) through
       - All succeed -> Close the circuit
       - Any fails -> Open the circuit again
       - Why: gradual recovery prevents overwhelming a
              just-recovered service

NON-FUNCTIONAL REQUIREMENTS

  NFR1: Thread Safety
        - Must handle concurrent calls
        - State transitions must be atomic

  NFR2: Low Overhead
        - State checks must be O(1)
        - No expensive operations on the hot path

  NFR3: Observable
        - Expose current state for monitoring
        - Log state transitions for debugging

content.text: Each requirement exists for a reason. Consecutive failure counting (FR2) means a single failure doesn't trip the breaker, only sustained problems do. The timeout (FR3) prevents us from immediately retesting a service that just failed. The limited half-open testing (FR4) prevents a thundering herd from overwhelming a recovering service. Thread safety (NFR1) is essential because HTTP handlers run concurrently.
Data Structure

For tracking state, we need a struct with the current state, failure count, success count (for half-open), timestamp of last failure (to check timeout), and configuration (thresholds, timeout duration). A mutex protects concurrent access. All operations are O(1) since we only read and write a few fields.

content.code:
CircuitBreaker struct:

  +------------------------------------------+
  | Configuration (immutable after create)   |
  |------------------------------------------|   O(1) to check
  | name         string                      |   state and
  | maxFailures  int       # trip threshold  |   update counters
  | timeout      Duration  # open duration   |
  | halfOpenMax  int       # test count      |
  +------------------------------------------+
  | State (protected by mutex)               |
  |------------------------------------------|   sync.Mutex guards
  | state        State     # current state   |   all state fields
  | failures     int       # consecutive     |
  | successes    int       # in half-open    |
  | lastFailure  Time      # for timeout     |
  | halfOpenCount int      # tests allowed   |
  | mu           sync.Mutex                  |
  +------------------------------------------+

Why this structure achieves O(1):
  - State check: read one field
  - Failure count: increment one int
  - Timeout check: one time comparison
  - No maps, slices, or complex lookups

content.text: The structure separates configuration (set once at creation) from mutable state (changes with each request). This makes the design clear: configuration is immutable and safe to read without locks, while state fields require mutex protection.
Implementation

Now let's implement the circuit breaker. The core is the Execute method, which wraps any function call with circuit breaker logic. It checks the current state, decides whether to allow the call, executes the function, and updates state based on success or failure. Pay attention to how the mutex is acquired and released to avoid holding it during the actual function call.

content.output:
$ go run circuit_breaker.go
=== Initial: Circuit Closed ===
State: CLOSED

=== Simulate Failures to Trip Circuit ===
Request 1: FAILED (service unavailable)
Request 2: FAILED (service unavailable)
  [api-service] State: CLOSED -> OPEN (tripped)
Request 3: FAILED (service unavailable)
Request 4: BLOCKED (circuit open)
Request 5: BLOCKED (circuit open)

State: OPEN

=== Requests While Open ===
Request 1: BLOCKED
Request 2: BLOCKED

=== Wait for Timeout ===

=== Test Requests in Half-Open ===
  [api-service] State: OPEN -> HALF-OPEN (testing)
Request 1: SUCCESS
Request 2: SUCCESS
  [api-service] State: HALF-OPEN -> CLOSED (recovered)
Request 3: SUCCESS
Request 4: SUCCESS

Final State: CLOSED

content.text: The output demonstrates the complete lifecycle. Requests 1-3 fail, incrementing the failure counter. On the third failure, the counter hits the threshold and the circuit trips to OPEN. Requests 4-5 are blocked immediately without calling the failing function, that's the "fail fast" behavior. While open, requests 1-2 are also blocked. After waiting 600ms (exceeding the 500ms timeout), the circuit transitions to HALF-OPEN on the next request. In half-open, three successful requests trigger the transition back to CLOSED, restoring normal operation.

Notice the key design decision: the mutex is released before calling the wrapped function. This prevents the circuit breaker from becoming a bottleneck. If we held the lock during the function call, all requests would serialize through the breaker, defeating the purpose. By releasing the lock, multiple calls can execute concurrently while state updates remain atomic.

items.label: Closed
items.description: Normal operation. Requests pass through. Track failures. Trip to Open when threshold exceeded.

items.label: Open
items.description: Failing fast. All requests rejected immediately. Wait for timeout before testing.

items.label: Half-Open
items.description: Testing recovery. Allow limited requests. Success -> Closed. Failure -> Open.

content.text: Testing State Transitions

Circuit breaker tests focus on verifying state transitions. We need to test three transitions: CLOSED to OPEN when failures exceed threshold, OPEN to HALF-OPEN after timeout expires, and HALF-OPEN to either CLOSED (on success) or OPEN (on failure). Using short timeouts (50-100ms) keeps tests fast while still exercising real timing behavior.

content.output:
$ go test -v circuit_breaker_test.go circuit_breaker.go
=== RUN   TestCircuitBreaker_TripsAfterFailures
  [test] State: CLOSED -> OPEN (tripped)
--- PASS: TestCircuitBreaker_TripsAfterFailures (0.00s)
=== RUN   TestCircuitBreaker_Recovery
  [test] State: CLOSED -> OPEN (tripped)
  [test] State: OPEN -> HALF-OPEN (testing)
  [test] State: HALF-OPEN -> CLOSED (recovered)
--- PASS: TestCircuitBreaker_Recovery (0.06s)
=== RUN   TestCircuitBreaker_HalfOpenFailure
  [test] State: CLOSED -> OPEN (tripped)
  [test] State: OPEN -> HALF-OPEN (testing)
  [test] State: HALF-OPEN -> OPEN (tripped)
--- PASS: TestCircuitBreaker_HalfOpenFailure (0.05s)
PASS
ok      command-line-arguments  0.118s

content.text: Each test exercises a specific state transition. TestCircuitBreaker_TripsAfterFailures verifies that N consecutive failures trip the circuit and subsequent calls are blocked. TestCircuitBreaker_Recovery verifies the full recovery path: trip, wait for timeout, succeed in half-open, close. TestCircuitBreaker_HalfOpenFailure verifies that a single failure in half-open sends us back to open, not closed.

Notice how the tests use short timeouts (50ms) to keep tests fast. In a real test suite, you might use dependency injection to provide a mockable clock, avoiding sleep entirely. But for this demonstration, real sleeps work fine and prove the timeout logic actually works.
Production Considerations
Our implementation covers the core pattern, but real systems need additional features. Here are the most important considerations and common pitfalls to avoid.

content.title: Sliding Window vs Consecutive Failures
content.message: Our implementation counts consecutive failures, resetting on any success. This means a pattern like fail-success-fail-success-fail never trips the circuit. For some services, you want a sliding window: "5 failures in the last 60 seconds" trips regardless of intermittent successes. Choose based on your failure patterns.

content.title: Thundering Herd in Half-Open
content.message: When the timeout expires, many waiting requests might all try to become the "test" request simultaneously. Our halfOpenCount limits this, but if you have thousands of concurrent requests, even a few test requests can overwhelm a recovering service. Consider allowing exactly one test request and queuing others.

content.text: Real systems also need fallback functions. When the circuit is open, instead of returning an error, you might return cached data, a default value, or call an alternative service. This provides graceful degradation instead of hard failures.

content.title: Additional Features for Real Systems
content.message: Production circuit breakers typically add: metrics (trip count, reject count, state duration), logging on state transitions, different thresholds for different error types (5xx vs timeout), health check endpoints for monitoring, circuit breaker registry for managing multiple breakers, and configuration hot-reload.

content.text: Quick Reference

content.code:
CIRCUIT BREAKER QUICK REFERENCE

States:
  CLOSED    -> Normal, counting failures
  OPEN      -> Blocking all calls, waiting for timeout
  HALF-OPEN -> Testing with limited requests

Transitions:
  CLOSED -> OPEN:      failures >= threshold
  OPEN -> HALF-OPEN:   timeout expired
  HALF-OPEN -> CLOSED: enough test successes
  HALF-OPEN -> OPEN:   any test failure

Key Methods:
  Execute(fn)    Wrap a call with circuit breaker logic
  State()        Get current state for monitoring

Configuration:
  maxFailures    Failures before tripping (3-10 typical)
  timeout        How long to stay open (10-60s typical)
  halfOpenMax    Test requests before closing (1-5 typical)

Thread Safety:
  - Mutex protects all state fields
  - Release lock before calling wrapped function
  - Re-acquire lock to update state after call

Common Libraries:
  - sony/gobreaker: Popular, well-tested
  - afex/hystrix-go: Netflix Hystrix port
  - rubyist/circuitbreaker: Simple, lightweight

content.text: Clean Architecture organizes code into layers with clear dependencies. The core business logic (domain) has no dependencies on external concerns like databases, web frameworks, or UI. This makes the system testable, maintainable, and flexible to change.
The Dependency Rule

Dependencies point inward. Outer layers depend on inner layers, never the reverse. The innermost layer (Domain) knows nothing about databases, HTTP, or any external technology. This inverts the typical dependency direction where business logic depends on infrastructure.

content.code:
Clean Architecture Layers (outside-in):

+----------------------------------------------------------+
|                   Frameworks & Drivers                   |
| HTTP handlers, CLI, gRPC servers, database drivers, UI   |
| +------------------------------------------------------+ |
| |                  Interface Adapters                  | |
| |  Controllers, Presenters, Gateways, Repositories     | |
| | +--------------------------------------------------+ | |
| | |             Application (Use Cases)              | | |
| | |   Orchestrates domain logic, defines app flow    | | |
| | | +----------------------------------------------+ | | |
| | | |                   Domain                     | | | |
| | | |  Entities, Value Objects, Domain Logic       | | | |
| | | |       (NO external dependencies)             | | | |
| | | +----------------------------------------------+ | | |
| | +--------------------------------------------------+ | |
| +------------------------------------------------------+ |
+----------------------------------------------------------+

Dependency Direction: ALWAYS inward
  - Frameworks depend on Interface Adapters
  - Interface Adapters depend on Use Cases
  - Use Cases depend on Domain
  - Domain depends on NOTHING external

content.text: Domain Layer

The domain contains business entities and rules that exist independent of any application. These are the concepts your business cares about, expressed in code. Domain entities have no idea they'll be stored in a database or displayed in a web page.

content.output:
$ go run domain.go
Account: Alice
Balance: 100.00 USD
After $30 withdrawal: 70.00 USD
Withdraw $100 failed: insufficient funds
Deposit to inactive: account is inactive

content.text: The domain code has no imports from external packages (except standard library). Business rules (can't withdraw more than balance, can't transact on inactive accounts) are in the entity methods. This domain works the same whether it's used by a web app, CLI, or test.
Application Layer (Use Cases)

Use cases orchestrate domain entities to accomplish application-specific goals. They define repository interfaces (ports) that adapters will implement. Use cases know the flow but not the infrastructure details.

content.output:
$ go run usecase.go
Before transfer:
  Alice: 100.00 USD
  Bob: 50.00 USD

After $30 transfer:
  Alice: 70.00 USD
  Bob: 80.00 USD

content.text: TransferUseCase defines AccountRepository interface (what it needs), not how it's implemented. InMemoryAccountRepo is an adapter that implements the interface. The use case doesn't know if it's talking to an in-memory map, PostgreSQL, or a mock. This is Dependency Inversion in action.
Project Structure

content.code:
Typical Go Clean Architecture Layout:

myapp/
├── cmd/
│   └── server/
│       └── main.go          # Wires everything together
│
├── internal/
│   ├── domain/              # Innermost: entities, value objects
│   │   ├── account.go       # Account entity
│   │   ├── money.go         # Money value object
│   │   └── errors.go        # Domain errors
│   │
│   ├── usecase/             # Application layer: use cases
│   │   ├── transfer.go      # TransferUseCase
│   │   ├── create_account.go
│   │   └── ports.go         # Repository interfaces (ports)
│   │
│   ├── adapter/             # Interface adapters
│   │   ├── repository/      # Database implementations
│   │   │   ├── postgres/
│   │   │   │   └── account.go  # PostgresAccountRepo
│   │   │   └── memory/
│   │   │       └── account.go  # InMemoryAccountRepo
│   │   │
│   │   └── handler/         # HTTP/gRPC handlers
│   │       └── http/
│   │           └── account.go  # HTTP handlers
│   │
│   └── config/              # Configuration
│       └── config.go
│
└── pkg/                     # Public packages (optional)
    └── money/               # Reusable money type

Key insight: domain/ and usecase/ have NO imports from adapter/.
Adapters depend inward, never the reverse.

items.label: Domain
items.description: Entities, value objects, domain services. No external dependencies. Business rules that exist independent of application.

items.label: Use Cases
items.description: Application-specific logic. Orchestrates domain. Defines repository interfaces (ports). Knows WHAT to do, not HOW.

items.label: Adapters
items.description: Implements interfaces defined by use cases. Connects to external systems (DB, HTTP, etc). Can be swapped without changing core.

content.text: Interface Adapters: HTTP Handlers

Interface adapters translate between the use case layer and external systems. HTTP handlers receive requests, convert them to use case inputs, invoke the use case, and format the response. They know about HTTP but not about database implementations.

content.output:
$ go run http_adapter.go
Before: Account 1: 10000 cents, Account 2: 5000 cents

Handler registered at POST /transfer
Handler type: *main.TransferHandler
After: Account 1: 7000 cents, Account 2: 8000 cents

content.text: The handler translates between HTTP and use case: it parses JSON into a DTO, converts DTO to domain objects, calls the use case, and maps domain errors to HTTP status codes. The handler knows nothing about how accounts are stored.
Dependency Injection: Wiring in main.go

The entry point (main.go) is where you wire everything together. It creates concrete implementations (adapters) and injects them into use cases and handlers. This is the only place that knows about all layers.

content.output:
$ go run main_wiring.go
Wired: Handler -> UseCase -> Adapters
Handler: *main.TransferHandler
UseCase: *main.TransferUseCase
Repo: *main.PostgresAccountRepo
Logger: main.ConsoleLogger

--- Executing transfer ---
[LOG] transfer 5000 USD from acc-1 to acc-2
[PostgreSQL] SELECT * FROM accounts WHERE id = 'acc-1'
[PostgreSQL] SELECT * FROM accounts WHERE id = 'acc-2'
[PostgreSQL] UPDATE accounts SET balance = 5000 WHERE id = 'acc-1'
[PostgreSQL] UPDATE accounts SET balance = 15000 WHERE id = 'acc-2'

content.text: Main.go is the composition root: it creates concrete types and wires them together. Use cases receive interfaces, not concrete types, so you can swap PostgresAccountRepo for InMemoryAccountRepo in tests without changing any use case code.
Hexagonal Architecture (Ports and Adapters)

Clean Architecture and Hexagonal Architecture (Ports and Adapters) share the same goal: isolate business logic from external concerns. The terminology differs: hexagonal uses 'ports' (interfaces) and 'adapters' (implementations). Ports are inbound (driving) or outbound (driven). In Go, the practical implementation is identical.

content.code:
Hexagonal Architecture (Ports and Adapters) to Clean Architecture Mapping

+---------------------------------------------------------------+
|                     DRIVING SIDE (input)                      |
|  Inbound Adapters: HTTP handlers, CLI, gRPC servers, tests    |
|  Inbound Ports: Use case interfaces (what the app can do)     |
|                              |                                |
|                              v                                |
|  +---------------------------------------------------------+  |
|  |                    APPLICATION CORE                     |  |
|  |   Domain: Entities, Value Objects, Business Rules       |  |
|  |   Use Cases: Application-specific orchestration         |  |
|  +---------------------------------------------------------+  |
|                              |                                |
|                              v                                |
|  Outbound Ports: Repository interfaces, external service APIs |
|  Outbound Adapters: PostgreSQL repo, S3 client, email sender  |
|                     DRIVEN SIDE (output)                      |
+---------------------------------------------------------------+

Key insight:
  - Ports = interfaces (defined by the core)
  - Adapters = implementations (connect to external world)
  - Go's implicit interfaces make ports lightweight

In Go, keep interfaces close to where they're used:
  - Outbound ports: defined in usecase/ package
  - Inbound ports: often just the use case struct's public methods

content.title: When to Use Clean Architecture
content.message: Clean Architecture adds complexity. Use it when: the domain has complex business rules, you need to test business logic without infrastructure, you expect requirements to change, multiple interfaces (web, CLI, gRPC) use the same core. For simple CRUD apps, it may be overkill.

content.text: Testing Clean Architecture

Each layer can be tested independently. Domain entities are tested with pure unit tests (no mocks needed). Use cases are tested by injecting fake repositories. Handlers are tested by injecting stubbed use cases. This separation makes tests fast, focused, and reliable.

items.label: Domain Tests
items.description: Pure unit tests. Test entity methods and value objects with real inputs/outputs. No mocks, no dependencies.

items.label: Use Case Tests
items.description: Inject fake/in-memory repositories. Test business flow orchestration. Verify correct calls and state changes.

items.label: Adapter Tests
items.description: Integration tests for real adapters (PostgreSQL, HTTP). Use testcontainers or test servers.

items.label: Handler Tests
items.description: Inject stubbed use cases. Test HTTP request/response mapping and error code translation.

questions.question: In Clean Architecture, which layer defines repository interfaces (ports)?
options: Domain layer
Use Case / Application layer
Interface Adapters layer
Frameworks & Drivers layer
questions.explanation: Repository interfaces are defined by the Use Case layer because use cases need to specify what data operations they require. The adapters layer implements these interfaces with concrete database code. This follows the Dependency Inversion Principle: inner layers define interfaces, outer layers implement them.

questions.question: According to the Dependency Rule, which statement is TRUE?
options: Domain layer imports from the Use Case layer
Use Case layer imports from the HTTP handler package
HTTP handlers import from the Use Case layer
Database adapters import from the Domain layer only
questions.explanation: Dependencies point inward. Outer layers (HTTP handlers) can import inner layers (Use Cases), but never the reverse. Domain is innermost and has no external imports. Use cases don't know about HTTP handlers. Database adapters import from use cases (to implement their interfaces) and domain (to work with entities).

questions.question: Where should you create concrete implementations and wire them together?
options: In the domain layer
In each use case constructor
In main.go (composition root)
In the HTTP handler package
questions.explanation: Main.go is the composition root, the only place that knows about all concrete types. It creates adapters (PostgresRepo, ConsoleLogger), injects them into use cases, and injects use cases into handlers. This keeps other layers decoupled from concrete implementations.

questions.question: What is the relationship between Clean Architecture and Hexagonal Architecture?
options: They are completely different patterns
Hexagonal is a simplified version of Clean Architecture
They share the same goals with different terminology (ports = interfaces, adapters = implementations)
Clean Architecture is only for web apps, Hexagonal is for microservices
questions.explanation: Both architectures aim to isolate business logic from external concerns using dependency inversion. Hexagonal uses 'ports' (interfaces) and 'adapters' (implementations), while Clean Architecture uses layers. In Go, the practical implementation is identical: define interfaces in inner layers, implement them in outer layers.

questions.question: An HTTP handler receives a request and needs to call a use case. What should the handler do?
options: Pass the raw http.Request to the use case
Parse the request into a DTO, convert to domain objects, call the use case, map errors to HTTP status codes
Store the request in a database directly
Forward the request to the domain layer
questions.explanation: HTTP handlers are interface adapters. They translate between the HTTP world and the application core. They parse requests into DTOs, convert DTOs to domain objects, invoke use cases with those objects, then translate domain errors to appropriate HTTP status codes. The use case never sees HTTP-specific types.

content.text: Good OOP design enables good testing. When code follows SOLID principles and uses dependency injection, you can test components in isolation by substituting real dependencies with test doubles. Go's interfaces make this natural and framework-free.
Test Doubles: Mocks, Stubs, Fakes

Test doubles replace real dependencies during testing. A stub returns canned responses. A mock verifies interactions. A fake is a working but simplified implementation. In Go, you create these by implementing the same interface as the real dependency.

Stubs are simple: set what to return, use it. Mocks record calls for assertions. Fakes actually work but are simplified (in-memory vs real database). Choose based on what you're testing: stubs for simple tests, mocks for interaction verification, fakes for integration-like tests.
Table-Driven Tests

Go's idiomatic testing style uses table-driven tests. Each test case is a row in a table (slice of structs). This makes it easy to add cases and see all scenarios at once. Combined with test doubles, it's powerful.

content.output:
$ go run table_demo.go
=== Table-Driven Tests ===
PASS success
PASS invalid email: got expected error
PASS user not found: got expected error
PASS save fails: got expected error

content.text: Each test case configures the stub differently. Adding a new scenario is just adding a struct to the slice. The test loop handles setup, execution, and verification uniformly. This is standard Go testing practice.
Testing Design Patterns

Patterns like Strategy and Decorator are inherently testable because they depend on interfaces. You can test each strategy independently, test decorators by mocking the wrapped component, and verify composition works correctly.

content.output:
$ go run pattern_demo.go
=== Testing Strategy Pattern ===
PASS: Pay called with correct total: $60.00
PASS: Real payment: Charged $99.99 to card 1234
PASS: Empty cart totals $0.00

content.text: MockPayment records what was passed to Pay, letting us verify Checkout calculated the total correctly. We can test the service logic independently from real payment processing. The interface boundary makes this natural.

content.title: Testing Tips
content.message: Keep test doubles simple, one test file. Name them clearly (StubX, MockX, FakeX). Test behavior, not implementation. One assertion per test where possible. If testing is hard, the design might need improvement, not more mocking.

items.label: Stub
items.description: Returns canned data. Use when you just need a dependency to return something. Simplest test double.

items.label: Mock
items.description: Records calls for verification. Use when you need to assert HOW something was called (args, frequency).

items.label: Fake
items.description: Working but simplified. Use when you need realistic behavior (in-memory DB, test server).

content.text: Design Smells That Hurt Testability

Some design choices make testing difficult or impossible. Recognizing these patterns helps you write more testable code from the start. The common theme: code that creates its own dependencies instead of receiving them.

content.output:
$ go run design_smells.go
Test 1 PASS: Order rejected at 8am: orders not accepted before 9am
Test 2 PASS: Order placed at 10am
Test 3 PASS: Payment failure handled: payment failed: card declined

content.title: Common Testability Killers
content.message: Global variables and singletons (can't reset between tests). Hard-coded file paths or URLs. Direct use of time.Now() or rand (non-deterministic). Creating dependencies inside methods instead of injecting them. Concrete types instead of interfaces at boundaries.

content.text: Writing Real Go Tests

The examples above use main() for demonstration. In real code, you write tests using Go's testing package with t.Run for subtests. This integrates with go test and gives you proper test output, coverage, and parallel execution.

content.output:
$ go run testing_example.go
Running tests (simulated go test output):

    --- PASS: TestEmailService_SendWelcome/valid_email_sends_successfully
    --- PASS: TestEmailService_SendWelcome/invalid_email_rejected_before_sending
    --- PASS: TestEmailService_SendWelcome/sender_failure_propagates_error

PASS: 3/3 tests passed

content.text: The test function follows Go conventions: TestXxx naming, table-driven structure, t.Run for subtests. Each subtest gets its own mock instance, so tests are isolated. The Arrange-Act-Assert pattern makes test logic clear.

Good OOP design and good testability go together. If you can't easily substitute a dependency in tests, that's a design smell. Interfaces at boundaries, dependency injection, and small focused types make testing natural. In Go, you rarely need mocking frameworks, just simple structs implementing interfaces.

questions.question: What is the main difference between a stub and a mock?
options: Stubs are faster than mocks
Stubs return canned data; mocks record calls for verification
Mocks are only used for database testing
Stubs require a testing framework; mocks don't
questions.explanation: A stub returns pre-configured responses (canned data) and is used when you just need a dependency to return something. A mock records how it was called (arguments, frequency) so you can verify interactions. Both are test doubles that implement the same interface as the real dependency.

questions.question: Which design choice makes code HARDEST to test?
options: Accepting interfaces as constructor parameters
Creating database connections inside methods
Using small, focused interfaces
Separating business logic from infrastructure
questions.explanation: Creating dependencies (like database connections) inside methods means tests can't substitute them with test doubles. This forces tests to use real databases, making them slow, flaky, and hard to set up. Accepting dependencies through constructors (dependency injection) allows tests to inject mocks or fakes.

questions.question: In Go, how do you typically create a mock for testing?
options: Use a mocking framework like Mockito
Define a struct that implements the same interface
Use reflection to generate mocks at runtime
Mock functions using build tags
questions.explanation: In Go, you create a mock by defining a simple struct that implements the same interface as the real dependency. Thanks to Go's implicit interface satisfaction, the mock just needs to have methods with matching signatures. No framework is needed, just a struct with fields to record calls and configure return values.

questions.question: What is table-driven testing in Go?
options: Testing database tables
Using a slice of test cases where each case is a struct
Testing with CSV files as input
Running tests in parallel across multiple tables
questions.explanation: Table-driven testing is Go's idiomatic testing style where you define test cases as a slice of structs. Each struct contains the inputs, expected outputs, and test name. A single loop runs all cases using t.Run for subtests. This makes it easy to add cases and see all scenarios at once.

questions.question: Why would you inject a Clock interface instead of using time.Now() directly?
options: time.Now() is deprecated in Go
Clock interface is faster than time.Now()
Tests can control time by providing a mock clock with fixed time
Clock interface uses less memory
questions.explanation: Injecting a Clock interface allows tests to control time. With a mock clock returning a fixed time, you can test time-dependent logic deterministically. For example, testing 'orders not accepted before 9am' by setting the mock clock to 8am. Direct use of time.Now() makes such tests impossible or flaky.

content.text: Sorting is one of the most common operations in programming. Go's sort package makes it easy to sort slices of any type. You'll use sorting constantly: to prepare data for binary search, to group similar items together, or as a first step in many algorithms.
Why Sorting Matters
Many problems become much easier once data is sorted. For example, finding duplicates, searching efficiently, or solving two-sum problems. Sorting is often the first step in an optimal solution.

items.label: Unsorted search
items.description: O(n) - must check every element

items.label: Sorted + binary search
items.description: O(log n) - eliminate half each step

items.label: Finding duplicates unsorted
items.description: O(n^2) or O(n) with extra space

items.label: Finding duplicates sorted
items.description: O(n) - duplicates are adjacent

content.text: Built-in Sorting Functions
Go provides convenience functions for sorting slices of common types. These sort in-place (modify the original slice) and sort in ascending order by default.
Check if Already Sorted
Sometimes you need to verify if data is sorted before processing. Go provides functions to check without modifying the slice.
Reverse (Descending) Sort
To sort in descending order (largest first), wrap your slice type with sort.Reverse. This flips the comparison logic.

content.title: IntSlice vs []int
content.message: sort.IntSlice is a type that implements sort.Interface. You need it for sort.Sort() and sort.Reverse(). For simple ascending sort, just use sort.Ints() directly.

content.text: Custom Sorting with sort.Slice
The real power comes from custom sorting. sort.Slice lets you define exactly how to compare elements. You provide a "less" function that returns true if element i should come before element j.
Sorting 2D Slices (Intervals)
A common pattern is sorting intervals or pairs. You can sort by the first element, second element, or any combination. This is essential for interval merging, scheduling, and meeting room problems.
Sorting Structs
When working with structs, sort.Slice lets you sort by any field. This is useful for sorting objects by priority, timestamp, score, etc.
Stable Sort

A stable sort preserves the relative order of equal elements. Use sort.SliceStable when the original order matters for ties. For example, sorting by age while keeping alphabetical order for people with the same age.
Binary Search with sort.Search

Once data is sorted, you can search in O(log n) time using binary search. Go's sort.Search finds the first index where a condition becomes true. Think of it as finding the "boundary" in a sorted array.
Check if Element Exists
To check if a specific value exists in a sorted slice, find where it should be and verify it's actually there.

content.title: sort.Search Requires Sorted Data
content.message: Binary search only works on sorted slices. The condition function must be monotonic: it returns false for indices 0..k-1 and true for indices k..n-1. If the condition is never true, sort.Search returns len(slice).

content.text: Common Sorting Patterns

items.label: Sort + Two Pointers
items.description: Two Sum, 3Sum, container with most water

items.label: Sort by start
items.description: Merge intervals, insert interval

items.label: Sort by end
items.description: Greedy scheduling, non-overlapping intervals

items.label: Sort + Binary Search
items.description: Find target, count occurrences, search insert position

items.label: Custom comparator
items.description: Largest number, sort by frequency

content.time: O(n log n) for sorting, O(log n) for binary search
content.explanation: Go uses pdqsort (pattern-defeating quicksort), a hybrid algorithm that's O(n log n) worst case. Binary search halves the search space each step, giving O(log n).

content.text: Two pointers is a technique where you use two index variables to traverse a data structure. Instead of using nested loops (O(n^2)), two pointers often let you solve problems in a single pass (O(n)). It's one of the most common patterns in coding interviews.
When to Use Two Pointers

Two pointers work well when you need to find pairs, compare elements from different positions, or partition/rearrange arrays. The key insight is that moving pointers strategically eliminates possibilities without checking every combination.

items.label: Opposite Direction
items.description: Start at both ends, move toward middle (sorted arrays, palindromes)

items.label: Same Direction
items.description: Both start at beginning, fast/slow pattern (remove duplicates, partition)

items.label: Fixed Gap
items.description: Maintain fixed distance between pointers (sliding window variant)

content.text: Pattern 1: Opposite Direction (Converging Pointers)

Start with one pointer at the beginning and one at the end. Move them toward each other based on some condition. This works great for sorted arrays because you can decide which pointer to move based on whether the current sum/comparison is too small or too large.
Example: Two Sum in Sorted Array

Given a sorted array, find two numbers that add up to a target. The brute force approach checks all pairs in O(n^2). With two pointers, we can do it in O(n): if the sum is too small, move the left pointer right (to get a larger number); if too large, move the right pointer left.
Example: Valid Palindrome
Check if a string reads the same forwards and backwards. Compare characters from both ends moving inward. If any pair doesn't match, it's not a palindrome.
Example: Container With Most Water

Given heights of vertical lines, find two lines that form a container holding the most water. The area is limited by the shorter line. Start with the widest container (both ends), then try to find taller lines by moving the shorter pointer inward.

content.title: Why Move the Shorter Line?
content.message: Moving the taller line can only decrease or maintain the height (still limited by shorter line) while decreasing width. Moving the shorter line might find a taller line, potentially increasing the area despite smaller width.

content.text: Pattern 2: Same Direction (Fast/Slow Pointers)

Both pointers start at the beginning. The 'fast' pointer scans through all elements, while the 'slow' pointer marks where to write or tracks a boundary. This is perfect for in-place array modifications.
Example: Remove Duplicates from Sorted Array
Given a sorted array, remove duplicates in-place and return the new length. The slow pointer tracks where the next unique element should go. The fast pointer scans for unique elements.
Example: Move Zeroes to End
Move all zeroes to the end while maintaining the relative order of non-zero elements. The slow pointer marks where the next non-zero should go. Swap non-zeroes to the front.
Example: Remove Element
Remove all occurrences of a value in-place. Similar to move zeroes, but we're removing a specific value.
Pattern 3: Three Pointers (3Sum)

For problems involving three elements (like 3Sum), fix one element with a regular loop and use two pointers on the remaining array. This reduces O(n^3) brute force to O(n^2). The array must be sorted first.

content.title: Handling Duplicates in 3Sum
content.message: The tricky part of 3Sum is avoiding duplicate triplets. After finding a valid triplet, skip over duplicate values for both left and right pointers. Also skip duplicates for the outer loop variable i.

content.text: Common Two Pointer Problems

items.label: Two Sum (sorted)
items.description: Opposite direction, O(n)

items.label: Valid Palindrome
items.description: Opposite direction, compare from ends

items.label: Container With Most Water
items.description: Opposite direction, maximize area

items.label: Remove Duplicates
items.description: Same direction, in-place modification

items.label: Move Zeroes
items.description: Same direction, partition array

items.label: 3Sum / 4Sum
items.description: Fix element(s) + two pointers

items.label: Merge Sorted Arrays
items.description: Same direction on two arrays

items.label: Linked List Cycle
items.description: Fast/slow pointers (different speeds)

content.title: Two Pointer Template
content.message: For opposite direction: left, right := 0, len(arr)-1; for left < right { ... }. For same direction: slow := 0; for fast := 0; fast < len(arr); fast++ { if condition { slow++ } }.

content.time: O(n) for two pointers, O(n^2) for 3Sum
content.explanation: Two pointers traverse the array once (or converge from ends). Each pointer moves at most n times, so total is O(n). 3Sum has an outer loop O(n) times two pointers O(n), giving O(n^2).

content.text: Sliding window is a technique for processing contiguous sequences (subarrays or substrings) efficiently. Instead of recalculating everything from scratch for each position, you 'slide' a window across the data, updating only what changes. This reduces many O(n^2) or O(n*k) problems to O(n).
What is a Sliding Window?

Imagine looking through a window at a row of houses. You can only see a few houses at a time. As you walk down the street, the window 'slides': a new house enters your view on one side, and another leaves on the other side. You never go back to recount houses you've already passed.

items.label: Fixed Window
items.description: Window size stays constant (e.g., max sum of k consecutive elements)

items.label: Variable Window
items.description: Window grows/shrinks based on conditions (e.g., smallest subarray with sum >= target)

items.label: With HashMap
items.description: Track character frequencies inside window (e.g., longest substring without repeats)

content.text: Pattern 1: Fixed Size Window
When the window size k is fixed, initialize with the first k elements, then slide by adding the new element and removing the oldest. This avoids recalculating the entire window each time.
Example: Maximum Sum of Subarray of Size K

Find the maximum sum among all contiguous subarrays of exactly size k. Brute force would sum k elements for each starting position: O(n*k). With sliding window, we maintain a running sum and update it in O(1) for each slide.

content.title: Fixed Window Template
content.message: Initialize: sum first k elements. Slide: for i := k; i < n; i++ { add nums[i], remove nums[i-k], update result }. The window always contains elements from i-k+1 to i.

content.text: Pattern 2: Variable Size Window (Shrinkable)

When finding the smallest or largest window satisfying a condition, use two pointers: 'right' expands the window, 'left' shrinks it. Expand until the condition is met, then shrink while still valid to find the minimum.
Example: Minimum Size Subarray Sum
Find the smallest contiguous subarray with sum >= target. Expand the window until sum reaches target, then shrink from the left to find the minimum length while still valid.
Pattern 3: Sliding Window with HashMap
For substring problems involving character frequencies or uniqueness, combine sliding window with a hashmap. The map tracks what's inside the current window, making it easy to check validity.
Example: Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters
Find the length of the longest substring with all unique characters. Use a map to track the last position of each character. When you see a repeat, jump the left pointer past the previous occurrence.

content.title: Check if Character is in Current Window
content.message: When checking for repeats, verify the previous occurrence is within the current window (idx >= left). Characters outside the window don't cause conflicts.

content.text: Example: Minimum Window Substring (Hard)

Find the smallest substring of s that contains all characters of t (including duplicates). This combines variable window with character frequency counting. Expand until all characters are covered, then shrink to minimize.
When to Use Sliding Window

Look for keywords like 'contiguous', 'substring', 'subarray', 'consecutive', 'window of size k', 'minimum/maximum length'. If the problem asks about contiguous elements with some constraint, sliding window is likely the approach.

items.label: Fixed window
items.description: Max/min/average of every k elements, string anagrams

items.label: Shrinkable (find min)
items.description: Smallest subarray with sum >= k, minimum window substring

items.label: Expandable (find max)
items.description: Longest substring with at most k distinct chars, max consecutive ones

items.label: With frequency map
items.description: Anagram search, permutation in string, all unique characters

content.title: Variable Window Template
content.message: for right := 0; right < n; right++ { add nums[right] to window; for window is invalid OR (for min problems) window is valid { remove nums[left]; left++ } update result }. For max length: update result after inner loop. For min length: update result inside inner loop.

content.time: O(n) - each element enters and leaves window at most once
content.space: O(1) for fixed window, O(k) for hashmap where k is character set size
content.explanation: The right pointer visits each element once. The left pointer also moves at most n times total (never backwards). So total operations are O(2n) = O(n), not O(n^2).

content.text: Backtracking is a systematic way to explore all possible solutions by building them incrementally. When you hit a dead end (a choice that can't lead to a valid solution), you 'backtrack' by undoing the last choice and trying a different path. It's like exploring a maze: go forward until you hit a wall, then go back and try another direction.
When to Use Backtracking

Backtracking is ideal when you need to find all solutions (or one solution) that satisfy certain constraints. Common problems include generating combinations, permutations, subsets, solving puzzles, and constraint satisfaction problems.

items.label: Subsets/Combinations
items.description: Choose which elements to include (order doesn't matter)

items.label: Permutations
items.description: Arrange elements in different orders (order matters)

items.label: Constraint Satisfaction
items.description: Find arrangements that satisfy rules (N-Queens, Sudoku)

items.label: Path Finding
items.description: Find all paths in a graph or grid

content.text: The Backtracking Template

Every backtracking solution follows the same pattern: (1) Choose an option, (2) Explore by recursing, (3) Unchoose (undo) to try the next option. In Go, we typically define the recursive function as a closure so it can access the result slice and current state.

content.title: Critical: Always Copy Slices Before Saving
content.message: When saving a solution, use append([]int{}, current...) to make a copy. If you just append current directly, all saved solutions will share the same underlying array and get corrupted as you backtrack. This is the #1 backtracking bug in Go.

content.text: Example 1: Generate All Subsets

Generate all possible subsets (the power set) of a given array. For each element, we have two choices: include it or skip it. Every intermediate state is a valid subset, so we save at every step, not just at leaves.
Example 2: Generate Combinations
Generate all combinations of k elements from n elements. This is like subsets, but we only save when we have exactly k elements. We stop exploring branches that can't possibly reach k elements.

content.title: Pruning Optimization
content.message: Pruning means cutting off branches early when you know they can't lead to valid solutions. In combinations, if you need 3 more elements but only 2 remain, there's no point exploring further. Good pruning can dramatically speed up backtracking.

content.text: Example 3: Generate Permutations

Generate all orderings (permutations) of elements. Unlike subsets where order doesn't matter, permutations care about order: [1,2] and [2,1] are different. We use a 'used' array to track which elements are already in the current permutation.
Subsets vs Permutations: Key Difference

items.label: Subsets
items.description: Use 'start' parameter, loop from start to end. Each element considered once. [1,2] same as [2,1].

items.label: Permutations
items.description: Use 'used' array, loop from 0 every time. Same elements, different orders. [1,2] different from [2,1].

content.text: Example 4: N-Queens (Constraint Satisfaction)

Place N queens on an N×N chessboard so no two queens attack each other (same row, column, or diagonal). This is a classic constraint satisfaction problem. We place one queen per row and backtrack when we can't place a queen safely.

content.title: Diagonal Trick
content.message: For \ diagonals, all cells have the same (row - col) value. For / diagonals, all cells have the same (row + col) value. Store these in maps to check diagonal attacks in O(1).

content.text: Common Backtracking Problems

items.label: Subsets / Power Set
items.description: Generate all 2^n subsets

items.label: Combinations
items.description: Choose k from n elements

items.label: Permutations
items.description: All orderings of n elements

items.label: Combination Sum
items.description: Find combinations that sum to target

items.label: Palindrome Partitioning
items.description: Split string into palindromes

items.label: N-Queens / Sudoku
items.description: Place items satisfying constraints

items.label: Word Search
items.description: Find word path in grid

items.label: Generate Parentheses
items.description: All valid combinations of n pairs

content.time: O(2^n) for subsets, O(n!) for permutations, varies with pruning
content.space: O(n) for recursion stack + O(result size) for storing solutions
content.explanation: Backtracking explores exponential or factorial solution spaces. The time complexity is often unavoidable because you need to generate all solutions. However, good pruning can eliminate large portions of the search tree and dramatically improve average case performance.

content.text: Dynamic Programming (DP) is a technique for solving problems by breaking them into smaller overlapping subproblems and storing the results to avoid redundant computation. Instead of solving the same subproblem multiple times, you solve it once and remember the answer. This transforms exponential-time solutions into polynomial time.
When to Use Dynamic Programming

DP is applicable when a problem has two properties: (1) Optimal substructure, meaning the optimal solution can be built from optimal solutions to subproblems, and (2) Overlapping subproblems, meaning the same subproblems are solved multiple times. Common signals include 'minimum/maximum', 'count ways', 'is it possible', and recursive solutions with repeated work.

items.label: Memoization (Top-Down)
items.description: Start with the main problem, recurse into subproblems, cache results

items.label: Tabulation (Bottom-Up)
items.description: Start with smallest subproblems, build up to the answer iteratively

content.text: The Problem with Plain Recursion

Consider the Fibonacci sequence: fib(n) = fib(n-1) + fib(n-2). A naive recursive solution recalculates the same values exponentially many times. fib(5) calls fib(3) twice, fib(2) three times, and so on. For fib(40), this takes billions of operations.
Approach 1: Memoization (Top-Down DP)

Memoization adds caching to recursion. Before computing a subproblem, check if you've already solved it. If yes, return the cached result. If no, compute it, cache it, then return. This is the easiest way to convert a recursive solution to DP.

content.title: Map vs Slice for Memoization
content.message: Use a map when keys are sparse or non-integer. Use a slice when keys are dense integers 0 to n, as slice access is faster. Initialize slice values to -1 or another invalid value to distinguish 'not computed' from 'computed as 0'.

content.text: Approach 2: Tabulation (Bottom-Up DP)

Tabulation builds the solution iteratively from the smallest subproblems up. Create a table (usually an array), fill in base cases, then fill remaining cells in order so each cell's dependencies are already computed. No recursion needed.
Space Optimization
Often you don't need the entire table, just the most recent values. For Fibonacci, each value only depends on the previous two, so we only need two variables instead of an array of n elements.
Example: Coin Change (Classic 1D DP)

Given coin denominations and a target amount, find the minimum number of coins needed. For each amount, try using each coin and take the minimum. This is unbounded knapsack: you can use each coin unlimited times.
Example: Longest Common Subsequence (2D DP)

Find the length of the longest subsequence present in both strings. A subsequence maintains relative order but doesn't need to be contiguous. Use a 2D table where dp[i][j] represents the LCS of the first i characters of text1 and first j characters of text2.
Space-Optimized 2D DP
When each row only depends on the previous row, you can reduce O(m*n) space to O(n) by keeping only two rows. Alternate between them as you iterate.
The 5-Step DP Strategy
When facing a DP problem, follow these steps systematically:

items.label: 1. Define State
items.description: What does dp[i] or dp[i][j] represent? Be precise.

items.label: 2. Find Recurrence
items.description: How does current state relate to previous states?

items.label: 3. Base Cases
items.description: What are the smallest subproblems with known answers?

items.label: 4. Iteration Order
items.description: Fill table so dependencies are computed first.

items.label: 5. Space Optimization
items.description: Can you reduce to O(n) or O(1) space?

content.text: Common DP Patterns

items.label: Linear DP
